papers.title: "If we don't act now, someone will die": Temporal riskwork in action
papers.authors: Agnieszka Latuszynska, Eivor Oborn, Trish Reay
papers.abstract: In this ethnographic study, we develop the concept of temporal riskwork -- actions taken to alter the temporal dynamics of risk -- by examining how riskworkers navigated situations of multiple dynamically evolving risks under severe time constraints. In such contexts, decisions about how and when to act are critically interdependent and made with attention to assessing urgencies, priorities and volatility of risk. Our study revealed how risk can present both synchronic and diachronic competing temporal demands, requiring temporally complex riskwork. We studied a mental health crisis team where actors collectively responded to clients’ urgent, often accelerating risks in high-stakes, time-pressured environments. We contribute to the literature by developing a model of temporal riskwork that explains how actors can collectively manage a set of ongoing risks by engaging in two connected temporal processes: decelerating synchronic risk momenta and redirecting diachronic risk trajectories. More generally, our model explains how riskworkers can collectively manage the temporal complexity of multiple concurrent risks, integrating their assessments and actions in complex, dynamic contexts.

papers.title: International Power
papers.authors: Ernest Liu, David Y Yang
papers.abstract: An interconnected world increases economic efficiency while giving certain countries leverage over others. We aim to describe and understand international power stemming from trade. Using an illustrative model of trade with possibilities of bilateral disputes and ex-post hold-ups, we highlight that bilateral asymmetry in import dependence can be a source of power towards one another. We construct the model-implied measure of international power — asymmetric bilateral import dependence, weighted inversely by sectoral trade elasticities — across country pairs over the past 20 years. Combining this measure with comprehensive data on bilateral engagement events and a high-frequency measure of bilateral geopolitical relationships, we examine the consequences and strategic causes of international power. We present two main empirical results. First, increases in international power between countries — which raise the credibility of threats of trade disruptions — induce more bilateral engagement and negotiations. Second, evidence suggests that worsened geopolitical relationships — in anticipation of future disputes — prompt countries to build up greater international power through adjusting trade activities.

papers.title: Fine Stratification of Survey Experiments
papers.authors: Max Cytrynbaum
papers.abstract: This paper studies a two-stage model of experimentation, where the researcher first samples representative experimental participants from an eligible pool, then assigns each sampled unit to treatment or control, using matched k-tuples randomization at both stages. To implement such designs, we develop a fast algorithm for matching units into k-tuples for any k ≥ 2 and any dimension of covariates. By surveying 200 recent experimental working papers, we estimate that our algorithm newly enables multivariate fine stratification with provable match quality guarantees in about 48% of recent papers. We show that finely stratified sampling and assignment both nonparametrically reduce the variance of treatment effect estimation, with the gains from stratified sampling increasing in the size of the eligible pool and how well covariates predict treatment effect heterogeneity. We develop new inference methods that fully exploit the efficiency gains from both design stages, allowing researchers to report smaller standard errors if they designed a representative experiment. An application to nine published experiments quantifies the efficiency gains.

papers.title: The Labor Demand and Labor Supply Channels of Monetary Policy
papers.authors: Sebastian Graves, Christopher Huckfeldt, Eric T. Swanson
papers.abstract: Monetary policy is typically understood to affect employment through labor demand, with the role of labor supply receiving less consideration. We estimate the response of labor market flows to high-frequency changes in interest rates around FOMC announcements and Fed Chair speeches, and find that a contractionary monetary policy shock leads to a significant increase in labor supply: workers reduce the rate at which they quit jobs to nonemployment, and non-employed individuals increase their job-seeking behavior. These effects are quantitatively important: holding supply-driven labor market flows constant, the decline in employment from a contractionary monetary policy shock would be twice as large. To interpret our findings, we estimate a heterogeneous agent model with frictional labor markets and an active extensive margin of labor supply. The model rationalizes existing estimates of modest labor supply responses to idiosyncratic transfers with our new evidence of a large labor supply response to an aggregate shock.

papers.title: Online Job Selection: Reward Rate vs. Remaining Value
papers.authors: Mohammad Reza Aminian, Will Ma, Linwei Xin
papers.abstract: High-throughput systems, such as cloud spot markets, adaptive large language model inference, and order consolidation in logistics, operate under capacity constraints. In these settings, decision makers must allocate fixed resources among a stream of requests with heterogeneous reward rates and service durations. A critical tension arises when capacity is saturated; the system must decide whether to continue serving an active job to harvest its remaining value or to preempt it in favor of a new arrival. This trade-off is especially subtle when a new job offers a lower immediate reward rate but a longer service duration, potentially outweighing a high-rate job near completion. To address this challenge, we introduce a general and parsimonious online allocation framework for capacity-constrained resources, where preemption is nonresumable and yields partial rewards. This abstraction captures the essential dynamics of modern resource management problems, including but not limited to those discussed earlier. We derive intuitive index-based policies and provide constant-factor competitive-ratio guarantees for their performance without requiring any forecasts of future demand. In particular, we show that two naive index-based policies have competitive ratios of 1/2 and [Formula: see text]. Our main methodological contribution is to develop a flexible framework for defining “quasiutilities” that couples the states of an online algorithm versus an offline algorithm, which reduces the design of online index-based policies to an offline geometrical problem. The framework allows us to optimize the index function, leading to an exponential-index-based policy that has an improved competitive ratio of 0.68. papers.title: When GenAI Increases Inequality: Evidence from a University Debating Competition
papers.authors: Antonio Roldán-Monés
papers.abstract: Research on Generative AI (GenAI) and work reports both productivity-compressing and inequality-expanding effects, leaving open a central question for organizations: Who benefits from GenAI and on which specific tasks? I address this question through a randomized controlled trial in competitive university debating, where participants are randomly assigned access to GenAI. Although most previous experimental work examines the impact of GenAI on written activities and across individuals, this setting allows me to study the impact of GenAI on a knowledge-intensive spoken activity and to identify heterogeneous effects across subtasks. I find that GenAI expands performance inequality in this setting. Consistent with recent theories on GenAI and work, results show that high-ability participants experience significantly larger gains from GenAI usage than their lower-ability counterparts in judgment-intensive subtasks, whereas lower-ability individuals only improve their performance in less expert components of debating, where GenAI can be used as a substitute. If these inequality-expanding effects generalize to similar spoken settings where complex ideas must be internalized and explained, rather than simply written, they would have important implications for understanding the impact of GenAI on work and inequality. This paper was accepted by Maria Guadalupe, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01063 .

papers.title: Scalable Just-in-Time Price Elasticity Estimation
papers.authors: Jingbo Wang, Yufeng Huang
papers.abstract: This paper presents a scalable, nonparametric approach to estimating point-wise price elasticities designed for real-time pricing decisions. A key challenge in these settings is correcting for price endogeneity while remaining computationally efficient. We address this by leveraging nonparametric control functions to decompose the identification of causal elasticities into a sequence of scalable intermediate prediction tasks. We implement this framework with bootstrap averaged (bagged) nearest neighbors, which admits a closed-form representation that enables scalable, real-time implementation. We establish uniform consistency of our estimator and show in Monte Carlo simulations that it robustly recovers local elasticities across a diverse range of data-generating processes. We demonstrate the method’s practical usefulness by applying it to the New York City ride-sharing market, recovering substantial spatial-temporal heterogeneity in price elasticity and updating citywide elasticity estimates in less than one minute, which provide a “just-in-time” input for algorithmic pricing systems. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Funding: J. Wang acknowledges financial support from the Research Grants Council of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region, China [Grant 14508924]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04791 .

papers.title: Machine Learning Vast Dynamic Conditional Covariance Matrices: The Spirit of “Divide and Conquer”
papers.authors: Zhoufan Zhu, Ke Zhu
papers.abstract: Large-scale portfolio selection requires accurate forecasts of high-dimensional dynamic conditional covariance matrices (CCMs). This task is challenging because the number of covariance elements grows quickly with the number of assets, whereas the available time-series observations are limited and noisy. In this paper, we propose a novel graph-based quantiled (GRAND) CCM estimator in the spirit of “divide and conquer.” By extracting information from the extensive asset features, the GRAND method leverages a new graph-based deep learning network, called the self-grouping autoencoder (SGA), to learn the conditional quantiles of returns. Using those learned conditional quantiles, the GRAND method further learns (co)variances of CCM element-wisely via the quantiled conditional moment (QCM) method, and finally, it makes the resulting assembled CCM estimator positive semidefinite through a projection. Because of the use of the SGA network and the QCM method in an element-wise way, the GRAND method is blessing dimensionality in learning the CCM of a large-scale portfolio, while keeping the computation manageable and maintaining causal semantics. From an extensive empirical analysis of the Chinese stock market, we show that the GRAND method can produce much better tangency portfolios than its competitors, and provide dynamic causal graphs to study variance and quantile connectedness of all stocks for interpreting systemic risk and forecasting the business cycle. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72503203 and 72573142]; the Natural Science Foundation of Fujian Province [Grants 2025J01036 and 2025J08009]; the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities [Grant 2

papers.title: Action-Oriented Narratives: How Innovation Emerges from Crowd Discussions
papers.authors: Claudio Biscaro, Arvind Malhotra, Ann Majchrzak
papers.abstract: Crowds are increasingly invited to tackle complex innovation problems. However, our understanding of how crowds solve these problems has limited our ability to utilize them effectively. In this article, we examine how a crowd tasked with finding ways to preserve New Zealand’s native flora and fauna achieves solutions to this complex innovation problem through discussion. Our analysis reveals that discussions leading to innovative solutions differ from those leading to non-innovative solutions: innovation-yielding discussions (1) mobilize more Resources than Constraints, (2) converge on a single Goal, and (3) specify few (often one) responsible Subject(s); vis-à-vis discussions leading to non-innovative solutions often surfaced multiple goals—thereby sustaining multiple problem framings—while subjects remained vague, implicit, or multiplied, and constraints frequently outnumbered resources. Moreover, we show how the specific weavings of these discursive elements support the crowd’s navigation of the complex innovation problem. Three discursive maneuvers—subject-goal anchoring, repurposing distant knowledge, and layering resources—are fundamental navigational tools used by the crowd to form what we call “action-oriented narratives”: simple, dynamic, and evolving linguistic structures that enable collective problem exploration, while giving room for localized improvisation. We contribute to the literature on problem solving by showing how specific linguistic activities alter individuals’ capacity to contribute to and solve complex problems. We also contribute to the literature on linguistic structures supporting innovation by showing that the types of discussions that support innovation depend on the openness of the setting. papers.title: Legal Chameleons: Political Ideology, Institutional Histories, and Firms’ Management of Identity Cues
papers.authors: Yong Hyuck Kim, Jose N. Uribe, Maxim Sytch
papers.abstract: This study examines how foreign firms strategically manage the salience of foreignness when facing unfavorable domestic evaluators. Foreign firms do so by altering the ethnic composition of the agents representing them before the evaluators. We examine this question in the context of Asian firms’ selection of legal counsel in U.S. federal courts. Prior research suggests that foreign firms may anticipate less favorable evaluations in courts that have historically favored domestic over foreign firms and in those with conservative judges. We argue that, in such evaluative settings, Asian firms adjust the ethnic composition of their external legal teams to manage the salience of foreignness, and that such adjustments are especially likely in courts that combine judge conservatism with pro-domestic ruling histories. We test these arguments using data on U.S. patent litigation from 2000 to 2016 and validated measures of courts’ political ideology and pro-domestic ruling histories. We find that Asian firms reduce the proportion of Asian-origin lawyers and increase the proportion of White lawyers when litigating in conservative courts, particularly when these courts also have pro-domestic ruling histories. By contrast, the ethnic composition of lawyers representing domestic firms remains stable across courts. Evidence of implicit bias against Asians among legal professionals provides additional support consistent with the theorized mechanism. Post hoc analyses reveal that adjusting the ethnic composition of external legal teams attenuates the likelihood of unfavorable outcomes in conservative courts. These findings contribute to research on liability of foreignness by identifying agent selection as a specific mitigation mechanism in evaluative arenas. Funding: This research was

papers.title: Not Learning from Others
papers.authors: John J. Conlon, Malavika Mani, Gautam Rao, Matthew Ridley, Frank Schilbach
papers.abstract: We study social learning using experiments where two people independently learn relevant information and can share it to make accurate private decisions. Across three experiments, people are substantially less sensitive to information others discover than to equally-relevant information they discovered themselves. This holds when they must learn information from others through discussion; when the experimenter perfectly communicates the information; and even when participants observe others’ information with their own eyes. Our results therefore stem not from a failure to elicit information from others but a systematic tendency to underweight it relative to one’s own information. Our findings illustrate a powerful barrier to social learning that might underlie many documented cases of failure to learn from others.

papers.title: Carbon home bias
papers.authors: Patrick Bolton, Marc Eskildsen, Marcin T. Kacperczyk
papers.abstract: Institutional investors apply stricter carbon screens abroad than at home. Using global equity holdings for roughly 13,400 institutions across 48 countries over 2005–2024, we show that higher firm emissions predict lower foreign institutional ownership with no corresponding reduction at home; the domestic-foreign ownership gap widens with emissions, and domestic ownership rises with Scope 3 emissions. This carbon home bias remains in within-investor and within-firm comparisons and is not explained by the country-pair determinants of ordinary home bias. It operates through both re-entry (foreign high emitters face a higher hurdle to re-enter a portfolio) and exit (a higher hazard of leaving it). This bias intensified after the Paris Agreement and did not unwind during the subsequent anti-ESG reaction. It is concentrated in discretionary rather than index-constrained holdings; at the extensive margin, the incremental bias is largest among pension funds—institutions particularly associated with formal investment-policy restrictions, and better covered by European than by U.S. filings—rather than among managers best placed to exploit an informational advantage. Overall, the evidence is more consistent with institutional constraints and screening policies than with a simple information-advantage explanation.

papers.title: The effect of relative performance information on the performance of task novices
papers.authors: Kaitlin Hudspeth, Ivo D. Tafkov

papers.title: Generative AI And Creative Goods: Market Expansion, Crowd-Out, and Copyright
papers.authors: Samuel G Goldberg, H Tai Lam
papers.abstract: We study how generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) affects creative goods markets using data from a large stock images marketplace. In December 2022, the platform announced it would allow artists to sell GenAI-produced images, subject to two conditions: all GenAI images must be labeled, and GenAI would be prohibited in certain markets. We exploit this policy variation using a difference-in-differences design. We estimate a 136% increase in image production and 47% increase in active artists, accompanied by a 15% decline in non-GenAI production and 29% decline in non-GenAI active artists. On the demand side, total sales increase by 82%, but non-GenAI sales fall by 28% and non-GenAI sales rates decline by 3 percentage points. We use image embeddings to develop novel measures of image quality, characteristics, and market composition.We find that quality (measured as predicted sales probability) increases by 9 percentage points overall and 2 percentage points for non-GenAI content, suggesting low-quality non-GenAI artists exit. Our product characteristic measures indicate that GenAI production is heavily concentrated in characteristic space, potentially limiting the value of these images to the market. Non-GenAI production responds to GenAI by differentiating into niches. We discuss implications for copyright policy and the longer-run sustainability of original creative work.

papers.title: The Economic Dynamics of City Structure: Evidence from Hiroshima’s Recovery
papers.authors: Kohei Takeda, Atsushi Yamagishi
papers.abstract: We provide new theory and evidence on the resilience of internal city structure after a large shock, analyzing the atomic bombing of Hiroshima. Exploiting newly digitized data, we document that the city structure recovered within five years after the bombing. Our new dynamic quantitative model of internal city structure incorporates commuting, forward-looking location choices, migration frictions, agglomeration forces, and heterogeneous location fundamentals. Strong agglomeration forces in our estimated model explain Hiroshima's recovery, and we find an alternative equilibrium where the city center did not recover. These results highlight the role of agglomeration forces, multiple equilibria, and expectations in urban dynamics.

papers.title: Determinants of Norm Compliance: Moral Similarity and Group Identification
papers.authors: Alexander Schneeberger, Erin L. Krupka
papers.abstract: What determines whether someone complies with a social norm? The social identity approach offers a mechanism for norm compliance: A person who feels similar to a group identifies more with that group and, in turn, complies with the group’s norms. Using an experiment, we test whether similarity in values increases identification and adherence to a group rule. To do so, we varied the similarity/dissimilarity between the values of an individual and members of a social group and measured group identification and rule compliance. We find that moral similarity in progressivism increases group identification, and group identification can increase compliance with rules from the social group. However, our results also suggest that this relationship can be disrupted. Because of our design and empirically verified in our study, social norms do not differ between treatments. As a consequence, observed behavior changes are attributable to increased group norm sensitivity and not changes in group norms. We advance the study of social identity by testing a causal pathway between group identification, group norm sensitivity, and behavior change. Our contribution to the management literature is to extend the empirical rationale, and cautionary notes, for investing in value-alignment between individuals and organizations. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Max Planck Institute for Research on Collective Goods and the University of Michigan School of Information for financial support. They also gratefully acknowledge support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft (DFG, German Research Foundation) under Germany’s Excellence Strategy (EXC 2126/2 – 390838866), and from the Center for Social and Econom

papers.title: Widely Used Measures of Overconfidence Are Confounded with Ability
papers.authors: Stephen A. Spiller
papers.abstract: Measures of overconfidence are used both to assess biases in people’s beliefs regarding their own abilities and to identify correlates of those biases. Proposed correlates of overconfidence include narcissism, social status, (low) task anxiety, savings, planning, and many more. Research on these correlates typically explicitly or implicitly claims that the associations with overconfidence are not attributable to ability (i.e., latent inputs enabling successful task performance, including inputs that vary across people, states, or contexts). I argue that several typical approaches used to measure overconfidence are not sufficient to support such claims. This argument follows from two underappreciated properties of these measures of overconfidence. First, performance is an imperfect measure of ability: accounting for performance does not sufficiently account for ability. Second, self-evaluations of performance should reflect ability in addition to performance: because performance is ambiguous, people should incorporate prior beliefs about their ability. These properties imply that multiple commonly used measures of overconfidence are confounded with ability. I support these analytical results by reexamining previously published findings. In the first analysis, I find that overconfidence predicts subsequent performance, consistent with measures of overconfidence serving as a signal of ability. In the second set of analyses, I find that some purported associations between overconfidence and other constructs could be attributed to ability instead. I close with recommendations to recognize and reduce the potential for mistaken inferences. papers.title: Screening, Investment Incentives, and the Welfare Trade-Offs of Privacy
papers.authors: Anastasios Dosis, Casey G. Rothschild
papers.abstract: This paper studies how information disclosure affects investment incentives and contracting efficiency. We analyze a class of principal-agent models in which information helps the principal screen the agent but also facilitates surplus appropriation, thereby weakening the agent’s incentive to invest before contracting. Efficient privacy regimes balance these two forces. Along the frontier of efficient information policies, more privacy is associated with stronger investment incentives and higher agent payoff. We characterize conditions under which full privacy, full disclosure, or intermediate privacy is efficient. The results provide guidance for intellectual property and innovation policy by identifying when additional privacy fosters or hinders economic efficiency and innovation. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01507 .

papers.title: Gatekeepers and Kingmakers: Do Superplatforms Distort Digital Competition?
papers.authors: Umit G. Gurun, Zheng Liu, Steven Chong Xiao
papers.abstract: The rising dominance of superplatforms raises concerns about conflicts of interest and externalities on innovation, because they act as both marketplace gatekeepers and strategic investors. Studying Google’s dual role via Google Ventures (GV) and the Android marketplace, we find Google-backed startups receive 115% more reviews, 12% higher ratings, and 77% fewer bug complaints than their iOS counterparts—despite no major app updates. These gains are consistent with selective review removal and platform promotion. Using a difference-in-differences approach with iOS versions as controls, we isolate treatment from selection effects. Our findings challenge platform neutrality and highlight subtle mechanisms of competitive distortion. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, information systems. Supplemental Material: The Online Appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03354 .

papers.title: Demand for Research and the Composition of Scientific Response: Intellectual Distance, Research Productivity, and Research Outcomes
papers.authors: Jino Lu
papers.abstract: When demand for research in a domain increases, scientific progress depends not only on whether more research is produced, but also on which scientists produce that research. This distinction is especially important in emerging domains, where technological trajectories remain uncertain and progress often requires the generation and integration of heterogeneous scientific knowledge. This study examines how academic scientists respond when demand for research increases in a domain and what research outcomes they produce within that domain. Empirically, I exploit the Zero Emission Vehicle (ZEV) mandate, which led to an unanticipated increase in demand for electric vehicle (EV) research. I find that scientists became more likely to produce EV research after the mandate. However, this response varied systematically across scientists: as intellectual distance from the EV domain increased, more-productive scientists were less responsive than less-productive scientists. Yet among scientists who produced EV research, the research outcomes of scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater novelty, while those of more-productive scientists from more distant domains were associated with greater scientific impact and greater use in downstream EV inventions. These findings suggest that increased demand for research shapes not only the volume of scientific activity in a domain, but also the composition of scientists who produce that research. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2023.17926 .

papers.title: Reconceptualizing Network Change: Robustness and Resilience of Interorganizational Networks
papers.authors: Maxim Sytch, Sukanya Roy, Pavel Ivanov Zhelyazkov
papers.abstract: Existing research on interorganizational network dynamics has largely treated network change as gradual, local, and primarily oriented toward private organizational advantage. Yet contemporary cooperative interorganizational systems are highly interconnected across industrial sectors and geographies and are routinely exposed to shocks that simultaneously disable multiple organizations or relationships among them. These shocks stem from disruptions such as pandemics, natural disasters, wars, sanctions, or cascading partner failures, and they can rapidly reconfigure whole-network architectures and undermine collective outcomes. In light of this new reality, we reconceptualize interorganizational networks as loci of frequent, punctuated change at the whole-network level, with primary implications for collective outcomes. We develop this reconceptualization through a robustness-resilience lens, defining network robustness as an interorganizational network’s capacity to maintain its collective outcomes in the immediate aftermath of a shock, and network resilience as its capacity to recover and potentially surpass preshock collective outcomes over the longer term. We then outline the theoretical and methodological opportunities that this robustness-resilience perspective opens for the study of network change. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2024.19624 .

papers.title: Keep calm and bank on: Bank run risks and the role of public communication
papers.authors: Damiano Sandri, Francesco Grigoli, Yuriy Gorodnichenko, Olivier Coibion

papers.title: Taxing Homeowners Who Can't or Won't Borrow
papers.authors: Francis Wong
papers.abstract: Using high-frequency administrative data covering millions of US homeowners, I document three novel facts about homeowner responses to property tax increases driven by rising home values. First, non-migrating homeowners cut consumption, exhibit financial distress, and do not borrow against their higher home values. Second, heterogeneity analysis shows that consumption responses do not vary by liquidity, consistent with savings target behavior. In contrast, distress responses are concentrated among liquidity-constrained homeowners. Many homeowners report being debt averse and therefore unwilling to borrow in order to avoid illiquidity and distress. Third, tax hikes induce migration—partly by displacing illiquid homeowners—but do not accelerate neighborhood change. A simple welfare framework reveals that the largest costs of property taxes arise from financial distress, suggesting welfare gains from policies that limit taxes for liquidity-constrained households.

papers.title: Limits of Disclosure in Search Markets
papers.authors: Raphael Boleslavsky, Silvana Krasteva
papers.abstract: This paper examines competitive information disclosure in search markets with a mix of selective consumers, who search costlessly, and casual consumers, who incur positive search costs. Selective consumers incentivize truthful disclosure; casual consumers, concealment. With both types, the equilibrium features partial disclosure, which persists despite intense competition. Casual consumers may search actively, but only in small markets. While selective consumers benefit from increased competition, casual consumers may be harmed. Changes in search costs have non-monotone effects: the equilibrium approaches full disclosure as the cost approaches zero or the mean valuation. When costs are high, further increases raise equilibrium informativeness and the welfare of selective consumers, while reducing the welfare of casual consumers.

papers.title: Information Design with Supplemental Investment
papers.authors: Lin Nan, Lin Qiu, Xiaoyan Wen, Ronghuo Zheng
papers.abstract: This paper features a setting with two-dimensional information asymmetry on a firm’s fundamental (good or bad type) and the nature of its supplemental investment (improving upside potential, or mitigating downside risk). We examine the firm’s optimal design of the information system when the system can only address the dimension of fundamental. We show that, with only single-dimensional information asymmetry regarding the firm’s fundamental, greater informativeness on the firm’s fundamental type always improves efficiency. However, with two-dimensional information asymmetry, increasing informativeness about firm fundamental no longer guarantees higher efficiency and can be detrimental. The optimal information system trades off reducing information asymmetry and preserving firms’ incentives to invest, and it could be uninformative or optimistically biased, depending on the level of credit risk, which in our setting is higher when supplemental investment is more likely to improve upside rather than protect downside. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00524 .

papers.title: Optimal Incentive Design for Decentralized Dynamic Matching Markets
papers.authors: Chen Chen, Pengyu Qian, Jingwei Zhang
papers.abstract: In decentralized dynamic matching markets, agents can benefit from sharing resources, but they will collaborate only if properly incentivized. Motivated by applications such as multihospital kidney exchanges and job-hunting markets, this paper proposes novel monetary and nonmonetary mechanisms to incentivize collaboration in such decentralized dynamic markets. We study a model in which multiple self-interested agents manage local multiway dynamic matching problems. Jobs of different types arrive stochastically at each agent, expire after a limited time, and yield rewards when matched. An agent’s job backlog and actions are the agent’s private information, and each agent aims to maximize its long-run average matching reward. We design simple mechanisms that incentivize agents to submit all jobs upon arrival, thereby enabling centralized matching. Our first mechanism, the marginal-value (MV) mechanism, reimburses agents based on the MV of their submitted jobs. This can be implemented in a nonmonetary way by randomly selecting an agent (with a specified probability) to perform a match and collect the associated matching reward. We show that under the MV mechanism, full job submission constitutes an approximate Nash equilibrium—that is, the gain from unilateral deviation vanishes as the number of agents grows. To further eliminate incentives for deviation, we propose a refined mechanism, the MV-plus-credit (MVC) mechanism, and show that, when the number of agents exceeds a constant threshold, full job submission constitutes a stronger oblivious equilibrium. Numerical experiments based on kidney exchange data demonstrate that the gains from deviation under our mechanisms are small even in moderately sized markets. This paper was accepted by Peng Sun, optimization and decisio

papers.title: Learning from a Biased Sample
papers.authors: Roshni Sahoo, Lihua Lei, Stefan Wager
papers.abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that this problem is equivalent to an augmented convex risk minimization problem. We give statistical guarantees for learning a model that is robust to sampling bias via the method of sieves, and propose a deep learning algorithm whose loss function captures our robust learning target. We empirically validate our proposed method in a case study on prediction of mental health scores from health survey data and a case study on intensive care unit length-of-stay prediction. This paper was accepted by Vivek Farias, data science. Funding: This research was supported by NSF grant SES-2242876. RS is furthe

papers.title: Stockouts and the Success of New Products
papers.authors: Diego Aparicio, Duncan I. Simester
papers.abstract: We investigate how stockouts of existing products influence the success of new product introductions. Our findings reveal that stockouts on incumbent items at the time a new product is launched are associated with higher sales of the new product for at least six months. This positive spillover is specific to new products and is most potent at the start of the product life cycle. To establish causality, we use instrumental variables based on historical stockouts and contemporaneous stockouts in other stores. Analysis of individual-level transaction data corroborates a trial-and-adoption mechanism: Stockouts of existing items prompt consumers to trial the new product, leading to increased repeat purchasing. By identifying inventory as a driver of product trial, this research highlights the importance of strategically timing new product launches and documents a previously unrecognized tradeoff for inventory policies. This paper was accepted by David Simchi-Levi, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.02602 .

papers.title: Deep Tangency Portfolio
papers.authors: Guanhao Feng, Liang Jiang, Junye Li, Yizhi Song, Yuanzhi Wang
papers.abstract: We develop a deep learning framework to directly estimate tangency portfolio weights by augmenting benchmark factors with a long-short deep factor derived from high-dimensional characteristics. Guided by a Sharpe ratio maximization objective, the deep factor plays two key roles: (i) providing a natural hedge against benchmark risks and (ii) capturing multimarket signals to enhance the performance of the benchmark. In an empirical application to U.S. corporate bonds using 132 firm-level bond, equity, and option characteristics, the deep factor achieves an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio exceeding one, and the deep tangency portfolio benchmarked against the market factor yields a Sharpe ratio over two, outperforming portfolios spanned by common observable or latent factors. These results demonstrate that bond risk signals are fundamentally dense, requiring the nonlinear integration of multimarket information to span the efficient frontier. This paper was accepted by Agostino Capponi, finance. Funding: G. papers.title: Proximity-Based Delivery Policies: Efficiency, Coverage, and Fairness
papers.authors: Zhongbin Wang, Shiliang Cui, Yongjian Li, Qian Zhang
papers.abstract: The growing demand for rapid food and grocery delivery has prompted many restaurants and retailers to develop their own on-demand delivery services. Although hiring additional couriers can expand delivery capacity, it is often prohibitively costly. As a cost-effective alternative, we propose a proximity-based delivery (PBD) policy that prioritizes the delivery of orders from customers located closer to the vendor, in contrast to the traditional first-come-first-served (FCFS) approach. We show that PBD can substantially reduce average delivery delays without requiring additional couriers; however, it may raise fairness concerns, because distant customers experience longer wait times, potentially shrinking market coverage and exacerbating service disparities. To address this issue, we introduce an incentive-compatible PBD (IP) policy, where nearby customers are incentivized to pay for priority, whereas distant customers receive compensation to offset longer delays. We demonstrate that this mechanism can restore fairness to levels comparable to FCFS while preserving efficiency, expanding market demand, and enhancing consumer surplus, particularly in moderately dense markets with moderately delay-sensitive customers. We further show that vendors can enhance these benefits through optimal pricing and benefit from less extreme staffing adjustments due to a “pull-to-center” effect. Our findings highlight the operational, economic, and ethical dimensions of proximity-based delivery, and offer a practical framework for balancing speed, profitability, consumer welfare, and equity. Finally, we conduct a mini case study using empirical data to demonstrate the real-world applicability of our approach. This paper was accepted by Jeannette Song, operations management. Funding: Z. Wang

papers.title: Short-horizon capital in a bank-centered financial system: Japanese mutual fund launches relative to the U.S.
papers.authors: Toshiki Honda, Alan Guoming Huang, Daisuke Miyakawa, Sho Nishiuchi, Russ Wermers
papers.abstract: The median time from launch to peak assets under management (AUM) is nine months for Japanese active domestic equity mutual funds, versus 4.6 years for comparable U.S. funds. Japanese funds also grow much less from launch to peak, as strong initial inflows quickly give way to persistent outflows, while U.S. funds continue to attract net inflows for years. We link this compressed life cycle to Japan’s bank-centered, concentrated distribution system and front-loaded sales compensation. A larger launch size and higher sales load each predict earlier peak AUM in Japan, but not in the U.S.; within Japan, stronger distribution networks are associated with larger launches and earlier peaks, while longer pre-inception sales periods are associated with larger launch sizes and higher sales loads. The evidence shows that the same market-based financial product can follow different life cycles when embedded in different national systems of intermediation and compensation. Japan’s prolonged weak equity-market environment provides an additional context in which investors may reassess newly launched funds as realized performance becomes observable. Our findings suggest that incentives rewarding initial sales can mobilize capital rapidly without generating durable asset retention in an institutional environment such as Japan’s.

papers.title: Adapting to the new abnormal: multinational corporations’ foreign subsidiary investment and country resilience to climate change
papers.authors: Chang Hoon Oh, Jorge E. Rivera, Jennifer M. Oetzel
papers.abstract: As climate change (CC) increasingly disrupts infrastructure, supply chains, labor availability, and public services, multinational corporations (MNCs) face growing uncertainty when selecting locations for foreign expansion. We examine whether host-country CC resilience has become an important determinant of international investment and how firm capabilities shape this relationship. Drawing on socio-ecological resilience theory and the resilience and turbulence framework, we analyze Global Fortune 500 firms investing across 155 countries between 2003 and 2017. We find that MNCs establish more wholly owned subsidiaries in countries with higher CC resilience, indicating that resilience is emerging as a strategic location-specific advantage. This relationship is stronger for firms with well-developed ESG capabilities and prior experience operating in resilient countries, but weaker for firms with greater financial slack. Our findings suggest that managers should incorporate CC resilience into location decisions alongside traditional economic and institutional criteria while considering their firms’ resource and capability profile to assess how effectively they can leverage host-country CC resilience. For policymakers, the results indicate that strengthening CC resilience can improve not only adaptation to CC but also national competitiveness in attracting MNC foreign direct investment. Overall, CC resilience is becoming a strategic determinant of where MNCs choose to invest.

papers.title: Populism, polarization and green investment
papers.authors: Anders Anderson, David T. Robinson

papers.title: Deterrence or Backlash? Arrests and the Dynamics of Domestic Violence
papers.authors: Sofia Amaral, Gordon B. Dahl, Timo Hener, Victoria Kaiser, Helmut Rainer

papers.title: Organizational Goal Hierarchies in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: A Dynamic Behavioral Perspective
papers.authors: David Diwei Lv, SAKU Mantere
papers.abstract: This paper theorizes how artificial intelligence (AI) disrupts organizational goal hierarchies by altering the rate and rhythm at which strategic purposes and operational means evolve. Rather than assuming that goals shift uniformly, we introduce the concept of goal flow: a dynamic and nonuniform change across a system of goals. AI technologies play a dual role in goal flow, as they disintegrate goal systems by accelerating goal evolution at different intensities across strategic and operational goals, while simultaneously enabling new forms of integration by augmenting social processes of learning, bargaining, and control. By elaborating this dual role in four types of integration work—aligning, directing, filtering, and sustaining—the paper reconceptualizes goal hierarchies as dynamic systems, augmented by AI.

papers.title: Prospect Theory and Currency Returns: Empirical Evidence
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Qi Lei Xu, Roman Kozhan, Mark Taylor
papers.abstract: We empirically investigate the role of prospect theory in the foreign exchange market. A currency-level measure of prospect-theory value, constructed from the historical distribution of exchange rate returns, negatively forecasts future currency excess returns. A long–short strategy based on this measure yields approximately 5% per annum. Predictability is stronger when arbitrage is limited. Bank order flow is positively associated with prospect-theory value, with inter-dealer and proprietary trading primarily driving this relation. Funds trade against prospect-theory value, acting as arbitrageurs. Overall, our findings suggest that investors evaluate currencies based on historical return distributions, consistent with prospect theory.

papers.title: Trended Momentum
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Charlie Xiaowu Cai, Lin Peng, Kevin Keasey
papers.abstract: Drawing on cognitive psychology and behavioral theories of pattern recognition and heuristic processing, we offer a new perspective on momentum by highlighting how clear price trends shape investor expectations. Trend clarity (TC) materially strengthens momentum returns: the highest trend-clarity quintile earns annualized returns of 12.68%, compared with 6.90% for a conventional momentum strategy. We also show that TC affects momentum trading intensity within Hong and Stein’s (1999) multiperiod return-chasing model. Additional tests indicate that trading on clear trends is a central feature of momentum, distinct from existing explanations and observable across asset classes and global markets.

papers.title: Bringing culture back in: An institutional analysis of budgeting and power in an emerging economy context
papers.authors: Paromita Rakhi, Sven Modell
papers.abstract: This paper examines how notions of culture and power intertwine in the shaping of budget-related practices within a large public sector organisation in Bangladesh. Drawing on institutional theory, we advance a view of power as a dynamic and relational, yet institutionally embedded, phenomenon. We examine how the power originating in cultural norms, which are firmly institutionalised in Bangladeshi society, is reinforced and weakened by micro-level dynamics in the organisation under investigation. We also show how the interplay between cultural norms and micro-level dynamics is conditioned by the influence of international donor agencies and other actors, who are relatively peripheral to the organisation, and how this gives rise to variations in the operation of power and budget-related practices. Examining how this interplay manifests itself under conditions of institutional stability, we provide a nuanced perspective on how power is implicated in budgeting and a systematic, contingent conception of how variations in budget-related practices emerge. We discuss the implications for institutional research on budgeting and institutional theory in general.

papers.title: Unemployment Benefits and Unemployment in the Great Recession: The Role of Equilibrium Effects
papers.authors: Marcus Hagedorn, Fatih Karahan, Iourii Manovskii, Kurt Mitman
papers.abstract: Equilibrium labor market theory suggests that unemployment benefit extensions affect unemployment by impacting both job search decisions by the unemployed and job creation decisions by employers. The existing empirical literature focused on the former effect only. We develop a new methodology necessary to incorporate the measurement of the latter effect. Implementing this methodology in the data, we find that benefit extensions raise equilibrium wages and lead to a sharp contraction in vacancy creation and employment and a rise in unemployment.

papers.title: Market Response to Racial Uprisings
papers.authors: Bocar Ba, Roman G. Rivera, Alexander Whitefield
papers.abstract: Do investors anticipate that demands for racial equity will impact companies? We explore this question in the context of the Black Lives Matter (BLM) movement—the largest racially motivated protest movement in U.S. history—and its effect on the U.S. policing industry using a novel dataset on publicly traded firms contracting with the police. It is unclear whether the BLM uprisings were likely to increase or decrease market valuations of firms contracting heavily with police because of the increased interest in reforming the police, fears over rising crime, and pushes to “defund the police”. We find, in contrast to the predictions of economics experts we surveyed, that in the three weeks following incidents triggering BLM uprisings, policing firms experienced a stock price increase of seven percentage points relative to the stock prices of nonpolicing firms in similar industries. In particular, firms producing surveillance technology and police accountability tools experienced higher returns following BLM activism–related events. Furthermore, policing firms’ fundamentals, such as sales, improved after the murder of George Floyd, suggesting that policing firms’ future performances bore out investors' positive expectations following incidents triggering BLM uprisings. Our research shows how—despite BLM’s calls to reduce investment in policing and explore alternative public safety approaches—the financial market has translated high-profile violence against Black civilians and calls for systemic change into shareholder gains and additional revenues for police suppliers.

papers.title: Intermediate Input Prices and the Labor Share
papers.authors: Juanma Castro-Vincenzi, Benny Kleinman
papers.abstract: We argue that the relative price of materials is an important determinant of the labor share of income. When materials and primary inputs are complements and the profit share is positive, a higher price of materials lowers the labor share and raises the profit share of value added, without requiring markups or returns to scale to change. We show that materials-price fluctuations align with U.S. labor-share trends, provide causal evidence on this mechanism across industries and commuting zones, and quantify its importance in a dynamic quantitative model. Finally, we use our mechanism to rationalize differential labor-share trends across countries. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

papers.title: How to Get Away with Merger: Stealth Consolidation and Its Effects on US Dialysis
papers.authors: Thomas Wollmann

papers.title: Sample Range as Subjective Variability and Implications for Experience-Based Decision Making
papers.authors: Tianwei Liu, Benjamin Scheibehenne
papers.abstract: Variance and standard deviation are common metrics of statistical variability in the management and decision-making literature. In everyday contexts, however, information about sample range prevails. Range is arguably easier to comprehend and compute than variance, yet it often yields equivalent judgments about variability. Hence, we reason that decision makers often rely on range to judge variability. We test this hypothesis across four behavioral experiments (total n = 1,093). When comparing the variability of two number sets, decision makers predominantly based their judgments on sample range rather than sample variance when the two metrics disagree (experiment 1). Sample range tends to increase with sample size, whereas sample variance does not. Consistent with the range as variability hypothesis, decision makers perceived distributions as more variable after observing larger samples (experiment 2). This perceived variability, in turn, influenced risky decisions, as larger sample sizes led to decreased valuations of uncertain rewards for risk-averse decision makers (experiment 3). In further support of the hypothesis, when asked to mentally simulate new samples from a previously experienced distribution, participants generated more numbers within the observed range and fewer numbers outside of it than the true distribution implies (experiment 4). To model the data, we propose a “cognitive fence” idea as a potential psychological explanation for how experience shapes subjective variability. We conclude by discussing implications for research on overconfidence, distributional learning, risk perception, and communication. This paper was accepted by Jack Soll, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are avail

papers.title: The Impact of Mandatory Audit Firm Rotation on Competitive Pricing Strategies for New Audit Engagements: Evidence From the European Union
papers.authors: Ditmir Sufaj, Simon Dekeyser, Marleen Willekens
papers.abstract: Mandatory audit firm rotation was introduced in the European Union (EU), in part, to make the audit market more dynamic by bringing audit engagements to market more frequently. However, it creates a countervailing economic force: By limiting the duration of auditor–client relationships, mandatory rotation shortens the period over which auditors can recoup first‐year fee discounts through fees earned in subsequent years. Consistent with this argument, we find that first‐year fee discounts decline substantially after mandatory firm rotation took effect in the EU, particularly in countries with stricter limits on auditor tenure. Thus, greater opportunities to compete for new engagements do not necessarily translate into greater first‐year fee discounts. Our findings highlight that regulators should consider not only how frequently audit engagements are brought to market but also how limits on auditor tenure shape the pricing incentives associated with competing for new clients.

papers.title: The Long-Run Economic Effects of Medical Innovation and the Role of Opportunities
papers.authors: Sonia R. Bhalotra, Damian Clarke, Atheendar S Venkataramani

papers.title: From Design to Disclosure
papers.authors: S. Nageeb Ali, Andreas Kleiner, Kun Zhang
papers.abstract: We study the role of hard information in contractual and market settings in which the receiver can flexibly adjust allocations and transfers in response to the sender's disclosure. These settings include monopoly pricing, insurance contracting, and policy negotiations. Across these settings, the sender is worst off if she reveals her type completely because the receiver would then adjust the terms of trade to extract her surplus. Taking this feature as our central departure from the literature, we characterize the entire set of equilibrium payoffs in these disclosure games. We prove an equivalence result: a payoff profile can be approximated by an equilibrium of the disclosure game if and only if it can be achieved through information design. Thus, there exist equilibria in which the sender obtains approximately her commitment payoff.

papers.title: Temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements
papers.authors: Jeffrey J. Reuer, Toby X. Li
papers.abstract: Research Summary We examine temporal tradeoffs and contracting dynamics in buyer–supplier agreements by investigating how suppliers' contractual terms change when contracting with initial clients versus new clients in the future. We use information economics and research on certifications in interorganizational relationships to delve into the mechanisms leading to potential improvements in suppliers' contractual terms. We situate the empirical analysis in the context of onshore oil and gas drilling projects to examine the liabilities for project‐related risks that startup drillers assume when contracting with client producers. Evidence indicates that when drillers initially work for prominent client producers, the drillers assume more risks in these first contracts, but fewer risks in subsequent agreements with other client producers. We argue and show that the degree to which a specific driller obtains better terms in future deals owing to its initial client's prominence will be attenuated when subsequent clients have more information on the value of the driller's resources and capabilities. Specifically, the resulting reduction in risks borne by the driller will be smaller when the driller was founded by a serial entrepreneur and when the subsequent client is vertically integrated into drilling operations. Managerial Summary This study examines the contracting dynamics that startups experience as suppliers in buyer–supplier agreements. Startups often bear more risk in initial deals to build credibility, especially when contracting with prominent clients, and such affiliations can then lead to improved terms for startups in subsequent contracts with other clients. However, this follow‐on benefit of working with a prominent client depends upon whether subsequent clients

papers.title: The Consequences of Pay Standing under Pay Range Transparency
papers.authors: Meredith Lauren Woehler, Tae‐Youn Park
papers.abstract: Pay range transparency—that is, disclosing the minimum and maximum pay for a job rather than individuals’ actual pay—has become the most prevalent form of pay transparency. Yet, existing theories explain employee reactions to pay information through present-focused, interpersonal comparisons with coworkers’ pay. We theorize that pay range transparency instead directs employees to interpret their structural pay standing—their pay position relative to the disclosed range boundaries—as a forward-looking signal of the organization’s recognition and structural room for pay growth. Drawing on expectancy theory, we propose that structural pay standing has a curvilinear (attenuated-positive) effect on job satisfaction, intention to stay, and job performance, mediated by pay growth uncertainty: pay near the range minimum offers weak evidence that contributions will be recognized, whereas pay near the maximum reveals limited structural room for further growth, a pattern we term a ceiling effect. Pay-related procedural justice attenuates these effects. Four studies—a natural experiment (n = 371), an online experiment (n = 603), a three-wave field study (n = 525), and an experimental-causal-chain study (n = 392)—support our theorizing, establishing structural pay standing as distinct from interpersonal pay standing and revealing an unrecognized trade-off of pay range transparency.

papers.title: Phantom Networks: Window on Agency in Social Mechanisms
papers.authors: Ronald S. Burt, Ray E. Reagans, Sonja Opper
papers.abstract: Our goal is to offer proof of concept for the idea that behavioral networks emerging with and beyond assigned treatment networks in experiments can provide a valuable window on agency. We call these often unobserved behavioral structures phantom networks. Most evidence of agency is entangled with audience—what people recall, how others attribute, or who is seen to act. We strip that away to observe agency directly in the ties participants build within and beyond what they are assigned. Their deviation from assignment is not error but structure in action, a behavioral trace of agency. We offer three exhibits of that “behavioral deviation” revealing agency in gendered brokerage, rival brokerage, and structural reproduction. Across the three exhibits, behavioral deviation shows how a team works (sometimes in surprising ways), not how well the team works. Teams perform as expected in theory, but the behavior responsible for their performance is made more apparent by watching behavioral deviation. We close with a summary proof of concept and discussion of next steps for particularly promising future work. Funding: This work was made possible by financial support from the University of Chicago Booth School of Business for data-processing software and financial support from MIT Sloan for transitioning our earlier experiment to the more flexible Empirica platform and funding the experiment trials on which we report here.

papers.title: Influence Without Authority: Bottom-Up Normalization of Organizational Corruption
papers.authors: Patricia Helena Hein, Shahzad Shaz Ansari
papers.abstract: Research on organizational corruption has largely portrayed normalization as a top-down, management-driven process. We know less about how employees with limited formal authority can escalate wrongdoing beyond isolated acts and drive its normalization. Drawing on a qualitative study of a German recruitment firm’s practices during the COVID-19 pandemic, we develop a three-phase model of bottom-up normalization of organizational wrongdoing. Less powerful actors first engage in tolerated rule-bending to demonstrate competence and indispensability and build influence through informal networks. When disruption threatens this influence and legitimate alternatives are unavailable, they may escalate to more serious wrongdoing to safeguard their standing by framing new opportunities as extensions of familiar rule-bending. Normalization then depends on their ability to sustain a cohesive coalition, secure support from actors with formal authority, and contain resistance. We make three contributions. First, we advance a relational view of corruption by showing how central positions in informal networks enable actors lacking formal authority to mobilize support across hierarchical levels and normalize wrongdoing. Second, we show how organizational corruption can become a means of building and preserving social influence, fostering a sense of accomplishment rather than guilt or shame. Third, we identify a disruption-driven pathway to normalization in which threats to less powerful actors’ social influence precipitate abrupt escalation from tolerated rule-bending to more serious wrongdoing.

papers.title: Earnings Instability
papers.authors: Peter Ganong, Pascal Noel, Christina Patterson, Joseph Vavra, Alex Weinberg
papers.abstract: This paper uses high-frequency administrative data to show that most U.S. workers experience substantial month-to-month fluctuations in pay, even within ongoing employment relationships. Monthly earnings instability is pervasive but is masked in annual data. Moreover, this instability is unequally distributed: lower-income, hourly workers face more instability than higher-income, salaried workers. Firm-driven fluctuations in hours account for a large share of this instability. Monthly earnings instability, in turn, increases spending volatility and job separations. Short-term earnings risk is therefore a significant feature of the labor market and falls disproportionately on the most financially fragile workers.

papers.title: Meritocracy and Homophily in Collegial Organizations
papers.authors: Paul-Henri Moisson, Jean Tirole
papers.abstract: In collegial organizations, homophily jeopardizes the recruitment of the most talented (“meritocracy”). We analyze the dynamics and welfare properties of an organization whose incumbent members coopt new ones in a forward-looking manner. We identify organizations in which meritocracy is likely to give way to favoritism and entrenchment, and investigate policy interventions (such as affirmative action, quality-based or diversity-based funding, discretionary overruling of majority decisions, blind hiring processes) and their unintended consequences.

papers.title: Corporate Contributions to Ballot Measure Campaigns: Real Effects and Valuation
papers.authors: Rüdiger Fahlenbrach, Alexei V. Ovtchinnikov, Philip Valta
papers.abstract: We analyze novel data on corporate contributions to ballot initiatives at the U.S. state level. Firms make large contributions to ballot measure campaigns in favor of or against specific initiatives. They contribute significantly more to business initiatives compared with ideological initiatives. Corporate campaign spending is systematically associated with the likelihood that a ballot measure passes. Contributing firms experience changes in sales growth following the passage of important ballot measures. Following successful (failed) initiatives, all firms in affected industries exhibit significantly more positive (negative) cumulative abnormal returns around the election, but contributing firms do more so than peers. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: R. Fahlenbrach gratefully acknowledges financial support from the Swiss Finance Institute. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06801 .

papers.title: The Asymmetry in Responsible Investing Preferences and Beliefs
papers.authors: Jacquelyn Humphrey, Shimon Kogan, Jacob S. Sagi, Laura T. Starks
papers.abstract: Empirical stylized facts in the literature concerning “sin” versus “angel” stocks display marked asymmetries in investor behavior. Through a set of experiments, we examine whether such biases can be micro-founded via individuals’ preferences and belief formations. With respect to portfolio allocation decisions, we find that the responses to negative environmental and social externalities are several times larger in magnitude than their responses to comparable positive externalities, ceteris paribus. Negative externalities also modestly increase pessimism about future investment performance, whereas positive externalities have little discernible effect on beliefs. This asymmetry is pervasive across our sample, exhibits heterogeneity across individuals, and is comparable to or greater in magnitude than estimates observed in loss aversion analyses. These findings help rationalize several existing stylized empirical facts documented in the responsible investing literature and carry implications for the growing body of theoretical work modeling the role of nonpecuniary investor preferences in asset pricing. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06826 .

papers.title: Opinion Trumps Fact: Entry and Competition in Online Political News
papers.authors: Aaron Chatterji, Sharique Hasan, William D. Miles, Dror Shvadron
papers.abstract: This paper examines how new entrants influenced content strategies in the U.S. online political news business from 2014 to 2021. Using a novel measure of article opinionation that captures the extent to which an article displays editorializing and persuasive language, we provide correlational evidence that new entrants produce articles that are more opinionated than those of incumbents, even when reporting on the same event. We then show that there is an economic rationale for this content strategy: opinionated articles receive more engagement on Twitter, and this engagement translates to increased webpage visits, crucial for advertising revenue. Consistent with these incentives, we provide evidence that news providers increase the average opinion level in their articles in response to competition and advertiser pressure. These shifts are accompanied by a possibly unintended consequence: opinionated content is associated with greater anger and hate speech in social media engagement. This paper was accepted by Alfonso Gambardella, business strategy. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01487 .

papers.title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
papers.authors: Jose A. Cervantez, Sophia L. Pink, Linda W. Chang, Aneesh Rai, Katherine L. Milkman
papers.abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. Another study shows that when women are overrepresented, the effect of descriptive feedback reverses in direction, increasing the subsequent selection of men (due to concerns about fairness), but this effect is significantly smaller in magnitude than the feedback effect produced when women are underrepresented. Practically, the effects of descriptive feedback were 45%–80% as large as simulating a strict quota requiring that at least one woman or racial minority be selected for a given opportunity, highlighting that descriptive feedback is a light-touch but potentially powerful intervention for promoting diversity. This paper was accepted by George Wu, behavioral econ

papers.title: Human Performance at Solving 0-1 Knapsack Problems: Results from a Large-Scale Field Experiment
papers.authors: Sumit D. Agarwal, Joel Goh, Wenlan Qian, Xin Zou
papers.abstract: The 0-1 knapsack problem is a fundamental problem of discrete choice that permeates many diverse fields and applications, but relatively little is known about what instances human solvers find more difficult than others. This paper reports the results of the first large-scale randomized controlled field experiment investigating this question, conducted in partnership with a global mobile gaming platform. A total of 100,000 different knapsack instances were predesigned for this study and randomly assigned to each player attempt at the knapsack problem. For our base-case analysis, there were 17,950,838 distinct player accounts who made a total of 150,284,195 submitted solution attempts. Contrary to expectations, players performed better on problems that were rated as more difficult by two traditional measures of knapsack difficulty (the Pearson correlation between value and weight vectors and Sahni complexity), but performed worse on problem instances that featured large optimality gaps from a suite of heuristic solution algorithms. These suggest that optimality gaps can serve as promising measures of human-perceived knapsack difficulty and potentially could be used to measure human-perceived problem difficulty for other types of discrete choice problems. We found evidence that players improved their performance with repeated attempts at the knapsack task overall, but less-experienced players of the mobile game improved more quickly than more-experienced players. Through the construction of a new measure of human-perceived difficulty rating for each knapsack instance, we found evidence that players who were assigned to instances with a higher difficulty rating in the past tended to perform better on future attempts. This paper was accepted by Manel Baucells, behavioral ec

papers.title: Connectors and Influencers
papers.authors: Frédéric Moisan, Syngjoo Choi, Sanjeev Goyal
papers.abstract: We study a setting in which personal acquisition of information is costly and maintaining personal contacts to share information socially is also costly. The theory predicts star networks, with small groups sustaining an active hub and large groups allowing in addition for an inactive hub equilibrium. Experiments with small (8 subjects) and large (50 subjects) groups show star-like networks throughout. In small groups, behavior matches the active hub prediction. In large groups, hubs are inactive or engage in activity far in excess of the active hub equilibrium depending on how much information subjects are given on their own and others’ earnings. The hub’s activity level shapes relative earnings of subjects and the overall performance of the group. This paper was accepted by Roberto Weber, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: This work was supported by H2020 Future and Emerging Technologies [IBSEN Contract 662725]; the Keynes Fund, University of Cambridge; and the Creative-Pioneering Researchers Program, Seoul National University. S. Goyal acknowledges financial support from the Center of Behavioural Institutional Design and Tamkeen [New York University Abu Dhabi Research Institute Award CG005]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07308 .

papers.title: Should birds of a feather flock together: How public criticism shapes pressures for sustainability conformity and differentiation
papers.authors: N Piyasinchai, Matthew G. Grimes
papers.abstract: Research Summary While firms face pressure to engage in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) practices, it is unclear how they should specifically engage given the breadth of sustainability‐related concerns. Drawing on optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations research, we argue that public criticism directed toward an industry creates oscillating pressures for firms to conform with or deviate from industry ESG norms. Using data on 8176 global companies from 2013 to 2022, we find that although ESG conformity benefits investor evaluations, once industry peers' public criticism accumulates beyond a threshold, ESG differentiation is rewarded, particularly when firms increase material ESG practices and reduce immaterial ones. Our study reveals how public criticism dynamically reshapes the evaluative processes by which investors determine firm legitimacy, bridging optimal distinctiveness and social evaluations literatures. Managerial Summary Our research indicates that firms often adopt similar ESG practices as their industry peers, which usually enhances investor evaluations. However, this conformity can backfire and become a liability when industry peers face significant criticism. In such scenarios, firms that adopt distinctive ESG practices compared to the industry tend to receive greater rewards, especially when differentiation involves increasing material ESG practices and reducing immaterial ones. Therefore, while adopting ESG norms can be beneficial, managers should be vigilant of public opinion and ready to deviate from those norms when necessary.

papers.title: Silent female representation and tech entrepreneurial project evaluation: The role of evaluators' genders
papers.authors: Yan Anthea Zhang, Lun Li, Jizhen Li, Xiwei Yi
papers.abstract: Research Summary We examine how the nature of female representation in tech entrepreneurial projects may be related to the evaluations of the projects. We argue that silent female representation —i.e., women are present but do not speak in representing projects—may reinforce the stereotyped view of women, resulting in lower project evaluations relative to male‐only projects, whereas active female representation may not lead to evaluation penalty. We further predict that the negative association between silent female representation and project evaluation is stronger when the evaluators are women than when they are men. Conducted in a unique setting wherein female and male evaluators on panels, independently and confidentially, rated funding applications represented by various mixes of male and female entrepreneurs, our study provides evidence that is consistent with these predictions. Managerial Summary It is widely recognized that female entrepreneurs face greater challenges than their male counterparts when seeking external financial resources in the tech sector. This funding disparity may start from evaluation disparity. We find that projects with silent female representation—i.e., women are present but do not speak—receive lower evaluations than male‐only projects, whereas projects with active female representation receive evaluations comparable to male‐only projects. We also find that female evaluators are more likely than male evaluators to penalize projects with silent female representation. Our research offers valuable insights into strategies for fostering gender equality in traditionally male‐dominated fields.

papers.title: Partisan Banks and Creditor Coordination Within Loan Syndicates
papers.authors: Robert M. Bushman, Sang Woo Sohn, Jianxin Zhao
papers.abstract: We investigate how firm‐level partisanship influences interactions between banks in the syndicated loan market. Because politically divergent banks hold conflicting perceptions of economic conditions, ideological distance between banks impedes consensus and elevates expected coordination costs.
