We find that greater political distance between a lead arranger and a participant reduces the participant's likelihood of joining a syndicate and lowers its retained loan share relative to the lead. The relation between political distance and loan share differences intensifies during periods of high national political polarization. Moreover, greater political diversity within a syndicate is associated with less restrictive loan covenants and higher interest spreads, reflecting a trade‐off where lenders sacrifice contingent control to avoid costly renegotiation gridlock. Validating our disagreement mechanism, we show that following presidential elections, banks politically misaligned with the incoming administration issue significantly more pessimistic macroeconomic forecasts than aligned banks.

papers.title: Do Fund Managers’ Commitments to Responsible Investing Affect Private Information Acquisition, Information Environment, and Corporate Sustainability?
papers.authors: Sumit D. Agarwal, Johan Sulaeman, Yue Zhang, Zhe zong
papers.abstract: We investigate the effects of mutual funds’ commitments to responsible investing on their information acquisition activities and the corresponding externalities for other stakeholders. After committing to responsible investing (via United Nations Principles for Responsible Investment (UNPRI)), fund managers increase private information acquisition activities, that is, corporate site visits, particularly focusing on environmental and social issues. These visits generate negligible private investment value for the visiting funds. However, the information environment at the stock level improves following these visits with lower consensus analyst forecast errors. In addition to the information production role of these visits, they also generate positive externalities for other stakeholders through incremental improvements in the sustainability practices of the firms receiving sustainability-focused site visits from UNPRI fund managers. Collectively, the paper highlights the private costs and social benefits of responsible investing. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal and J. Sulaeman acknowledge research support from Sustainable and Green Finance Institute [Grant WBS A-0006413-00-00]. Y. Zhang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72402239] and China Scholarship Council. This work was supported by the Ministry of Education, Singapore [Social Science and Humanities Research Thematic Grant SSRC2024-SSHRTG-022]. Any opinions, findings and conclusions or recommendations expressed in this material are those of the author(s) and do not reflect the views of the Social Science Research Council (Singapore) and the Ministry of Education (Singapore). Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data

papers.title: Biodiversity Risk in the Corporate Bond Market
papers.authors: Sevgi Soylemezgil, Cihan Uzmanoglu
papers.abstract: We show that a biodiversity risk premium has emerged in the U.S. corporate bond market following the United Nations Biodiversity Conference (COP15) in October 2021. COP15 placed biodiversity on the global regulatory agenda and raised transition risks for exposed firms. After COP15, a one standard deviation increase in a firm’s biodiversity footprint is associated with a 7% increase in its secondary market yield spreads, whereas this relation is insignificant before COP15. The biodiversity effect is also present in primary bond markets, most pronounced for medium-term bonds and distinct from climate-related mechanisms. Furthermore, a higher biodiversity footprint is associated with a lower likelihood of issuing medium-term bonds after COP15, consistent with firms managing their biodiversity-related risks. Evidence from firms’ biodiversity dependencies suggests that physical biodiversity risks are also priced in the bond market. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07660 .

papers.title: Whiplash: Congestion Dissipation in a Disrupted Circulatory Shipping System
papers.authors: Ming Hu, Chaoyu Zhang
papers.abstract: The (post)pandemic period was marked by numerous port disruptions, leading to delays and rising costs for shippers. We build a fluid model in transient states to investigate how a disruption at one port can affect the disrupted port and its counterpart in another country in a circulatory container shipping system, where a stream of fleets moves goods back and forth between the two ports. Port disruption leads to two types of congestion: the inbound backlogs, which occur when ships are unable to enter the port, and the outbound backlogs, which arise when goods are unable to be loaded onto ships for transport to other ports. We analytically characterize the system’s recovery time, measured from the onset of the port closure until normal operations are restored, and the dynamics of inbound and outbound backlogs during recovery. We identify a whiplash effect in which outbound backlogs alternate between ports, creating oscillatory congestion patterns because of the disruption-induced uneven spatial distribution of ships. Our analysis reveals that simply increasing ship capacity may not expedite system recovery, highlighting the importance of coordination between port authorities and shipping companies when jointly planning capacity expansions. Furthermore, we examine several extensions of the model. We use the two-port system as a building block to analyze bipartite and cyclic network structures, and we also consider scenarios in which a port experiences multiple disruptions. In all cases, the whiplash effect persists, thereby demonstrating the robustness of our findings. Finally, we use the prediction from our theoretical model as a feature and apply machine learning techniques to predict the time that vessels spend in Shanghai Port after a typhoon disruption and show that

papers.title: When Data Scientists Meet Domain Experts: Artificial Intelligence, Epistemic Conflict, and Knowledge Transformation
papers.authors: Mayur Prataprai Joshi, Ning Su, Mark Zbaracki
papers.abstract: Predictive artificial intelligence (AI) models developed by data scientists promise to transform organizational knowledge, yet in practice, the predictions remain inscrutable to domain experts. Existing explanations situate the problems in the opacity of the AI tools, failed adoption, or jurisdictional conflict but offer limited insight into how to make the knowledge accessible. Here, we show how the problem emerges from the competing epistemic stances of data scientists and domain experts, which create conflict over how to produce and evaluate knowledge. We then ask how data scientists and domain experts address that conflict so that their work with AI satisfies each group’s standards for producing and evaluating knowledge. Drawing on an 18-month inductive study of three large Indian banks, we show that the data scientists produce new knowledge, but domain experts hold the power to decide whether it is deployed. Our findings distinguish between epistemic and jurisdictional conflict. We show that data scientists first try to address the epistemic conflict directly through assimilative practices that follow one epistemic stance or the other. When these practices fail to transform knowledge, data scientists learn to address the conflict indirectly through four bridging practices. These practices help the domain experts transform knowledge by embedding the data scientists’ predictions in the boundary objects and practices that the domain experts already use. Our findings reveal how power based on expertise rather than jurisdictional control can make possible the coproduction of knowledge. Funding: This research was supported in part by funding from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council [Grant 430-2024-01156] to M. Joshi.

papers.title: Dangerous Liaisons? Debt Supply and Convenience Yield Spillovers in the Euro Area*
papers.authors: Cristian Arcidiacono, Matthieu Bellon, Matthias Gnewuch
papers.abstract: The literature established that a sovereign bond’s “convenience yield” premium diminishes when that country issues more debt. But how is this convenience yield affected when another country issues sovereign debt? Using high-frequency identification and debt management offices’ communication, we find that an increase in German or French debt reduces convenience yields across the eurozone. Spillovers to low-risk countries are one-for-one while those to riskier countries are smaller. To rationalize these findings, we develop a model with heterogeneous credit risk. Safe sovereign bonds are close substitutes to hedge against idiosyncratic risk, explaining large spillovers, while risky bonds are poor substitutes.

papers.title: Government Guarantees and Dynamic Debt Runs
papers.authors: Jacopo Magnani, Yabin Wang
papers.abstract: This study quantifies the impact of public guarantees on the stability of bank wholesale funding. We study the Chinese market for negotiable certificates of deposit (NCDs) around the first bank failure in two decades, the Baoshang event, which struck investors’ belief in government guarantees on wholesale bank debt. We document a sharp increase in NCD spreads, issuance failures, and runs, with weaker banks becoming more exposed to rollover risk after the event. Using a model of dynamic debt runs, we estimate that the perceived guarantee fell from 54% of creditor losses before the event to approximately zero after the event. The decline is largest for small banks, low-rated banks, and rural commercial banks. Our structural model also allows us to compare alternative policies aimed at stabilizing creditors’ willingness to roll over short-term debt.

papers.title: The Welfare Effects of Price Shocks and Household Relief Packages: Evidence from an Energy Crisis
papers.authors: Peter Levell, Martin O’Connell, Kate Smith
papers.abstract: Aggregate price shocks generate unequal welfare losses both across and within income groups.Policymakers face a trade-off: price subsidies direct more support to households facing larger losses, but create inefficiencies, while transfers are less distortionary but harder to target.We develop and implement a framework to quantify this trade-off using rich panel data on households' energy spending and incomes, alongside price and policy variation from the 2022-23 European Energy Crisis.Absent policy intervention, average household welfare losses would have equalled 6% of income, with some households facing much larger losses.The combination of an energy-price subsidy and universal transfers reduced both the mean and dispersion of losses, but incurred efficiency costs equal to 12% of total relief-package revenue costs.Optimal policy entails a strictly positive price subsidy, though its level is lower when transfers can be targeted using income and prior energy usage.

papers.title: Noisy Global Value Chains
papers.authors: Ha Bui, Zhen Huo, Andrei A. Levchenko, Nitya Pandalai-Nayar

papers.title: Aspiring to a Better Future: Can a Simple Psychological Intervention Reduce Poverty?
papers.authors: Kate Orkin, Robert Garlick, Mahreen Mahmud, Richard Sedlmayr, Johannes Haushofer, Stefan Dercon
papers.abstract: Do higher aspirations for the future motivate people living in poverty to make long-term investments? Do their aspirations increase when economic conditions improve? To answer these questions, we run a 415-village field experiment with 8,300 women living in poverty in rural Kenya. We design an 80-minute workshop to help people set higher aspirations and plan to achieve them. We cross-randomise this with large unconditional cash transfers. The workshop substantially raises aspirations, labour supply, investment, revenue, and living standards 17 months later, relative to a placebo workshop. Increases in aspirations are the most likely mechanism to explain the economic effects. Cash transfers also raise aspirations, which might help to explain why transfers increase labour supply and investment. We conclude that aspirations respond to both economic and psychological interventions, contribute to investment decisions and living standards, and are important considerations for development policy.

papers.title: Daddy’s Girl: Daughters, Managerial Decisions, and Gender Inequality
papers.authors: Maddalena Ronchi, Nina Smith
papers.abstract: Using Danish registry data, we study how managers’ gender attitudes shape gender inequality in the workplace by exploiting the birth of a daughter—as opposed to a son—as a plausibly exogenous shock to male managers’ gender attitudes. Comparing within-firm changes in women’s labour outcomes depending on the gender of the manager’s newborn child, we find that women’s relative earnings and employment increase by 4.4% and 2.9%, respectively, following the birth of the manager’s first daughter. These effects are driven by an increase in managers’ propensity to substitute male hires with female hires that have comparable education, hours worked, and earnings. Consistent with this substitution channel, we do not detect any significant effect on firm performance. Because these effects emerge rapidly and persist over time, we can rule out the need for prolonged exposure to gender issues or for personal incentives tied to improving conditions for their own daughters as prerequisites for managers to promote gender equality within their firms.

papers.title: What’s at Stake? Understanding the Role of Home Equity in Flood Insurance Demand
papers.authors: Yanjun Liao, Philip Mulder
papers.abstract: Changing flood insurance demand shifts climate risk across homeowners, lenders, and governments. We show that flood insurance take-up follows rising and falling home equity over the housing boom and bust across markets with different price dynamics. To isolate the causal effect of risk shifting on insurance demand, we study flood insurance policy renewals over the housing bust, exploiting granular differences in purchase timing that led policyholders to experience differential changes in skin-in-the-game exposure to flood risk for the same change in home equity. When homeowners have less equity exposure to flood losses, they are less likely to renew their policies. Lenders, in turn, have little incentive to require flood insurance when they can sell their mortgages to federally backed mortgage purchasers. This paper was accepted by Tomasz Piskorski, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01302 .

papers.title: Rethinking Distribution Shifts: Empirical Analysis and Modeling for Tabular Data
papers.authors: Tianyu Wang, Jiashuo Liu, Peng Cui, Hongseok Namkoong
papers.abstract: Different distribution shifts require different interventions, and algorithms must be grounded in the specific shifts they address. However, methodological development for robust algorithms typically relies on structural assumptions that lack empirical validation. Advocating for an empirically grounded data-driven approach to algorithm development, we build an empirical testbed comprising natural shifts across 8 tabular data sets, 172 distribution pairs over 45 methods, and 90,000 method configurations encompassing empirical risk minimization and distributionally robust optimization (DRO) methods. We find that Y|X-shifts are most prevalent in our testbed, in stark contrast to the heavy focus on X (covariate)-shifts in the machine learning literature, and that the performance of robust algorithms is no better than that of vanilla methods. To understand why, we conduct an in-depth empirical analysis of DRO methods and find that underlooked implementation details—such as the choice of underlying model class (e.g., LightGBM) and hyperparameter selection—have a bigger impact on performance than the ambiguity set or its radius. We illustrate via case studies how a data-driven understanding of distribution shifts can provide a new approach to algorithm development. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08298 .

papers.title: The Data-Driven Censored Newsvendor Problem
papers.authors: Chamsi Hssaine, Sean R. Sinclair
papers.abstract: We study a censored variant of the data-driven newsvendor problem, where the decision maker must select an ordering quantity that minimizes expected overage and underage costs based only on offline censored sales data rather than historical demand realizations. Our goal is to understand how the degree of historical demand censoring affects the performance of any learning algorithm for this problem. To isolate this impact, we adopt a distributionally robust optimization framework, evaluating policies according to their worst-case regret over an ambiguity set of distributions. This set is defined by the largest historical order quantity (the observable boundary of the data set), and contains all distributions matching the true demand distribution up to this boundary while allowing them to be arbitrary afterward. We demonstrate a spectrum of achievability under demand censoring by deriving a natural necessary and sufficient condition under which vanishing regret is an achievable goal. In regimes in which it is not, we exactly characterize the information loss due to censoring: an insurmountable lower bound on the performance of any policy, even when the decision maker has access to infinitely many demand samples. We then leverage these sharp characterizations to propose a natural robust algorithm that adapts to the historical level of demand censoring. We derive finite-sample guarantees for this algorithm across all possible censoring regimes and show its near-optimality with matching lower bounds (up to polylogarithmic factors). We moreover demonstrate its robust performance via extensive numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world data sets. This paper was accepted by Wolfram Wiesemann, data science. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files

papers.title: Banking on a Corporate Rebrand
papers.authors: Matthew Jaremski, Kris James Mitchener, Kilian Rieder
papers.abstract: Firms often rebrand to counter negative shocks, but can it work? Using a historical natural experiment, we analyze a large sample of companies from the same industry (banking) that shared very similar names, but overwhelmingly decided to change them in response to a common, negative news shock. U.S. entry into World War I in 1917 created a sudden anti-German backlash against anything that invoked an association with the now enemy. The shock itself was thus orthogonal to bank fundamentals and pre-existing trends, but pushed banks to reconsider their brands. After 1917, the few German-named banks that kept their tainted names saw significant declines in assets, deposits, and market share relative to other banks. However, German-named banks that rebranded mitigated much of the negative shock. Specifically, German-named banks that adopted a new non-ethnic brand name avoided between 75% and 85% of the anti-German effect, and those that adopted a new patriotic brand name were able to neutralize it completely. Overall, we find that “crisis rebranding” paid off in our historical setting regardless of the chosen brand, with patriotic rebranding proving the most effective at offsetting the exogenous shock. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: K. J. Mitchener thanks the Ciocca Center for Entrepreneurship and Innovation at Santa Clara University for funding this research (Grant 2024-CIOG11). Any views expressed in this paper exclusively represent those of the authors and do not reflect the official viewpoint of the Oesterreichische Nationalbank, the European Central Bank, or the Eurosystem. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03635 .

papers.title: Comparing Factor Models Under Regime Switching
papers.authors: Shamim Ahmed, Cesare Robotti, Daniel Tsvetanov, Xiaoxia Ye
papers.abstract: We compare factor pricing models using the “test-asset irrelevance” result but under regime switching. We show that the unconditional squared Sharpe ratio measure is no longer appropriate for model comparison when returns are subject to regime shifts. However, conditional on a given regime, model comparison can be performed using the conditional squared Sharpe ratio metric. We find that the Fama-French six-factor model that employs a cash-based profitability factor, the Barillas-Shanken six-factor model, and the Stambaugh-Yuan four-factor model are jointly the best-performing models under the bull regime. However, no model performs significantly better than others under the bear regime. Importantly, these findings are robust to regime uncertainty. We also find that unconditional model rankings closely mirror those in bull markets, overstating the superiority of the models identified as best performing in expansions by ignoring the performance convergence across models that emerges in downturns. This underscores the importance of evaluating factor models conditional on market regimes. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.04942 .

papers.title: The Economics of Waste Valorization
papers.authors: Yuefeng Li, Zhongbin Wang, Shenghai Zhou
papers.abstract: As the spread of waste imposes substantial environmental and economic burdens, a newer operational strategy, waste valorization, is gaining attention. This approach transforms production-generated byproduct waste into valuable, distinct products, creating intricate production and demand interdependencies that traditional strategies like remanufacturing and coproduction cannot fully capture. In this study, we examine the impacts of these interdependencies within a two-stage stochastic production decision model to determine optimal production quantities under waste valorization. Our findings reveal that a higher waste valorization rate does not always benefit the manufacturer, especially if the waste incurs disposal costs. When product demands are uncorrelated, the manufacturer’s optimal profit can exhibit an inverse U-shaped relationship with the valorization rate, attaining its maximum at a moderate level that maintains a perfect balance in production. Conversely, when product demands are correlated, the manufacturer employs a “pool-to-center” strategy, using different pooling policies to smooth production quantities and minimize disparities with respect to the valorization rate. Surprisingly, as demand randomness or correlation intensifies, the optimal profit becomes M-shaped, with profit maximum shifting toward either low or high valorization rates, a phenomenon we term “go-to-extreme.” Although waste valorization can yield both economic and environmental benefits, we caution that a more efficient waste valorization process may lead to negative outcomes for both the manufacturer and the environment. This analysis not only sheds light on how waste valorization contributes to waste reduction and economic value, but also provides insights for production decision making.

papers.title: Insurers’ Investments and Insurance Prices
papers.authors: Benjamin Knox, Jakob Ahm Sørensen
papers.abstract: We develop a theory in which stable funding from insurance underwriting allows insurers to earn the liquidity premium on illiquid assets and pass part of it back to policyholders through lower prices. Consistent with the model’s predictions, we show empirically that (1) insurance prices are lower when the liquidity premium is higher, for both life insurers and property and casualty insurers. (2) In the cross-section, insurers with more stable funding earn higher expected returns and set lower prices. (3) It is specifically the part of expected returns driven by stable funding that passes through to prices. The findings highlight the value of insurance underwriting as a stable source of funding, with benefits that flow back to policyholders. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: The authors acknowledge support from the FRIC Center for Financial Frictions [Grant DNRF102]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.09038 .

papers.title: Can Voluntary Corporate Transparency Curb Corruption? Community-Level Evidence from Oil and Gas Fields in Africa
papers.authors: Shirley S. Tang, Daniel Walter Elfenbein, Tatenda Marume Geofrey Pasipanodya
papers.abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substant

papers.title: Incumbents’ Alliances and (Non-)Adaptation During the Pre-Commercialization Stage of a New Technology
papers.authors: Jung‐Hyun Suh, J. P. Eggers
papers.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.

papers.title: Wrongdoers or Saviors? CEO Activism, Media Partisanship, and the Media’s Construction of CEO Infamy and Celebrity
papers.authors: G. Alessandra Rizzi, Vilmos F. Misangyi
papers.abstract: This study advances research on social evaluations by theorizing how partisan media construct CEO infamy through dramaturgical logics distinct from those underlying CEO celebrity. Moving beyond conceptualizations of infamy as merely negative celebrity, we argue that infamy emerges through simple melodramatic narratives casting CEOs as wrongdoers, whereas celebrity involves more complex dramatized narratives portraying CEOs as saviors. Focusing on CEOs’ liberal sociopolitical activism—a visible, ideologically-charged action that departs from conventional executive roles—we theorize that this behavior generates divergent constructions in partisan media: infamy in conservative outlets and celebrity in liberal outlets. We further argue that activism more readily generates infamy than celebrity because melodramatic narratives are simpler to construct and negative deviance is more readily perceived than positive deviance. We examine two moderators of these relationships. Firm performance differentially shapes these constructions, with poorer performance intensifying conservative-media infamy and stronger performance amplifying liberal-media celebrity. CEO social media engagement, conversely, attenuates both by constraining traditional media’s narrative discretion and reducing activism’s newsworthiness. We develop an LLM-based annotation system capturing CEO-directed sentiment, role attributions, and dramaturgical narratives in media articles. Analyzing 91,608 articles covering 705 S&P 500 CEOs across 45 ideologically polarized U.S. media outlets between 2016 and 2022, we find broad support for our hypotheses across our main and extensive supplemental analyses. Our findings advance understanding of CEO infamy and social evaluations more generally by revealing how partisan medi

papers.title: The Emergence of Psychological Safety or its Mirage
papers.authors: Patricia Satterstrom, Michaela June Kerrissey
papers.abstract: Leaders often strive to foster psychological safety in teams, and yet it may not emerge. This study builds grounded theory on how psychological safety emerges, or not, on teams. We draw on longitudinal ethnographic data from a matched pair case study of two teams over two years, including verbatim meeting transcripts that elicit the micro-processes affecting psychological safety and interviews that elucidate team members’ interpretations. We identify an illusion initially present on both teams in which surface markers of psychological safety existed but team members nonetheless continued to avoid interpersonal risk—what we call a psychological safety mirage. This occurred because external pressures on leaders spurred them to take self-protective actions that inadvertently reinforced interpersonal risk, despite their continued efforts to invite contributions. One team was eventually able to break from this mirage through a three-phase de-risking process that facilitated psychological safety emergence: (1) collectively recognizing the underlying risk faced by team members, (2) de-risking contributions by offering opportunities to build skills, through which safety was demonstrated and reinforced, and (3) enacting psychological safety, with all team members contributing, reinforcing, and sharing in the benefits of reduced interpersonal risk. This paper advances theory on psychological safety by conceptualizing a team-level de-risking process model that facilitates its emergence and by characterizing its mirage.

papers.title: How Firms Respond to Carbon Taxation
papers.authors: Arzi Adbi, Xiaoteng Wu
papers.abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

papers.title: Effortful vs. Opportunistic Consumption of Discretionary Time: How Time-Reporting Decisions Influence Extra-Role Effort
papers.authors: Sophie Maussen
papers.abstract: Employees often work under incomplete contracts, performing both contracted in-role tasks and valuable but noncontracted extra-role activities. Once employees have completed in-role tasks, discretionary time remains, which they may allocate to extra-role activities or consume opportunistically. This study examines how managers’ time-reporting decisions, as a less intrusive form of control, affect subordinates’ effort-allocation decisions. I propose two opposing predictions. First, managers’ control implementations may signal distrust, resulting in more opportunism and thus less extra-role effort. Second, I identify value signaling as a novel theoretical mechanism through which time-reporting decisions may increase extra-role effort. The main experiment manipulated two factors: the type of time report (aggregated versus disaggregated) and its implementation source (managerial choice versus random assignment) to isolate signaling effects from monitoring effects. Results reveal that when managers choose not to implement disaggregated time reporting—that is, reports that make discretionary time salient—subordinates significantly reduce their extra-role effort. Structural equation modeling shows that value signaling outweighs distrust signaling in driving employees’ effort-allocation decisions. In contrast, when the time-reporting format is randomly assigned, effort remains unchanged, underscoring the signaling role of managerial choice. An additional online experiment shows directionally consistent results with the main experiment. These findings reveal a hidden cost of not controlling and contribute to the literature on incomplete contracts, slack resources, and input-based controls in modern work contexts. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Funding:

papers.title: Colleagues That Work Together Move Together: How Co-Moving Among Newcomers Affects Individual and Team Performance
papers.authors: Emma Y. Zhao, Catherine Theresa Shea, Siyuan Li
papers.abstract: As teams and team membership become more dynamic, colleagues from the same prior team increasingly transition together to a new team as a cohort: a phenomenon known as co-moving. Drawing on theories of shared team experience and team receptivity, we develop a multilevel, multitheory, and multiperiod model to examine how co-moving affects individual and team performance. We theorize that co-movers carry forward proximal shared team experience that they can leverage immediately to support their own performance relative to solo movers, who must build new working relationships. However, we also theorize that co-movers’ proximal shared team experience hinders team performance, although these detrimental effects attenuate over time. We test our theory using archival data from the National Basketball Association, supplemented by qualitative interviews with individuals involved in professional basketball. Our findings reveal that co-movers exhibit better individual performance than solo movers on their new teams and in our robustness checks we find that greater shared tenure on the prior team further enhances this advantage. At the team level, teams with co-movers perform worse than teams with solo movers, and we find partial support that this disadvantage attenuates over time. Additional analyses show that co-movers’ individual performance advantage persists over time in the new team. The findings from our interviews illuminate how these processes unfold both on and off the court. Our research contributes to the literature on shared team experience and newcomer integration by highlighting a multilevel tradeoff: Although co-moving benefits individuals, it can initially undermine collective performance.

papers.title: The Role of Supply Chains in Climate Disclosure
papers.authors: Pietro Bonetti, Yang (Ellen) EN, Igor Kadach, Gaizka Ormazábal
papers.abstract: We examine the role of supply chains in shaping the public disclosure of climate information. We leverage a unique empirical setting enabled by CDP—the leading platform for corporate climate risk reporting—which allows customers to demand climate‐related information from their suppliers. Using a large international sample of customer–supplier pairs, we find a positive association between customers’ information demand and suppliers’ public disclosure on the CDP. While the estimated association is modest on average, it exhibits substantial cross‐sectional variation reflecting the disclosure incentives of both customers and suppliers as well as their relative bargaining power. We also find descriptive evidence consistent with one potential implication of the documented association for corporate decision‐making: shifts in supply network relationships toward greener and more transparent suppliers. Overall, our findings contribute to ongoing debates on how to foster climate disclosure.

papers.title: Intertemporal Dynamics of Cost Asymmetry
papers.authors: Eti Einhorn, Efrat Shust
papers.abstract: We study the intertemporal dynamics of asymmetric cost behavior in a competitive setting. Our analysis delves into the primitives of cost asymmetry and explores its dynamic evolution over time. The analysis yields the result that cost behavior is asymmetric by default and path‐dependent, transpiring as cost stickiness following prior resource expansion and taking the form of cost anti‐stickiness after previous resource contraction. The analysis further suggests that the magnitude of cost asymmetry, either stickiness or anti‐stickiness, is decreasing in demand uncertainty and competition intensity, increasing in adjustment costs and time discounting, and greater for small demand shocks than for large demand shocks. By highlighting cost asymmetry as a dynamic, rather than static, phenomenon, and by providing new, testable predictions regarding the direction and magnitude of cost asymmetry across firms and over time, our results offer theoretical grounding for the empirical cost asymmetry literature and may also help investors and other stakeholders interpret cost behavior in light of firms' recent history of expansion or contraction and their competitive environment.

papers.title: Labor Market Tightness and the Reversal of Inequality Trends in Germany
papers.authors: Christian Dustmann, Martin Friedrich, Carl Gergs, Uta Schönberg
papers.abstract: Germany experienced a sharp rise in wage inequality over the two decades leading up to the Great Recession. However, a remarkable trend reversal occurred in 2010—well before the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015—when wages at the bottom of the distribution began to grow more rapidly than those higher up. This paper attributes the reversal to an increasingly tight labor market after the Great Recession, supported by strong domestic demand, and operating through several interrelated and mutually reinforcing channels. Consistent with this hypothesis, job-to-job transition rates and between-job wage growth rose markedly after the recession, especially for workers at the lower rungs of the job ladder. Concurrently, workers increasingly moved from low-paying to higher-paying firms, compressing the worker-weighted distribution of firm wage premia. Tighter labor markets also reduced assortative matching between workers and firms, lowered the skill premium, and weakened firms’ monopsony power.

papers.title: Collusion through Common Leadership
papers.authors: Alejandro Herrera-Caicedo, Jessica Jeffers, Elena Prager
papers.abstract: This paper studies whether common leadership, defined as two firms sharing executives or board directors, contributes to collusion. Using an explicit measure of labor market collusion from unsealed court evidence, we find that the probability of collusion between two firms increases by 11 percentage points after the onset of common leadership, a ninefold increase over the baseline rate. These results are not driven by closeness of product or labor market competition. Our findings are consistent with the increasing attention toward common leadership under Clayton Act Section 8. Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

papers.title: Beliefs and the Incentive Effects of Preferential College Admissions: Evidence from an Experiment and a Structural Model
papers.authors: Michela Maria Tincani, Fabian Kosse, Enrico Miglino

papers.title: Competition in Markups: A Theory of the Lerner Index in Networks and General Equilibrium
papers.authors: Lingxuan Wu
papers.abstract: What determines demand elasticities and markups in production networks, where firms' demand and pricing are interdependent? I propose competition in markups, an equilibrium concept in which firms choose markups, taking other firms' markups as given. In partial equilibrium with vertical structures, it links upstream demand elasticities to downstream characteristics without backward induction and ties pass-through to the curvature of final demand. In general equilibrium with arbitrary industry networks, it microfounds firms' demand elasticities and markups through their within-industry market shares and four industry-level network statistics---cycle, substitution in production, substitution in consumption, and consumer-price impact. Empirical analysis of Compustat firms from 1997 to 2019 confirms the predicted variation of industry demand elasticities and firm markups. Relative to an exogenous-markup benchmark, endogenous markups dampen the aggregate TFP impact of a productivity shock to an industry's largest firm by 6% for the median industry, and by up to 48% across industries.

papers.title: The Impact of Commercial Real Estate Regulations on U.S. Output
papers.authors: Fil Babalievsky, Kyle Herkenhoff, Lee E. Ohanian, Edward C. Prescott
papers.abstract: Commercial real estate accounts for about 20% of the U.S. capital stock and is highly regulated. Yet relatively little is known about how these regulations affect economic activity or consumer welfare. This paper develops a spatial general equilibrium model of the U.S. economy with commercial real estate regulations and congestion effects, the latter providing a rationale for such regulations. The model constructs a panel of commercial real estate regulation indices for major U.S. metropolitan areas by exploiting variation in the share of parcel value attributable to land versus structures in tax assessor records compiled by Cotality. We find that a moderate relaxation of commercial real estate building regulations across U.S. cities generates large allocative efficiency gains, increasing output by 2.7% to 5.3% and welfare by 2.8% to 8.0% of lifetime consumption. We then extract the component of our regulatory indices that covaries with specific zoning attributes in LightBox data, including zoning height limits, and use it to simulate local deregulation policies. Relaxing height limits in New York City raises its output by 2.9%.

papers.title: The role of financial markets in the unraveling of credit
papers.authors: Elena Asparouhova, Peter L. Bossaerts, Anh Tran
papers.abstract: We investigate how long an insolvent debtor can avoid default when survival benefits creditors collectively, but individual creditors gain from early repayment. Standard theory predicts that debt is not rolled over and default is immediate. Previous experimental studies of related environments suggest that liquidation is delayed, and we confirm that pattern here. We then study how secondary markets affect outcomes. The duration of the credit pool is unaffected, but average net payoffs increase because claims are held longer before redemption. With markets, realized payoff dispersion is significantly higher. Prices do not predict liquidation timing but correlate with realized payoffs.

papers.title: The Effect of Non‐US Tax Authority Monitoring on Income Shifting by Affiliates of US Multinationals: Evidence From EDGAR Search Activity
papers.authors: Sabrina Chi, Anh Persson, Terry J. Shevlin, Oktay Urcan
papers.abstract: Governments worldwide are concerned that multinational enterprises (MNEs) shift profits across borders to avoid taxes. While prior research shows that home‐country tax enforcement can reduce tax avoidance, far less is known about whether foreign tax authorities (FTAs) can constrain income shifting by MNE affiliates. We measure FTA monitoring using data on FTAs' downloads of US MNEs' annual reports filed with the SEC. We find that FTA monitoring is more intensive in higher‐tax‐rate countries with a larger MNE presence, consistent with those jurisdictions facing stronger incentives to monitor income shifting. More importantly, we find that monitoring by an affiliate's local tax authority does not systematically reduce income shifting by US MNE affiliates, whereas aggregate monitoring in the MNE group affects an affiliate even when its own local FTA is not observably monitoring it. This result is consistent with a spillover effect of FTA monitoring. This association is stronger when FTAs operate under information‐exchange treaties, when company disclosures are more detailed, and when enforcement capacity is greater. We also find positive associations between aggregate FTA monitoring and subsequent tax avoidance and tax settlements of US MNEs. Our findings suggest monitoring by multiple FTAs effectively combats MNE tax avoidance and have implications for how tax administrations design and coordinate monitoring efforts.

papers.title: Channeled Attention and Stable Errors
papers.authors: Tristan Gagnon-Bartsch, Matthew Rabin, Joshua Schwartzstein
papers.abstract: People persist in mistaken beliefs even in settings with high stakes, abundant data, and repeated opportunities to learn—settings where standard arguments imply they should correct their errors. We develop an attention-based framework for understanding why errors persist. When a person channels his attention through the lens of his potentially misspecified model, exposure to data is not the same as tracking the statistics necessary to tell him his model is wrong. A model is attentionally stable when the data the person deems relevant will, in the long run, fail to make the model look implausible. Models that erroneously rule things out—e.g., beliefs that a variable doesn’t matter or that a distinction doesn’t exist—tend to be attentionally stable because they divert attention away from data that would refute the models. Conversely, models that erroneously rule things in are less likely to be stable. Whether an error is discovered depends on the structure of the decision problem but is not tightly linked to its level of harm; arbitrarily costly errors can persist while trivially inexpensive ones may be detected. Nevertheless, no error is robust both to changes in the decision environment and to shocks that expand attention: every channeled-attention error is vulnerable to some perturbation that would reveal it. We use the framework to analyze the stability of psychological biases and empirical misconceptions, as well as to explain why fresh eyes catch mistakes, why people use overly coarse rather than overly fine categorizations, and why people recognize errors in others that they miss in themselves.

papers.title: When Insurers Exit: Climate Losses, Fragile Insurers, and Mortgage Markets
papers.authors: Parinitha Sastry, Ishita Sen, Ana-Maria Tenekedjieva
papers.abstract: This paper uses a range of natural experiments to show how mispricing of climate risk in mortgages and property insurance creates large taxpayer exposures and leads to excess credit flows to risky areas. Our central finding is that the government-sponsored enterprises’ (GSEs) policies for evaluating property insurers are a crucial source of this mispricing. We assemble a comprehensive new dataset on both mortgages and insurance to analyze these dynamics in Florida from 2009-2018. We begin by documenting a breakdown in the quality of insurance provision, with new under-capitalized and under-diversified insurers dominating insurance markets. These fragile insurers have high rates of insolvency, which we show causally increases mortgage defaults after natural disasters. We find that the GSEs’ reliance on third-party ratings of insurers leads them to accept insurance from companies at high risk of insolvency without pricing for it. This creates large taxpayer exposures, with an estimated 25% of the GSEs’ expected losses in Florida coming from insurance fragility. Most starkly, we show that private lenders strategically respond to the GSE mispricing. Mortgage denial rates are sensitive to insurance quality in the jumbo segment where loans are retained, but not in the conforming segment where loans are offloaded to the GSEs. This suggests that, all else equal, fewer conforming mortgages would have been originated if lenders screened insurance fragility as they do in jumbos.

papers.title: Connecting Common Ratio and Common Consequence Preferences
papers.authors: Christina McGranaghan, Kirby Nielsen, Ted O’Donoghue, Jason Somerville, Charles D. Sprenger

papers.title: Fertility and Family Leave Policies in Germany: Optimal Policy Design in a Dynamic Framework
papers.authors: Hanna Wang
papers.abstract: I develop and estimate a life-cycle discrete-choice model of fertility and female labour supply to study the optimal design of a range of child-related policies. First, I examine two German reforms that introduced wage-contingent parental leave payments and expanded access to low-cost public childcare. I find that both reforms raised completed fertility, with the parental leave reform having a particularly strong impact on highly educated women. Second, I solve for a budget-neutral optimal policy portfolio that maximizes either aggregate welfare or fertility, while ensuring that welfare and fertility do not decline for any education group. I consider four prominent child subsidies as well as the degree of tax jointness. My results show that optimal policy has the potential to increase welfare by 0.5% or fertility by 5.7%. While the solutions are qualitatively similar, they prioritize different policy instruments depending on the specific objective being targeted.

papers.title: Deadly Disease, Fear, and Ostracism in the Credit Market
papers.authors: Sumit D. Agarwal, Pengsheng Lin, Yupeng Lin, Ruichang Lu, Xiaojun Zhang
papers.abstract: This paper exploits the 2014 U.S. Ebola outbreak as a natural experiment to examine how fear distorts mortgage credit allocation. We find a 3.8-percentage-point increase in mortgage denial rates for Black applicants during the outbreak, despite negligible infection risk. Approved Black borrowers have stronger credit profiles and lower default rates, yet are less likely to receive loan modifications when delinquent. These effects are absent in algorithm-driven FinTech lending and reverse quickly postoutbreak—patterns inconsistent with statistical discrimination. Robustness tests rule out alternative explanations related to political cycles, labor market impacts, applicant pool composition changes, and bank financial conditions. Consistent with diagnostic expectation theory, higher exposure to Ebola fear does not result in a significant learning effect during the COVID-19 pandemic. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Funding: S. Agarwal acknowledges the financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72495154]. Y. Lin gratefully acknowledges financial support from the NUS Research Grant [Grants A-8001725 and A-8004426]. R. Lu and X. Zhang acknowledge the financial support of the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 71903005, 72402005, and 72472001]. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01919 .

papers.title: Uncertainty Attitudes, Subjective Beliefs, and Decisions Under Uncertainty
papers.authors: Adeline Delavande, Jayant Vivek Ganguli, Friederike Mengel
papers.abstract: We conducted survey experiments to gather new data on uncertainty attitudes and subjective beliefs. Our survey targets a general population, focusing on health and financial decisions. We collect data on (i) individual attitudes toward risk and ambiguity, including individual-specific probability weighting and loss aversion, and (ii) individual probabilistic beliefs about events related to the decisions we consider. The joint availability of individual preference parameters and subjective beliefs allows us to study heterogeneity and cross-correlations across these parameters in depth and to estimate structural models of decision making under uncertainty that go beyond subjective expected utility. We find that both preferences and beliefs are highly heterogeneous. Compared with subjective expected utility, prospect theory combined with source-dependent probability weighting fits the data strictly better in some contexts and equally well in others. Prospect theory performs particularly well when the belief distribution is concentrated toward extreme values. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: A. Delavande acknowledges funding from the Economic and Social Research Council Research Centre on Micro-Social Change [Grants ES/L009153/1 and ES/S012486/1] and the National Institute on Aging [Grant P01AG008291]. J. Ganguli acknowledges research support from the Economic and Social Research Council [Grant ES/K00168X/1]. F. Mengel acknowledges support from the European Research Council [Grant DYNNET-805017]. Ethical approval was obtained by the Ethics Social Sciences subcommittee at the University of Essex in August 2015. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.

papers.title: Benefiting from Culture Wars: Resource Mobilization in Polarized Issue Domains
papers.authors: Ludovica Castiglia, Fabrizio Ferraro
papers.abstract: Organizations engaging with contested social issues may struggle to mobilize resources due to disapproval from hostile audiences. Yet, some may benefit from increased support from sympathetic audiences, leaving unclear when such support will outweigh opposition. We propose that variation in audience reactions depends partly on how contestation is structured. We theorize that ideological polarization—the extent to which opposing stances on an issue sort along ideological lines—may enhance resource mobilization in contested issue domains. As polarization increases, contested issues pit opposing identities against each other and heighten threats to sympathetic audiences’ worldviews. New ventures in more polarized domains may attract greater support as sympathetic audiences respond by investing in aligned ventures, a mechanism we term “compensatory investment.” This relationship strengthens under conditions that heighten identity threat: when issues are highly salient, making them central political battlegrounds, and when audiences on both sides rely on core moral foundations to evaluate the issue, so that disagreements are experienced as moral violations. Analyses of U.S.-based Kickstarter campaigns (2009–2020) support our predictions and provide evidence consistent with compensatory investment. Our study highlights polarization as a key source of issue heterogeneity, introduces the mechanism of compensatory investment, and specifies when polarization enhances resource mobilization.

papers.title: Growth Paths in Early Machine Learning Ventures: Technical Configuration and Competitive Advantage Over Time
papers.authors: Jack Lewis Fraser, Pınar Özcan
papers.abstract: Machine learning capabilities have become important strategic assets, yet little is known about how their technical characteristics affect the competitive advantage of the firms that build them. Through an inductive, multicase study tracking six early-stage machine learning ventures in an accelerator program, we explore how their phases of specialization and exploration may be constrained by properties of the underlying technology. Our findings show how training data, learning paradigms, and model outputs depend on one another and on the applications they serve, and how these relationships change over time. This interdependence shapes firms’ growth paths, alternately expanding or limiting the strategic options available to them. Characteristics that confer an early competitive advantage can constrain later growth. We discuss the implications for strategy research on competitive advantage and path dependence in machine learning ventures.

papers.title: Presidential Address: Human Finance: Incorporating Insights from the Life Sciences
papers.authors: Ulrike M. Malmendier
papers.abstract: Many of the key determinants of human behavior identified in the life sciences, such as stress response, impulse control, and mood regulation, remain absent from standard economic and finance models. This paper illustrates how such insights can enhance economic models in the context of inflation expectations. Combining a retrospective survey that elicits personal inflation histories with an experimental intervention that induces the reexperiencing of historic inflation, I show that physiological, emotional, and cognitive stress markers predict heightened inflation expectations and sharper memory recall, while also shaping personal economic narratives. These findings suggest novel policy tools to counter the persistent scars of economic distress and crisis experiences, for example, by designing experiences to provide predictability and control.

papers.title: Private debt versus bank debt in corporate borrowing
papers.authors: Sharjil Haque, Simon Mayer, Irina Stefanescu
papers.abstract: Using administrative bank loan-level data matched to private debt deals, we study the interaction between private and bank debt for a large segment of dual borrowers. These firms use private debt for investment and bank credit lines for liquidity insurance. Private debt carries higher spreads and commonly features flexible, equity-like terms that are associated with greater reliance on bank credit lines. Relative to bank-only borrowers, dual borrowers obtain more and larger credit lines and draw them more intensively following liquidity shocks. Our findings suggest that private debt substitutes for bank term loans but complements banks’ provision of credit lines.

papers.title: Countercyclical Risk Aversion: Evidence from 10 Million Auto Insurance Transactions in China
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Huafeng Chen, Yinglu Deng, Pengfei Li, Hulai Zhang, Hao Zhou
papers.abstract: Whether risk aversion is time-varying and countercyclical is central to modern asset pricing, yet evidence remains limited and is based mainly on experimental, survey, or aggregate stock market data. We provide individual-level evidence from 10 million Chinese auto insurance contracts from 2011 to 2017, estimating policyholders’ risk aversion from deductible choices. We find that risk aversion is time-varying and countercyclical. The estimates are negatively related to lottery and stock trading, positively related to insurance sales and bond trading, and vary with psychological factors, including seasonal mood, “zodiac year,” and calendar events.

papers.title: U.S. Banks’ Exposures to Climate Transition Risks
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Hyeyoon Jung, João A. C. Santos, Lee Seltzer
papers.abstract: We propose a new approach to estimate banks’ credit exposures to transition risks that combines sectoral effects of climate policies from general equilibrium (GE) models with historical information on loans’ default risks. At worst, estimated exposures reach 14% of bank loan portfolio values. Accounting for historic loan payoff structures reduces exposures to 0.5%–2%. Exposures can increase by 3–5 percentage points due to aggregate economic shocks. Analyses surrounding climate transition events suggest our estimates can serve as an upper bound on banks’ transition risk exposures. Highlighting our measure’s novelty, emissions explain at most 60% of variation in banks’ exposures.

papers.title: How resolving enforcement ambiguity reduces tax compliance
papers.authors: Eric Floyd, Michael Hallsworth, John A. List, Robert Metcalfe, Kristian Rotaru, Ivo Vlaev
papers.abstract: Tax authorities often leave the consequences of non-compliance unspecified. We examine how disclosing those consequences affects tax payment and income reporting in four experiments. In a field experiment with HM Revenue and Customs, letters randomized to more than 200,000 taxpayers with outstanding income-tax debts increased payment when they warned of unspecified further action. Messages specifying financial or administrative costs did not produce the same benefit. An online payment experiment with 2050 taxpayers across fourteen conditions, including 1194 in the principal factorial design, found that revealing the maximum fine lowered the stated likelihood of paying. The reduction occurred at both modest and severe revealed maxima. It also occurred among participants who learned that the fine exceeded their prior estimate, contrary to the prediction from belief updating. An incentivized experiment with 827 participants extended the effect to income declarations with money at stake, although declarations differed between the two disclosed maxima in this setting. A laboratory experiment with 239 participants recorded differences in pupil dilation across enforcement messages without detectable differences in measured visual attention. Together, the findings suggest that ambiguity about enforcement consequences contributes to compliance. The physiological evidence is consistent with an affective account of this relationship. Disclosing a maximum penalty can therefore have a behavioral cost that tax authorities should consider when communicating enforcement policy.

papers.title: When AI thinks about culture: comparing language-based and empirical measures of individualism–collectivism
papers.authors: Plamen Akaliyski, Wolfgang Messner
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate cultural insights, yet little is known about their cultural expertise and the extent to which their outputs replicate or correct for cultural stereotypes. This study compares country-level estimates of individualism–collectivism (I-C) derived from five different LLMs with a recently validated I-C index based on nationally representative surveys. The LLM-based estimates correlate highly with the survey-based index (up to r = 0.874) but also exhibit systematic deviation from the benchmark: Western societies are consistently overestimated on individualism, while Confucian East Asian societies are underestimated. Statistically, the type of benchmark-relative deviations suggests group-specific baseline distortions rather than random noise, with smaller and older models showing weaker alignment. Moreover, the deviations are systematically aligned with Hofstede’s original I-C rankings, suggesting that LLM-generated cultural representations may reflect information from legacy cultural frameworks alongside contemporary empirical patterns. These findings demonstrate both the potential and the risks of using LLMs as cultural interpreters. In consequential settings, LLM-generated cultural insights should be used responsibly—with calibration, human oversight, and awareness of potential biases. Used uncritically, they risk reinforcing outdated narratives that misdirect academic research and managerial decisions.

papers.title: Optimal Policy Rules in HANK
papers.authors: Alisdair McKay, Christian K. Wolf
papers.abstract: We characterize optimal policy rules in a business-cycle model with nominal rigidities and heterogeneous households. The policymaker has access to two instruments: the short-term nominal rate, and lump-sum transfer payments. A policymaker with a traditional dual mandate that targets aggregates uses the same policy rule as is optimal in the textbook New Keynesian model. We then consider a policymaker with a distributional objective. The optimal policy rule now contains an additional term, reflecting the effects of the policymaker’s instruments on consumption inequality. Since, in our model, monetary policy only has very limited distributional effects, this additional term does not materially change optimal monetary policy. Fiscal stimulus payments, on the other hand, have strongly progressive effects and are thus well-suited to cushion the distributional effects of cyclical fluctuations.

papers.title: Using Financial Accounting Information to Estimate the Income Shifting of US Multinationals
papers.authors: Scott Dyreng, Robert Hills, Kevin Markle
papers.abstract: Existing estimates of how much income US multinational corporations (MNCs) shift out of the United States differ dramatically, and most cannot identify which specific firms do the shifting. We use data from firms' public financial reports to derive firm‐year estimates of US MNCs' outbound income shifting. We find that aggregate US outbound income shifting is substantially lower than widely cited macroeconomic‐based estimates, with the gap driven primarily by double counting of foreign income in macroeconomic data rather than by differences in firms' sensitivity to tax rates. Income shifting is also highly concentrated among a small number of firms, primarily in intangible‐intensive industries such as computers and pharmaceuticals, while most MNCs shift little or no income. This concentration implies that size‐based thresholds embedded in the OECD's Pillar 2 and the US corporate alternative minimum tax will capture the most active income shifters but may also impose compliance burdens on many firms that shift minimal income. These findings have direct implications for policy‐makers designing international tax rules, tax authorities prioritizing audit resources toward high‐risk income shifters, and investors and lenders assessing MNCs' tax‐related exposures.

papers.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Sales Productivity: Field Experiments in Online Retail
papers.authors: Lu Fang, Zhe Yuan, Kaifu Zhang, Dante Donati, Miklós Sárváry
papers.abstract: We quantify the short-term impact of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) on sales performance through a series of large-scale randomized field experiments involving millions of users and products at a leading crossborder online retail platform. Over 2023–2024, the platform integrated GenAI into seven business workflows spanning customer service, consumer-product matching, advertising, and seller services. We find that GenAI adoption increases sales in most workflows, with effects ranging from no detectable impact to 16.3% depending on GenAI’s marginal contribution relative to baseline firm practices. Across the four GenAI applications with positive sales effects, the implied annual incremental value is roughly $5 per consumer—an economically meaningful impact given the retailer’s scale and the early stage of GenAI adoption. The gains operate primarily through higher conversion rates rather than larger cart values, consistent with GenAI improving the shopping experience by reducing search, information, communication, and personalization frictions. Importantly, these effects are not associated with worse postpurchase outcomes as product return rates and customer ratings do not deteriorate. Finally, we document substantial demand-side heterogeneity, with larger gains for less experienced consumers. Our findings provide novel, large-scale causal evidence on how GenAI shapes sales productivity in online retail, highlighting both its immediate value and broader potential. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: L. Fang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72501258 and 72192803], the Major Special Project in Philosophy and Social Sciences of the Ministry of Education of China [Grant 2026JZD

papers.title: The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
papers.authors: Rebecca L. Mitchell, James Garrett Matusik, Nicholas A. Hays
papers.abstract: Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

papers.title: Shadow banks on the rise: Evidence across market segments
papers.authors: Kim Fe Cramer, Pulak Ghosh, Nirupama Kulkarni, Nishant Vats
papers.abstract: This paper examines the comparative advantages of shadow banks across market segments. Combining credit bureau data on retail loans in India with weather shocks as a proxy for credit demand, we show that Fintechs respond more in uncollateralized markets. In contrast, non-Fintech shadow banks exhibit stronger responsiveness in collateralized markets. Exploiting geographic heterogeneity in the adoption of digital payments, we identify technology as the key advantage for Fintechs. Leveraging four natural experiments, we document the significance of lower regulation for non-Fintech shadow banks. Our results suggest that the comparative advantage of shadow banks differs across market segments.

papers.title: Are the Hedges of Funds Green?
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Huan Kuang, Bing Liang, Mila Getmansky Sherman, Tianyi Qu
papers.abstract: Over the past decade, hedge funds have increasingly embraced green investing. We develop a novel return-based measure of fund greenness and find that greener funds earn higher average returns, consistent with capturing a positive green premium, and are associated with lower risks, especially during adverse periods. We further show that performance gains are greatest among directional funds, whereas risk reduction is most pronounced among nondirectional funds. We also provide evidence that managers of these funds exhibit superior green investment skills through green stock selection and green factor timing. Finally, investors reward greener hedge funds only when they demonstrate strong performance.

papers.title: Why Do Union Jobs Pay More? New Evidence from Matched Employer-Employee Data
papers.authors: Pierre‐Loup Beauregard, Thomas Lemieux, Derek Messacar, Raffaele Saggio
papers.abstract: We use Canadian matched employer-employee data to assess the sources of the union pay premium. After controlling for worker heterogeneity using the two-way fixed effects approach of Abowd, Kramarz, and Margolis (AKM), we find that unionized firms pay about 15 log points more than non-unionized firms. Forty percent of this gap is linked to productivity differences between unionized and non-unionized firms as measured by value added per worker. The remaining gap reflects unions’ ability to extract more rents for workers. Our estimates imply that unions raise pay among unionized workers by around 9 log points, with considerable heterogeneity by industry and firm birth cohorts. The union effect grows to about 11 log points in an extension of the AKM approach where unions also affect the returns to unobservable worker characteristics.

papers.title: Political uncertainty, social legitimacy, and nonmarket strategy
papers.authors: Jonathan P. Doh
papers.abstract: The Decade Award–winning article by Darendeli and Hill (2016) presents a novel yet nuanced approach to the question of whether and how foreign firms can strategically navigate a volatile and unpredictable political environment. Their 2026 retrospective builds on their earlier contribution by showing how their insights have contributed to a number of contemporary IB research streams, including those addressing political risk, political action, and political ties. Going beyond their earlier contribution, in the retrospective, they describe the relational and physical pillars of social legitimacy (Darendeli & Hill, 2026). They then assess the efficacy of their original perspective in an environment characterized by heightened geopolitical conflict and political polarization. Finally, they develop a model that delineates four strategic approaches to legitimacy building in host countries. In this commentary, I offer perspectives that complement and extend their contributions by discussing (1) the nature of political uncertainty and the use of real options in responding to that uncertainty, (2) the literature on substantive versus symbolic CSR and how that might further extend some of their insights, and (3) research regarding when and how multinational enterprises provide public goods and services typically provided by government. I conclude by outlining how Darendeli and Hill’s (2016, 2026) insights have relevance for contemporary practice and policy.

papers.title: Is Informed Short Selling Concentrated in Family Firms? Evidence from a Reinvestigation
papers.authors: Ferhat Akbas, MINJIE HUANG, Felix Meschke
papers.abstract: We reinvestigate Anderson, Reeb, and Zhao's findings that informed short selling is unique to family firms and driven by information leakage from internal disputes. Using the same firm sample and more comprehensive short‐selling data, we find that short selling predicts future returns in both family and nonfamily firms. We also find no significant difference in abnormal short selling before negative earnings announcements. In extended sample periods, short selling continues to predict returns for nonfamily firms under both ownership‐based and familial‐link definitions. Overall, our evidence suggests that short sellers are broadly informed and that family firms are not uniquely vulnerable.

papers.title: China Walls
papers.authors: Tomy Lee, Daniel Nathan, Chaojun Wang
papers.abstract: We evaluate the enforcement of China Walls—information barriers within conglomerates. We focus on July 2018, when the SEC tightened enforcement around broker-dealer subsidiaries, and on the 25 million Israeli Shekel trades over 2018–2024. Our difference-in-differences design compares a dealer’s affiliate, connected, and unrelated funds on days when the dealer likely obtained valuable information. Before July 2018, dealers share information with their affiliate and connected funds. After July 2018: the sharing ceases only with the affiliate funds; price discovery slows; trading costs fall for affiliate funds and rise for other funds. Tightly enforced walls eliminated 99.0% of affiliate funds’ event-day profits.

papers.title: Economic Fundamentals and Short-Run Exchange Rate Prediction: A Machine-Learning Perspective
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Ilias Filippou, David E. Rapach, Mark Taylor, Guofu Zhou
papers.abstract: The exchange rate predictability puzzle—that fundamentals fail to forecast short-horizon exchange rate movements out of sample—has long resisted resolution. We show that fundamentals do matter, but their effects vary with global financial conditions. Using a rich set of country characteristics interacted with global state variables and machine-learning techniques to handle the high-dimensional data, we document that interactions between country characteristics and foreign exchange market volatility are particularly important, consistent with a “flight to fundamentals” during periods of financial stress. Our forecasts deliver substantial economic value and offer new insight into the carry trade.

papers.title: Housing Yields
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Stefano Colonnello, Roberto Marfè, Qizhou Xiong
papers.abstract: We build a granular data set of residential property yields using rental and sale listings from a major German real estate platform. With more than 1.5 million property-level rent-to-price ratios, we document a novel heterogeneity puzzle. About two-fifths of yield dispersion remains unexplained after controlling for extensive observable property characteristics and postal code-level time-varying factors using fixed effects.
