When we absorb finer neighborhood amenities through richer fixed effects, the unexplained share remains close to one-third. This evidence points to the importance of investors’ beliefs and preferences—rather than several alternative explanations we test—as sources of heterogeneity in risk premia.

papers.title: A Conditional Shrinkage Method for Portfolio Selection
papers.authors: Nathan Lassance, Alberto Martín-Utrera
papers.abstract: We develop a conditional shrinkage method for portfolio selection. Our approach builds on a decomposition of the mean-variance portfolio into the 1/N portfolio and an alpha component that offers large efficiency gains but is exposed to substantial estimation risk. We show that a linear shrinkage covariance matrix determines the portfolio’s relative exposure to these components, and our framework allows the shrinkage intensity to depend on a state variable that predicts their relative performance. We implement the method using investor sentiment and find that the estimated relation predominantly leads to greater shrinkage toward 1/N when sentiment is low, improving mean-variance efficiency while maintaining low turnover. JEL Classification: G11, G12.

papers.title: The DNA of neuroticism and financial decisions
papers.authors: Richard W. Sias, Laura T. Starks, Harry J. Turtle
papers.abstract: A polygenic score (PGS) capturing genetic predisposition toward neuroticism predicts heterogeneity in risk aversion, return beliefs, and stock market participation. This approach addresses key methodological and interpretive concerns associated with phenotypic measures of neuroticism. Risk aversion and return beliefs are important, but incomplete, channels linking the neuroticism PGS to stock market participation. The neuroticism PGS also predicts heterogeneity in demographic and behavioral characteristics previously shown to influence financial choices. These characteristics serve as key channels through which the genetic propensity for neuroticism shapes financial choices.

papers.title: The Anti‐SLAPP Statutes and Corporate Environmental Policies
papers.authors: Kevin C. W. Chen, Zhihong Chen, Chengzhu Sun
papers.abstract: We examine whether legal protection for civic participation affects corporate pollution. Polluters may deter public discipline through strategic lawsuits. Anti‐SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) statutes mitigate this threat by enabling prompt dismissal and recovery of legal costs. Using a difference‐in‐differences design, we find that enacting an anti‐SLAPP statute in a state significantly reduces toxic emissions from that state by increasing local public pressure. The reduction is greater when the statutes provide stronger protection, when local stakeholders have stronger incentives and abilities to discipline polluters, and when local public pressure increases more after the enactment. Plants lower emissions by improving abatement rather than by reducing output or relocating emissions. Our paper underscores the role of legal protection in environmental governance and informs policy debates over anti‐SLAPP legislation.

papers.title: Does the Salience of Climate-Related Risk Affect Asset Prices?
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Cloé Garnache
papers.abstract: Using regression discontinuity and difference-in-differences designs to compare prices of California homes across a new wildfire risk zone boundary, I identify null effects in the immediate vicinity of the new risk zone boundary. In contrast, prices of homes newly assigned to a riskier zone drop by 5.7% further away from the new risk zone boundary. These findings suggest that households do not respond to the risk salience triggered by the new risk zone assignment. Instead, they update their risk beliefs in response to rezoning in a way that is consistent with the actual wildfire risk.

papers.title: Does Climate Change Affect Firm Sales? Identifying Supply Effects
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Cláudia Custódio, Miguel A. M. M. Ferreira, Emilia García-Appendini, Adrian Lam
papers.abstract: We estimate the supply-side effects of climate change on firm sales by exploiting variation in local average temperature across suppliers of the same client. A 1°C increase in temperature leads to a 2.5% decline in annual sales. This effect is nonlinear, with stronger effects among suppliers in regions with the largest temperature increases and in cooler regions. Manufacturing and heat-sensitive industries are more affected, consistent with a reduction in labor productivity and labor supply when local temperatures rise. Nondiversified and financially constrained firms are also more affected, supporting the importance of operational and financial flexibility in adapting to climate change.

papers.title: Local Returns and Beliefs about the Stock Market
papers.authors: Tobin Hanspal, Clemens Wagner
papers.abstract: We show that investors extrapolate from recent stock returns of locally headquartered firms when forming beliefs about aggregate stock market outcomes. While it may be optimal to rely on local information, these effects are unrelated to how informative local returns are on predictions of aggregate outcomes. Evidence from a sample of retail investors suggests this belief extrapolation is driven by investors’ own holdings of local firms. Our findings suggest that beliefs about information contained in public signals vary systematically with geography, and are an important component of local biases in equity markets.

papers.title: The Cost of Regulatory Inaction: Evidence from IFRS Nonadoption
papers.authors: Miao Liu, Wanrong Xu, Rachel Xi Zhang
papers.abstract: Although extensive research examines the costs and benefits of adopting new disclosure regulations, little addresses the consequences of regulatory inaction. We investigate whether firms in nonadopting countries incur additional information losses, beyond the forgone benefits, when their foreign peers adopt International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS). Nonadopters bear an absolute liquidity cost as foreign peers adopt IFRS, consistent with negative externalities from IFRS and accompanying reforms. Exploiting heterogeneity across nonadopting countries, we observe more pronounced liquidity declines among firms with greater institutional ownership overlap with IFRS peers. This effect appears more pronounced when IFRS peers are domiciled in countries with concurrent enforcement reforms or greater comparability improvements. Further evidence shows shared intermediaries—investors and analysts—reduce information production for nonadopters as other firms in their portfolios adopt IFRS. Overall, regulatory inaction degrades information environments: resources shift to the new regime, worsening liquidity for firms in the old regime. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from commercial sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: G1; K22; M41; M48.

papers.title: Board–CEO Trust and Concealing Adverse News
papers.authors: Kee‐Hong Bae, Sadok El Ghoul, Zhaoran Gong, Omrane Guedhami, Lixin Nancy Su
papers.abstract: We investigate how generalized trust, a culturally rooted belief in the trustworthiness of unfamiliar others, influences board oversight. Using an ancestry-based measure of board–CEO trust based on ancestral origins and bilateral trust scores across countries, we find a significant positive relation between board–CEO trust and stock price crash risk, indicating higher bad-news hoarding. This relation remains robust across alternative crash risk measures, sample specifications, and trust measures. Firms with high board–CEO trust exhibit more asymmetric stock market reactions to good news versus bad news and a higher likelihood of material restatements. Analyses of insider trading patterns show that directors in high-trust firms are less informed than CEOs about adverse developments, supporting lax board monitoring rather than collusion between directors and CEOs. Overall, the evidence suggests that culturally inherited trust can weaken board oversight and reduce corporate transparency, consistent with an underexplored governance friction even within well-structured boards. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the study. JEL Classifications: G14; G34; G41; M12.

papers.title: The Effect of Cost Elasticity Choice on Loss Reversal
papers.authors: Edmond Tapero, Dan Weiss
papers.abstract: Although the prevalence of losses has been increasing over the years, little is known about how managerial decisions lead to reversing losses back to profits. We find cost elasticity choices, implied by operating actions made in advance, significantly increase the likelihood of loss reversal. We show loss firms with high cost elasticity exhibit significantly higher long-term survival rates and are therefore less likely to exercise the abandonment option than loss firms with low cost elasticity. The contributions are twofold. First, the findings shed light on a mechanism underlying loss reversal. We extend the loss literature by promoting the understanding of how ex ante cost elasticity choices affect the likelihood of loss reversal. Second, the findings enrich the cost accounting literature by demonstrating a unique performance implication of a cost elasticity choice. Data Availability: The data used in this study are obtained from third-party subscription databases, Compustat and CRSP, as described in the text. JEL Classifications: M41.

papers.title: National Audit Oversight and Foreign Investment
papers.authors: James Justin Blann, Phillip T. Lamoreaux, Beverly J. Larson
papers.abstract: Public audit oversight bodies have become ubiquitous following the establishment of the U.S. PCAOB in 2002. However, despite their cost and prominence, little is known of their economic implications, if any. We examine the relation between establishment of public audit oversight bodies (POBs) and cross-border investment. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that after a country establishes a POB, the country attracts more foreign capital. Our results suggest that total foreign portfolio investment (FPI) increases by approximately $11 billion for the average country that establishes a POB. The impact of POBs on foreign investment is dependent on the effectiveness of the POB in improving audit quality and the strength of a country’s existing institutional environment. Our study provides evidence of real economic effects of public audit oversight around the world, which adds to the literature on auditor oversight and to the broader literature on economic consequences of regulation. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M42; M48; F21; L51; G15; G18.

papers.title: Does Free Speech Law Contribute to Corporate Social Responsibility Behavior? Empirical Evidence
papers.authors: Paul A. Griffin, Hyun A. Hong, Boochun Jung, S. Katie Moon, Ji Woo Ryou
papers.abstract: People’s right to free speech can have profound effects on how firms discharge their social and environmental responsibilities. We examine these effects by analyzing the impact of the staggered enactment of anti-SLAPP free speech laws across U.S. states on firms’ corporate social responsibility (CSR) behavior. We theorize that, following the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, firms enhance their CSR activities as an economically effective means to counter negative publicity from stakeholders. Supporting this idea, we find that firm CSR activity increases after the enactment of anti-SLAPP laws, accompanied by an increase in stakeholder criticism of firms’ social and environmental practices. Further, we observe an increase in the level of CSR disclosure. The link between anti-SLAPP law enactment and subsequent CSR engagement is stronger in states with more comprehensive anti-SLAPP protections than in those with weaker protections. Data Availability: From public sources identified in the study. Some may require a subscription. JEL Classifications: A13; D80; K15; K22; L21; M14; O32.

papers.title: Private Firm Disclosures and Public Firms' Debt Choice
papers.authors: Fengqin Chen, JEFFREY A. PITTMAN, Walid Saffar
papers.abstract: Analyzing a cross-country sample, we provide evidence implying that private firm disclosure transparency narrows information asymmetry, which, in turn, lowers public firms' reliance on bank debt. Channel tests help substantiate that private firm disclosure elicits this positive externality, evident in lower monitoring demand, lower borrowing costs, and higher credit rating quality. Cross-sectional results suggest that the impact of private firm transparency is larger when public firms suffer worse information opacity, private firm disclosures are more important to their public peers, and bond markets are more developed. In relying on the staggered implementation of electronic business registers as a plausibly exogenous shock and a simulated disclosure scope as the instrumental variable, we continue to find that private firm disclosures reduce public firms' bank debt reliance, helping to alleviate endogeneity threats. Data Availability Statement: The data used in this study are obtained from publicly available sources identified in the paper. JEL Classifications: G32; G21; M41.

papers.title: Target Firm Material Contract Redactions and Valuation in Acquisitions
papers.authors: Paul A. Griffin, Hyun A. Hong, Kyungran Lee, Ji Woo Ryou
papers.abstract: We study whether and how the SEC’s confidential treatment program, which allows firms to redact proprietary information from material contracts, affects valuation in corporate acquisitions. We find that friendly acquisitions of redacting targets generate significantly higher positive announcement returns for both targets and acquirers compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. These positive returns are also more pronounced when targets are likelier to hold valuable proprietary information. In addition, friendly acquisitions of redacting targets achieve better long-term performance and recognize fewer subsequent goodwill impairments compared with acquisitions of nonredacting targets. Our findings of a robust association between target firm material contract redactions and target and acquirer announcement returns are consistent with a dual disclosure perspective, whereby redaction preserves target proprietary value, which is transferred privately to the acquirer through due diligence. Data Availability: Data are available from public sources identified in the paper; some require a subscription. JEL Classifications: D8; M41; M48.

papers.title: Environmental, Social, and Governance Ratings of Environmental, Social, and Governance Index Providers
papers.authors: Sonakshi Agrawal, Lisa Yao Liu, Shivaram Rajgopal, Suhas A. Sridharan, Yifan Yan, Teri Lombardi Yohn
papers.abstract: We explore the role of ESG raters’ business models in the production of their ratings, noting that increasingly ESG raters not only produce ESG ratings but also construct and sell ESG indices. We examine whether index licensing incentives are associated with how ESG ratings relate to stock returns. By comparing ratings across raters for the same firm, we control for fundamental ESG performance. We find that raters with strong index licensing incentives assign higher ESG ratings to firms with better stock performance compared to raters with weaker licensing incentives, and that this association is concentrated among index-eligible firms. We further show that index construction is significantly associated with stock returns, and that the high-incentive rater adjusts its ratings following index composition changes, whereas the low-incentive rater does not. Our findings highlight the need for greater transparency in the incentives of ESG rating producers. JEL Classifications: G24; M14; M40; M41; M48; Q56.

papers.title: The Evolution of the Market for Corporate Control
papers.authors: Mike C. Burkart, Samuel Lee, Paul Voß
papers.abstract: We consider an informed large shareholder who can choose between making a takeover bid herself and initiating a sale to another acquirer. Such takeover activism complements direct takeovers because the very choice mitigates the asymmetric information problem, thereby improving efficiency. As more investors enter the market for corporate control, takeover activism increasingly replaces direct takeovers as the prevailing mode of disciplinary control change, matching the evolution in practice. Our model shows how this evolution, characterized by a symbiotic relationship between investor activism and private equity, arises to overcome asymmetric information and collective action problems through intermediated transactions.

papers.title: Launching for the “Greater Good”: Spillover Effect of ESG Funds
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Fangyuan Ma, Linlin Ma, Yuan Wang, Bo Xu
papers.abstract: We examine the incentives for mutual fund families to launch ESG funds. Our analyses reveal that introducing a new ESG fund leads to a significant increase in capital inflows to sibling non-ESG funds in the family. This flow spillover accounts for a significant portion of the monetary awards for families to offer ESG funds. We also find that spillover is stronger among retail funds and cannot be attributed to changes in the ESG profiles or abnormal returns of the sibling funds. Further evidence suggests that affect-based judgments, particularly the halo effect, are the key drivers of this spillover effect.

papers.title: Market Return Decomposition and Equity Risk Premium Predictability
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Yanyan Lin, 吴冲锋, Guofu Zhou, Shunwei Zhu

papers.title: Who do you vote for? Same-race voting preferences in director elections
papers.authors: Johan Sulaeman, Qiaozhi Ye
papers.abstract: This article highlights racial and ethnic preferences in corporate director elections. Using a comprehensive dataset of mutual fund voting records, we discover that mutual fund managers are more likely to vote for director nominees who share their racial or ethnic identity. Funds managed by White-dominated teams exhibit the strongest same-race preferences, particularly those in fund families with scarce minority representation. Same-race voting preferences have detrimental implications for the career outcomes of minority director candidates and are associated with worse fund performance primarily when fund managers operate under weaker accountability. We investigate various potential mechanisms—including statistical discrimination, value maximization, conflicts of interest, social networks, and taste-based biases—and find that the evidence aligns most closely with a taste-based explanation for same-race preferential voting.

papers.title: Mandatory Disclosure and Peer Firms' Learning From Stock Prices
papers.authors: Jaewoo Kim, Hunter Pearson, Brady J. Twedt
papers.abstract: Theory posits that mandatory disclosure influences peer firms' learning from stock prices in two non‐mutually exclusive ways: intra‐industry information transfers and the reallocation of information acquisition efforts. Using mandatory segment disclosure as our setting, we document a decrease in investment‐ q sensitivity for peers of disclosing firms. This effect is stronger among peers with greater economic links to disclosing firms and peers with the greatest incentives to glean information from prices. Our findings provide novel evidence that mandatory disclosure can have significant negative externalities on peer firms' investment efficiency via a managerial learning from the stock price channel. These insights inform regulators assessing the economic consequences of mandatory disclosure, while also assisting managers who rely on information from stock prices to guide investment decisions.

papers.title: The Inflation Attention Threshold and Inflation Surges
papers.authors: Oliver Pfäuti
papers.abstract: The recent inflation surge brought inflation back on people's minds. I quantify when and how much attention to inflation changes and derive the macroeconomic implications of these attention changes. I estimate an attention threshold at an inflation rate of 4 percent, that attention doubles when inflation exceeds this threshold, and that supply shocks have stronger and more persistent effects on inflation in times of high attention. Developing a model featuring the attention threshold, I show that attention changes offer a joint explanation for inflation surges, inflation's co-movement with inflation expectations, and a long last mile of disinflation. (JEL D84, E12, E31, E43, E52)

papers.title: Union Bargaining Power and the Amenity-Wage Trade-Off
papers.authors: Lorenzo Lagos
papers.abstract: This paper studies how collective bargaining affects wages and amenities. By merging collective bargaining agreements (CBAs) to linked employer-employee data in Brazil, I combine rich contracted amenities with wage information. I implement a difference-in-differences strategy that exploits a court ruling enforcing CBA continuation (i.e., ultra-activity) to estimate the effects of union bargaining power. Strengthening unions raises wages and amenities without reducing employment—increasing retention despite some labor-labor substitution. A revealed-preference approach shows that amenities account for 45 percent of total compensation gains. These findings suggest that collective bargaining can offset monopsony power, but employers retain the right-to-manage workforce composition. (JEL J31, J32, J42, J51, J52, O15)

papers.title: The Returns to Government R&D: Evidence from US Appropriations Shocks
papers.authors: Andrew J. Fieldhouse, Karel Mertens
papers.abstract: Based on a narrative classification of all significant postwar changes in R&D appropriations for five major federal agencies, we find that an increase in nondefense R&D appropriations leads to increases in various measures of innovative activity and higher business-sector productivity in the long run. We structurally estimate the production function elasticity of nondefense government R&D capital using the SP-IV methodology of Lewis and Mertens (2024) and obtain implied returns of 140 to 210 percent over the postwar period. The estimates indicate that government-funded R&D accounts for one-fifth of business-sector TFP growth since WWII and imply substantial underfunding of nondefense R&D. (JEL D24, E23, H50, O31, O33, O38)

papers.title: Firm Adaptation in Production Networks: Evidence from Extreme Weather Events in Pakistan
papers.authors: Clare Balboni, Johannes Boehm, Mazhar Waseem
papers.abstract: This paper considers how far private adaptation may reduce future vulnerability to climate risks. Using data on monthly firm-to-firm transactions from Pakistan, we find that flood-affected firms are more likely to relocate to safer ground and shift purchases toward suppliers in less flood-prone regions and reached via less flood-prone roads. The results indicate that firms are imperfectly informed about flood risk and update their beliefs following floods. We quantify aggregate impacts using a spatial model of endogenous production network formation. The findings suggest that firms' learning will shape the economic impact of increasingly frequent climate-related disasters. (JEL D22, L14, O13, O14, Q54, R32)

papers.title: Durables and the Marginal Propensity to Spend
papers.authors: Nathan Zorzi, Martin Beraja
papers.abstract: Durables represent a large share of households' marginal propensity to spend (MPX). We develop a quantitative model of spending that takes durables into account and matches a rich set of empirical regularities simultaneously. Scaling the response of nondurables provides a poor approximation of the MPX on durables when it comes to its distribution in the population, its persistence over time, and its cyclicality. As an application, we study how the MPX varies with the size of stimulus checks and find that it declines more slowly compared to a model of purely nondurable spending. (JEL D11, E21, E32, E62, G51)

papers.title: The Unequal Economic Consequences of Carbon Pricing
papers.authors: Diego R. Känzig
papers.abstract: This paper studies the economic impacts of carbon pricing. Exploiting institutional features of the European carbon market and high-frequency data, I identify carbon policy shocks and trace their dynamic effects. A restrictive carbon policy shock raises energy prices, reduces emissions, spurs green innovation, but decreases economic activity—disproportionately burdening poorer households. Not only are the poor more affected because of their higher energy spending, but they also experience larger income losses. These indirect, general equilibrium effects via income and employment play an important role in the transmission of carbon pricing policies, accounting for about two-thirds of the aggregate consumption response. (JEL E23, E24, O44, Q41, Q54, Q55, Q58)

papers.title: The Causal Effects of Global Supply Chain Disruptions on Macroeconomic Outcomes: Evidence and Theory
papers.authors: Xiwen Bai, Jesús Fernández‐Villaverde, Yiliang Li, Francesco Zanetti
papers.abstract: We study the causal effects of global supply chain disruptions by constructing a new index of real-time port congestion using Automatic Identification System data from container ships and a spatial clustering algorithm. We develop a model with search frictions between producers and retailers that links upstream production slack to downstream supply shortages and captures output and price responses to supply chain shocks. The co-movements of output, prices, spare capacity, and market tightness provide novel identification restrictions. We find that demand and supply shocks drove US disinflation in 2020, while the inflation surge in 2021 was driven mainly by supply chain shocks. (JEL C43, E31, F14, F23, L14, L92)

papers.title: Residential Segregation and Unequal Access to Local Public Services in India: Evidence from 1.5 Million Neighborhoods
papers.authors: Sam Asher, Kritarth Jha, Paul Michael Novosad, Anjali Adukia, Brandon Tan
papers.abstract: We study residential segregation and access to public services across 1.5 million urban and rural neighborhoods in India. Muslim and Scheduled Caste segregation in India is high by global standards and only slightly lower than Black-White segregation in the United States. Within cities, public facilities and infrastructure are systematically less available in Muslim and Scheduled Caste neighborhoods. Nearly all regressive allocation is across neighborhoods within cities—at the most informal and least studied form of government. These inequalities are not visible in the aggregate data typically used for research and policy. (JEL H76, J15, O15, O17, O18, R23)

papers.title: Inequality and Racial Backlash: Evidence from the Reconstruction Era and the Freedmen's Bureau
papers.authors: Eric T. Chyn, Kareem Haggag, Bryan A. Stuart
papers.abstract: How do majority groups respond to narrowing inequality in racially polarized environments? We study this by examining the Freedmen's Bureau, an agency created after the US Civil War to aid former slaves and launch institutional reform in the South. Using new historical records and an event-study approach, we estimate the bureau's impact on political, social, and economic outcomes. Vote shares for Democrats, the party that previously championed slavery and opposed Black civil rights, initially eroded in bureau counties, but these impacts faded as federal oversight weakened. Racial backlash emerged rapidly and persisted, suggesting White majorities sought to offset Black progress. (JEL D63, D72, J15, N31, N41)

papers.title: The Effects of School Phone Bans: National Evidence from Lockable Pouches
papers.authors: Hunt Allcott, Jason Baron, Thomas Sean Dee, Angela Lee Duckworth, Matthew Aaron Gentzkow, Brian Aaron Jacob
papers.abstract: Schools across the U.S. have sharply restricted student use of phones during the school day. We evaluate one type of restriction—lockable phone pouches—using nationwide data combining a large-scale teacher survey, GPS pings, standardized test scores, and school administrative records, along with sales records from the largest pouch provider. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that pouch adoption substantially reduces phone use as measured by GPS pings and teacher reports. In the first year after adoption, disciplinary incidents increase, and we find suggestive evidence that student subjective well-being falls, consistent with short-term disruption. However, disciplinary effects fade, while the estimated effects on well-being appear to recover and become positive in later years. For academic achievement, average effects on test scores are consistently close to zero. High schools see modest positive effects, particularly in math, while middle schools see small negative effects. We find little evidence of effects on school attendance and no clear evidence of improvements in self-reported classroom attention or perceived online bullying.

papers.title: A Theory of Redistribution and Public Good Provision under Nondemocracy
papers.authors: Nicola Persico
papers.abstract: Two office-motivated politicians compete for power by making promises to citizens. Unlike in voting models, a citizens' political activity is observable and subject to retaliation if the citizen happens to back the wrong politician. In equilibrium, a citizen supports the politician that is expected to win the political contest, not the one who promises her the most. Consequently, the incentives for politicians to redistribute resources and provide public goods are different from those in voting models. Citizens who are better able to coordinate with others receive more resources in equilibrium. Transition to democracy is not voluntary in this model.

papers.title: A Model of Enclosures: Coordination, Conflict, and Efficiency in the Transformation of Land Property Rights
papers.authors: Matthew J Baker, Jonathan H. Conning
papers.abstract: Economists and historians have long debated how open-access areas, frontier regions, and customary landholding regimes transformed into private property. This paper analyses decentralized enclosure processes using the theory of aggregative games, examining how population density, enclosure costs, potential productivity gains, and local governance capacity, including the power to demand compensation, jointly determine the mix of property regimes. Depending on these fundamentals, private decisions to enclose may be strategic complements or substitutes. Strategic complements generate tipping points and socially destructive property races, whereas strategic substitutes produce smoother transitions and may leave enclosure below the social optimum. While policies to strengthen customary governance or compensate displaced stakeholders can realign incentives, addressing one distortion while neglecting others can worsen welfare.

papers.title: Materiality and investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility: A replication and extension of Flammer (2013)
papers.authors: Steve Kofford, Ben W. Lewis, Myles Melancon
papers.abstract: Research Summary We replicate and extend Flammer's (2013) event study of investor reaction to environmental corporate social responsibility. Flammer found that investors react positively to eco‐friendly events and negatively to eco‐harmful events, with positive reactions diminishing and negative reactions intensifying from 1980 to 2009. We confirm her results in a narrow replication and find that these time trends persist in a quasi‐replication extending the sample through 2019, despite major shifts in the institutional environment for sustainability investing. We then extend Flammer by incorporating financial materiality and find that the investor reactions and time trends Flammer observed are primarily concentrated in material events. Notably, investors drew this distinction throughout the 40‐year window we study, predating the institutionalization of materiality‐based sustainability analysis. Managerial Summary We examine how investors respond to companies' environmental actions. Analyzing 40 years of data on US‐listed public firms, we find that investors reward companies for eco‐friendly actions and penalize them for harmful ones. Over time, these reactions have shifted: investors have grown less enthusiastic about eco‐friendly actions and more critical of harmful ones. Importantly, investors react primarily to environmental actions that are financially relevant, or “material,” to the business and were doing so well before formal standards existed. Within material actions, positive reactions to eco‐friendly initiatives have weakened while negative reactions to eco‐harmful ones have grown stronger. These findings suggest that managers should prioritize environmental initiatives closely tied to their company's financial performance.

papers.title: Strategy as a theory of change
papers.authors: Sérgio G. Lazzarini, Todd R. Zenger, Teppo Felin
papers.abstract: Research Summary The theory‐based view argues that a strategist's task is to develop a theory to move the organization to an improved future state. Focusing on theorizing as a thought process of model creation, we propose a framework to specify hypothetical causal links and analyze their structure as a directed graph connecting inputs, activities, and indicators of problem resolution. We then propose a set of metrics operationalizing key theory attributes: complexity, equifinality, interdependence, and circularity. We discuss the strategic relevance of these attributes in terms of a theory's ability to promote comprehensive problem resolution as well as implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed solution. Our work represents a step toward operationalizing model creation in the theory‐based view and informs the design of strategic theories of change. Managerial Summary Strategists often theorize how to move their organizations toward an improved performance state. Yet most strategic analysis tools describe the organization's external environment or the internal components of its business model, without precisely specifying forward‐looking interventions that might cause the desired changes. In this paper, we represent strategic theories as a chain of causal interventions—inputs and activities that address relevant problems and lead to desirable outcomes. We propose a structured framework that helps managers develop theories and measure key attributes that influence comprehensive problem resolution and the ability to implement, evaluate, and replicate the proposed interventions. In this sense, our work helps managers mentally create their strategic theories and assess their usefulness as a roadmap to superior performance.

papers.title: Leveraging social legitimacy to navigate geopolitical fragmentation and populist polarization
papers.authors: Izzet Sidki Darendeli, TL Hill
papers.abstract: Although earning political legitimacy helps MNEs manage political risk, association with governments and political elites can become liabilities when regimes, alliances, and public sentiment shift. Reflecting on our study of MNE survival during abrupt regime change, we revisit social legitimacy as a complement to, and sometimes a substitute for, political legitimacy. We distinguish two foundations of social legitimacy: relational legitimacy, built through broad ties across societal constituencies, and material legitimacy, earned by providing products, services, and investments perceived as valuable by non-elite society. Although long recognized as a part of earning and maintaining a license to operate in any country, social legitimacy has become an increasingly important hedge against the ebbs and flows of political power driven by geopolitical fragmentation, populism, and polarization. Indeed, as geopolitics and populism make political affiliations more noticeable and more volatile, we suggest that efforts to earn social legitimacy play an increasingly important role in MNE nonmarket strategy. We identify theoretical and empirical questions concerning the sources, usefulness, and limits of earning social legitimacy; urge researchers and leaders to learn from and connect to non-elite sectors of society; and suggest ways that investment in social legitimacy can help MNEs navigate political turbulence worldwide.

papers.title: Do Experimental Asset Market Results Replicate? High‐Powered Preregistered Replications of 17 Key Results
papers.authors: Christoph Huber, Felix Holzmeister, Magnus Johannesson, Christian König-Kersting, Anna Dreber, Jürgen Huber, Michael Kirchler
papers.abstract: Experimental asset markets provide a controlled approach to studying financial markets. We attempt to replicate 17 key results from four prominent studies, collecting new data from 166 markets with 1,544 participants. Only three of the 14 original results reported as statistically significant were successfully replicated. We fail to replicate findings on emotions, self‐control, and gender differences in bubble formation but confirm that experience reduces bubbles and cognitive skills explain trading success. Our study demonstrates the importance of replications in enhancing the credibility of scientific results in this field.

papers.title: Decoupling voting and cash flow rights
papers.authors: Andre Speit, Paul Voß, András Danis

papers.title: Whose Job Is It, Anyway? The Effect of the Review Process on Employee Performance
papers.authors: A. Bross, Ryan D. Sommerfeldt
papers.abstract: Companies have widely adopted a system of work‐product reviews whereby the work of one individual is subsequently reviewed by another to ensure its quality. We examine how managers can effectively implement a review of employee work to improve performance. Organizations review employees' work to identify mistakes and improve work quality. However, reviews may also reduce employees' effort and initiative if they expect reviewers to identify and correct their errors for them. We use an experiment to examine how employee performance depends on who conducts the review and how feedback is provided. Specifically, participants' work was reviewed by either a superior or a peer, and the reviewer provided either general, high‐level guidance (autonomy‐oriented) or specific corrective information about errors (dependency‐oriented). Employees performed best when superiors provided high‐level guidance or when peers provided specific corrective feedback, with these benefits emerging over time. Guidance from a superior increased employees' sense of responsibility, whereas corrective help from a peer strengthened feelings of teamwork and cohesion. Review approaches that did not fit these combinations offered no clear performance benefit relative to having no review. The findings show that review effectiveness depends on matching the feedback approach to the reviewer's organizational rank. These results have important implications for managers, accountants responsible for internal controls, and audit professionals involved in designing and implementing the review process.

papers.title: Inflexibility and Leverage
papers.authors: Lifeng Gu, Dirk Hackbarth, Yuxin Luo
papers.abstract: Firms’ inflexibility to adjust their scale persistently explains capital structure variations in a comprehensive sample and randomly selected subsamples. Higher inflexibility leads to lower financial leverage, potentially due to higher default risk and lower value of tax shields. Contraction inflexibility determines leverage more than expansion inflexibility. Moreover, our inflexibility measure explains financial leverage significantly better than other variables that potentially capture certain aspects of adjustment costs for capital or labor. In addition, inflexible firms increase leverage more following a positive credit supply shock. Analyses employing instrumental variables estimation confirm our main finding. Our results suggest inflexibility shapes corporate financial policies. This paper was accepted by Bo Becker, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08672 .

papers.title: Multitype Information Acquisition in a Strategic Trading Model
papers.authors: Hui Ou‐Yang, Weili Wu, Xingtan Zhang
papers.abstract: We analyze information acquisition in a strategic trading model with multidimensional uncertainties. Our main result is that the equilibrium can exhibit multiplicity because of the integer nature of the number of informed traders and the strategic interactions across different types of informed traders. We show that the number of equilibria can be arbitrarily large. Moreover, asymmetric equilibria can arise even in symmetric settings. As information costs rise, fewer traders acquire information, yet prices can become more informative. These results shed light on the instability of financial markets and yield testable empirical predictions. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72472171 and 72372011]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08463 .

papers.title: Willingness to Compete in Dirty Competitions
papers.authors: Thomas Buser, Sahar Sangi
papers.abstract: Competitive environments often leave room for “dirty” practices such as sabotage, retaliation, or dishonesty. We use an online experiment to document aggregate levels and individual differences in the willingness to engage in dirty competition and in the willingness to enter competitions where the opponent may play dirty. We then use the experimental data to validate a set of survey questions that capture willingness to engage in dirty competition above general willingness to compete. We elicit these questions in a representative survey panel and show that willingness to engage in dirty competition is a strong predictor of holding a management or supervisory position and of working in the private—versus the public—sector, but also of worse self-esteem, worse social relationships, and increased feelings of guilt and shame. Men, younger people, and lower-educated people are on average more willing to engage in dirty competition. This paper was accepted by Dorothea Kübler, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01218 .

papers.title: Contest or Contract: Assessing the Effectiveness of Contests in Online Labor Markets
papers.authors: Jason Chan, Jiahui Mo, Tingting Nian, Nila Zhang
papers.abstract: Online labor markets have become increasingly popular among companies seeking global access to workers. Some platforms have adopted a contest-based scheme, allowing employers to review multiple submissions before selecting the best one. This practice raises a crucial question: Given a predefined budget, should employers choose a contest or contract scheme for tasks? This study examines the comparative effectiveness of contests versus contracts in achieving better job outcomes, focusing on design tasks characterized by high uncertainty. Using a comprehensive data set from a leading online labor market, we employ multiple empirical strategies, combined with machine learning and text mining techniques, to examine the impact of compensation schemes on job quality. Our results suggest that contract-based jobs yield better performance than contests in the context of ideation tasks. Further analysis, such as examining image similarity among pairwise solutions within a task, identifies “copying” behaviors as a key mechanism undermining the effectiveness of contests. In the public setting of contests, workers can observe others’ submissions and revise their own, leading to imitation rather than innovation. As competition intensity increases, workers have weaker incentives to exert effort, reducing solution quality. Consequently, the negative incentive effects in contests outweigh both the potential positive incentive and parallel effects. Moreover, although information availability can enhance work quality, contests inherently offer limited informational advantages compared with contracts. Taken together, our findings suggest that contract-based schemes are more effective than contests for design tasks, offering important implications for both employers and platform designers in

papers.title: Production-Based Option Pricing
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Andrea Gamba, Alessio Saretto
papers.abstract: We show that a structural model incorporating firms’ real options and financial leverage decisions can generate forward-looking equity distributions of various shapes, resulting in highly flexible implied volatility surfaces. In contrast, exogenously specified models with stochastic volatility and jumps can only generate smiles and downward-sloping curves. We explain the observed negative relationship between downward sloping implied volatility surfaces and the value of real options: real options contribute positively to equity skewness, and more so the more convex their payoff, which is the case when the real option is “at-the-money” and has the lowest value.

papers.title: Robust Auction Design with Support Information
papers.authors: Jerry Anunrojwong, Santiago Balseiro, Omar Besbes
papers.abstract: A seller wants to sell an item to n buyers. Buyer valuations are independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) according to a distribution unknown to the seller; the seller only knows that the support is included in [a, b]. To be robust, the seller chooses a dominant strategy incentive compatible mechanism that optimizes the worst-case performance relative to the ideal expected revenue the seller could have collected with knowledge of buyers’ valuations. Our analysis unifies the regret and the ratio objectives. For these objectives, we derive an optimal mechanism and the corresponding performance in quasi-closed form, as a function of the support information [a, b] and the number of buyers n. Our analysis reveals three regimes of support information and a new class of robust mechanisms. (i) When a/b is below a threshold, the optimal mechanism is a second-price auction (SPA) with random reserve, a focal class in earlier literature. (ii) When a/b is above another threshold, SPAs are strictly suboptimal, and an optimal mechanism belongs to a class of mechanisms we introduce, which we call pooling auctions (POOL); whenever the highest value is above a threshold, the mechanism still allocates to the highest bidder, but otherwise the mechanism allocates to a uniformly random buyer, that is, pools low types. (iii) When a/b is between two thresholds, a randomization between SPA and POOL is optimal. We also characterize optimal mechanisms within nested central subclasses of mechanisms: standard mechanisms that only allocate to the highest bidder, SPA with random reserve, and SPA with no reserve. We show strict separations in terms of performance across classes, implying that deviating from standard mechanisms is necessary for robustness. Lastly, we show that the same results

papers.title: From Employer Responsibility to Environmental Irresponsibility: Unintended Impacts of Social Insurance Law on Pollution Emissions
papers.authors: Yanan Li, Yu Qin, Wenjun Wang
papers.abstract: This study investigates the unintended effect of the introduction of the 2011 Social Insurance Law on corporate pollution emissions. Using a difference-in-differences framework, our analysis reveals that enhanced social insurance contributions lead to higher industrial pollution emissions, as measured by chemical oxygen demand and wastewater emissions. The mechanism analysis indicates that the enforcement of the law increases firms’ labor costs and financial distress, motivating them to reduce efforts on end-of-pipe treatment activities and measures taken during the production process, which results in higher pollution emission intensity. Our study highlights the potential conflict between employee protection and corporate environmental goals. Further analysis suggests that stronger environmental monitoring and environmental, social, and governance disclosure requirements can partially mitigate this tradeoff, providing valuable insights for policymakers. This paper was accepted by Caroline Flammer, sustainability. Funding: Y. Li acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72403026]. Y. Qin acknowledges research support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72342031]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00714 .

papers.title: Estimating the Pricing Kernel: A Simple Regression-Based Dimension-Reduction Approach
papers.authors: Bin Luo, Guofu Zhou, Ti Zhou
papers.abstract: We propose a simple framework for estimating the pricing kernel in factor space by constructing the mean–variance efficient factor portfolio via an ordinary least squares formulation with least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regularization. The method accommodates high-dimensional settings in which the number of candidate factors exceeds the sample size and automatically shrinks redundant factor weights toward zero. We show theoretically that the out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of the estimated portfolio converges to the theoretical maximum at the fastest rate among existing regression-based approaches. Applying the method to 174 characteristic-based factors together with the market factor, we obtain an out-of-sample Sharpe ratio of 3.59, substantially outperforming competing strategies and delivering the smallest aggregate pricing errors. The selected factors vary over time in both composition and number, averaging about 50. We further develop a model comparison test and reject the hypothesis that eight widely used sparse factor models are sufficient to span the pricing kernel. This paper was accepted by Kay Giesecke, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grants 72671091, 72371079, and 72501192, and Key Program 72432005] and the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangdong Province [Grant 2023B1515020045]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03608 .

papers.title: Affect-Infused Reflective Process in Responding to Burdensome Role Expectations: An Affect-Cognition Theory Extension of Yagil’s “I Don’t Want To”
papers.authors: Chang Su, Xiaoran Hu

papers.title: Are direct lenders more like banks or arm’s-length investors?
papers.authors: Young Soo Jang

papers.title: Innovation booms, easy financing, and human capital accumulation
papers.authors: Johan Hombert, Adrien Matray

papers.title: The Weight of Compliance: Anti-Money Laundering Enforcement, Banking Sector Composition, and Lending
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Şenay Ağca, Pablo Slutzky, Stefan Zeume
papers.abstract: We examine how strengthened anti-money laundering (AML) enforcement affects the U.S. banking sector. Heightened enforcement disproportionately raises compliance costs for small banks, especially in counties more exposed to money laundering. In these areas, small banks contract while large banks expand, increasing standardized, government-supported, and secured lending. While aggregate county-level credit does not decline differentially, local outcomes improve. Small establishments grow, non-tradable employment and wages rise, and real estate prices increase. The evidence is consistent with a reallocation mechanism in which AML enforcement shifts activity toward large banks, potentially improving intermediation quality through changes in the composition of local financial intermediation.

papers.title: Do PCAOB Inspection Deficiencies Related to Management Review Controls Affect Financial Reporting Decisions? Evidence From Goodwill Impairments
papers.authors: Kenneth L. Bills, Chris E. Hogan, Jennifer Puccia
papers.abstract: We examine whether PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to management review controls (MRCs) affect financial reporting decisions. Using the goodwill impairment setting, we find that firms are more likely to record goodwill impairments when their auditors have received more PCAOB inspection deficiencies related to goodwill MRCs. The association is stronger when inspection deficiencies are more likely to lead to changes to the design or implementation of an internal control (repeat deficiencies and deficiencies related to MRC precision). We observe some evidence that MRC inspection deficiencies increase the likelihood of goodwill impairment even when unrelated to goodwill, indicating that improving the audit of MRCs can broadly affect financial reporting. Our findings provide evidence that PCAOB inspections affect not only auditor behavior but also the financial reporting behavior of audit clients. Specifically, inspection feedback appears to influence reporting outcomes through changes in the audit and evaluation of MRCs, identifying a channel through which regulatory oversight affects issuers. The results have implications for audit firms seeking to remediate inspection deficiencies, for management and audit committees responsible for overseeing significant estimates and impairment analyses, and for regulators evaluating the broader effectiveness of the PCAOB inspection process.

papers.title: Safe Spaces: Shelters or Tribes?
papers.authors: Jean Tirole

papers.title: Conversations at Scale: Robust AI-Led Interviews
papers.authors: Friedrich Geiecke, Xavier Jaravel
papers.abstract: The advent of large language models (LLMs) creates new opportunities to conduct qualitative interviews at scale, with thousands of respondents, thereby bridging qualitative and quantitative methods. We develop a simple, versatile approach for researchers to run AI-led qualitative interviews, including voice interviews. We assess its robustness by drawing comparisons to human experts and with several respondent-based quality metrics. The versatility of the approach is illustrated through four broad classes of applications: eliciting key factors in decision making, political views, subjective mental states, and mental models of the effects of public policies. High performance ratings are obtained in all of these domains. Our applications highlight the potential of AI-led interviews as a tool for measurement, hypothesis generation, and discovering mechanisms.

papers.title: Selection into Financial Education and Effects on Portfolio Choice
papers.authors: Irina Gemmo, Pierre‐Carl Michaud, Olivia S. Mitchell
papers.abstract: We study the impact of a financial education program on portfolio choices in a setting that allows us to examine both participation decisions and differences in program benefits across individuals. We directly elicit willingness to pay for financial education and show that individuals with higher financial literacy, greater confidence in applying new knowledge, and higher expected returns are willing to pay more. Using incentivized portfolio allocation tasks, we develop outcome measures tailored to individual risk preferences and show that financial education improves decision quality along these dimensions. The program increases the share of participants who experience an improvement by 20 percentage points, corresponding to average gains of 3.2 percentage points of initial wealth. Individuals with the highest willingness to participate benefit disproportionately from the program, with important implications for the design and evaluation of financial education initiatives. By isolating a specific investment skill in a setting with voluntary participation, our design sheds light on how selection into financial education shapes measured program effects and informs the assessment of broader workplace and public training programs. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: The authors thank the Pension Research Council of Wharton School at the University of Pennsylvania, as well as the Retirement and Savings Institute at HEC Montréal, for generous research funding. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.08268 .

papers.title: Navigating the Rugged Data Landscape: The Impact of Data-Extrapolation Technologies on Knowledge Production
papers.authors: Soomi Kim
papers.abstract: Data-extrapolation technologies enable progress by importing and applying empirical patterns from one domain to another. Their reliance on empirical patterns, however, is also their limitation: these tools can only be applied where data are abundant. Using the setting of structural biology, I investigate the impact of a data-extrapolation technology on innovation. I exploit the variation in prior data availability to compare areas in which the tool was usable to those in which it was not. I find that the tool increased the quantity of research in data-rich areas: the resulting output yielded limited biological insights but was methodologically rigorous and contributed to downstream research. This paper was accepted by Toby Stuart, entrepreneurship and innovation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.04115 .

papers.title: Unpacking the micro–macro transmission mechanism: how home-country culture selectively shapes cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial internationalization
papers.authors: Razieh Sadraei, Vahid Sadeghi, Andrew Delios
papers.abstract: International business accounts treat national culture as a country-level antecedent that shifts average export propensity uniformly, leaving the individual-level mechanisms producing within-country heterogeneity in internationalization intensity unspecified. We address this micro–macro transmission gap using social cognitive theory, examining how individualism versus collectivism and risk avoidance versus tolerance selectively recalibrate three cognitive orientations in entrepreneurial export decisions: perceived self-efficacy, perceived opportunity availability, and fear of failure. Our multilevel analysis of 40,529 observations across 41 countries spanning 2010–2019 reveals divergent rather than uniform moderation: individualism amplifies self-efficacy and opportunity availability beliefs through the social validation pathway, while risk avoidance constrains opportunity availability beliefs and fear of failure through the anticipatory self-regulation and outcome expectancy pathways. Fear of failure’s directional relationship with internationalization is contingent on the expectations of failure costs that the home-country cultural environment establishes through the outcome expectancy pathway, rather than being uniformly inhibitory as prior frameworks assume. These findings advance international business microfoundations theory by specifying the observable transmission pathways through which national cultural dimensions produce heterogeneous export intensity outcomes within the same national context. For policymakers, the findings imply that interventions to strengthen self-efficacy or opportunity awareness work best when calibrated to a country’s cultural profile.

papers.title: The effect of prime brokers’ balance sheet constraints on hedge fund performance: Evidence from the GSIB surcharge
papers.authors: Yueting Jiang, Yiwen Shen

papers.title: Synthesizing Information-Driven Insider Trade Signals
papers.journal: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
papers.authors: Jens Heckmann, Heiko Jacobs, Patrick Schwarz
papers.abstract: We propose a novel approach to synthesize presumably information-driven insider trading signals for the cross section of stocks. We find that the resulting straightforward composite strategy can often forecast returns in a global sample. This predictability is strongest in equal-weighted portfolios, short holding periods, and insider-buying signals, and it improves further with global diversification. Cross-country analysis reveals that varying insider trading restrictions between countries have limited explanatory power for the performance of the composite strategy. Overall, the results are consistent with a short-term informational advantage of insiders, which might be due to the skillful interpretation of non-private news.

papers.title: Price Gouging and the Monopoly Option
papers.authors: Samuel Häfner, Curtis R. Taylor
papers.abstract: We investigate a dynamic oligopoly model with two phases: a normal phase where an essential input is available, and a disruption phase where firms must rely on inventories. Disruptions create an overcutting pricing incentive arising from the option to forgo sales and monopolize the market once rivals stock out. This monopoly option causes the price to jump to a supracompetitive level at the advent of the disruption and to remain above the competitive price path throughout. Price caps raise welfare, but reduce inventory investment. Government reserves reduce prices and raise buffer stocks, as do reserve mandates when financially feasible.

papers.title: Qualitative Research in the Age of AI: Considerations, Critiques, and Craft
papers.authors: Andrew J. Nelson, Anne‐Laure Fayard, Alex Michael Murray

papers.title: Measurement Error, Manipulation, and the Value of Short‐Term Performance in Job Retention
papers.authors: Naomi Rothenberg
papers.abstract: This paper studies how the accuracy of a short‐term performance measure affects its value when a principal decides whether to retain or fire an agent, who can manipulate that measure. Compared with ignoring performance and never firing the agent, the performance measure is valuable when the savings in the expected cost of the retention error is more than the expected cost of the firing error. A more accurate performance measure can have a non‐monotonic effect on its value: Greater accuracy improves the principal's ability to correctly identify the agent, which increases efficient firing, but it causes the incompetent agent to increase manipulation to avoid being fired, which increases inefficient retention. With a less accurate performance measure, the incompetent agent has weaker incentives for manipulation, and an increase in accuracy increases its value due to the identification effect. With a more accurate performance measure, the manipulation effect dominates, and an increase in accuracy decreases its value. The results imply that the principal prefers an imperfect performance measure when the agent can choose the level of manipulation.

papers.title: The economics of data unions: optimal data sharing and coordination
papers.authors: Lin William Cong, Simon Mayer
papers.abstract: We develop a model of data-driven competition in which product quality depends on users’ data contributions and firms’ investments in data infrastructure. Users’ inability to internalize the value generated by their data, together with firms’ strategic investment incentives, can lead to data underinvestment—limiting quality—or overinvestment—concentrating market power. We introduce a data union that coordinates users’ contributions and can be implemented through a data trust or intermediary that aggregates user data. By shaping data compensation, the union enables users to capture and internalize more of their data’s value, enhancing user welfare, especially when combined with data sharing among firms. We apply these insights to financial data, digital payments, and Open Finance. Our analysis shows that data portability can strengthen competition but, without coordination, may leave data investment too low or excessive.

papers.title: From Heterogeneous Firms to Heterogeneous Trade Elasticities: The Aggregate Implications of Firm Export Decisions
papers.authors: Rodrigo Adão, Costas Arkolakis, Sharat Ganapati

papers.title: Bargaining and Contract Forms in Distribution Channels: Why Do Slotting Fees Arise and Linear Contracts Persist?
papers.authors: Øystein Foros, Hans Jarle Kind, Greg Shaffer
papers.abstract: Two empirical patterns emerge in business-to-business settings, particularly in retail distribution channels such as grocery markets. First, linear contracts are widely observed alongside nonlinear contracts with fixed payments, despite the claimed efficiency advantages of the latter. Second, when fixed payments arise, they often flow from suppliers to retailers (slotting fees) rather than the reverse. We develop and analyze a model of multilateral bargaining in which a supplier negotiates separately with competing retailers to explain these patterns. The key mechanism is a trade-off between two distortions: under linear contracts, wholesale prices reflect bargaining power and can be either above or below the channel-profit-maximizing level, whereas under two-part tariffs, wholesale prices are set to maximize bilateral surplus independently of bargaining power but are systematically too low from an overall channel perspective because of rent shifting across relationships. As a result, neither contractual form uniformly dominates; instead, relative performance depends on how bargaining shapes gains from trade across firms. When bargaining leads to slotting fees, two-part tariffs yield higher channel profits than linear contracts, whereas when it would imply payments from retailers to suppliers, linear contracts may perform better. These findings offer a unified explanation for the persistence of linear contracts alongside two-part tariffs, the direction of fixed payments, and the conditions under which each contractual form is likely to arise. This paper was accepted by Miguel Villas-Boas, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.03426 .

papers.title: Looking Under the Hood of Commodity Currency Predictability
papers.authors: Alexandre Jeanneret, Valeri Sokolovski
papers.abstract: This paper revisits the exchange rate predictability of commodity currencies through the lens of market efficiency. Focusing on currencies with strong contemporaneous exposure to commodity prices, we show that changes in country-specific commodity export or import prices predict exchange rate fluctuations both in sample and out of sample. We establish four empirical facts: (i) the sign of the predictive relationship runs counter to standard risk-based explanations; (ii) predictability is concentrated at short horizons; (iii) predictability is driven by a small set of thinly traded currencies; and (iv) even sophisticated speculative traders adjust positions sluggishly in response to commodity price shocks in these currencies. Together, these findings suggest that predictability arises from the slow incorporation of information in less actively traded currencies, which is likely due to liquidity and position-building constraints, rather than from compensation for risk. The results also clarify the sources of commodity-based predictability in carry trade returns. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07249 .

papers.title: Excess Movement in Option‐Implied Beliefs
papers.authors: Ned Augenblick, Eben Lazarus
papers.abstract: We derive bounds on the rational variation in option‐implied beliefs about market returns. While risk preferences distort option‐implied (or risk‐neutral) beliefs away from subjective beliefs, one can nonetheless bound risk‐neutral belief movement under a general assumption on the stochastic discount factor. The resulting test requires no knowledge of the objective distribution and allows significantly more flexibility in discount rates than standard volatility tests. Implementing our test empirically using index options, we find that there is so much movement in risk‐neutral beliefs that the bounds are routinely violated. Our results imply significant excess index‐price volatility.

papers.title: Do long-term yields help to estimate short-term risk premia?
papers.authors: Andrea Berardi, Roger Brown, Stephen M. Schaefer
papers.abstract: We identify a new and important property of affine term structure models: at long maturities, the slope of the term structure of risk premia becomes “almost observable”. Exploiting this property by fitting models to long-maturity data dramatically improves the precision of estimates of risk premia and expected short rates across the term structure. In a Monte Carlo experiment we show that using rates with maturities up to 25 years, rather than 10 years as is standard in the literature, reduces the standard deviation of estimation errors in risk premia, expected short rates and term premia by over 70%. Applying this approach to US Treasury data, we find that variation in expected short rates accounts for a much larger share of variation in yields (and variation in term premia a correspondingly smaller fraction) than in the widely used estimates reported by the Federal Reserve. Accounting for time-variation in yield volatility is key to successful extraction of the risk premium information in long rates. Our approach therefore departs from much of the empirical literature in two important respects: it incorporates long-maturity yields and allows for time-varying yield volatility, whereas most existing studies ignore long-term yields and rely on constant volatility models.

papers.title: Optimal Flood Insurance in a Second-Best World: Fiscal Spillovers, Reclassification Risk, and Moral Hazard
papers.authors: Jonathan Gruber A B, Adam Solomon
papers.abstract: Intensifying climate change makes protection against natural disaster risk – either through ex ante insurance or ex post aid – a first-order public policy issue. Flood risk protection in the U.S. traditionally featured ex post aid through FEMA and heavily subsidized insurance through the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP). In an effort to correct subsidy-induced overbuilding and under-mitigation in flood-prone areas, the NFIP recently moved to actuarially fair insurance premiums. But this change has two unintended consequences: a fiscal spillover onto FEMA disaster aid as insurance coverage declines in flood-prone areas, and household exposure to uninsurable reclassification risk from uncertain climate projections. We develop a model of optimal flood insurance that incorporates the static and dynamic tradeoffs of subsidizing premiums. We then use a variety of identification strategies and data to estimate the five key parameters needed to implement this model. We find that the fiscal spillover and reclassification risk protection benefits significantly outweigh the moral hazard costs, and that the optimal subsidy to flood insurance is 51%, comparable to the level of subsidization before the recent reform.

papers.title: How New Products Enter Markets: Social Networks, Consumer Imports, and Retailer Learning
papers.authors: David Argente, Esteban Méndez, Diana Van Patten
papers.abstract: This paper studies how new varieties enter markets and become locally available. We provide causal evidence of demand externalities that operate in two steps. First, information about new varieties diffuses directly through real-world social ties among consumers. Second, early purchases generate an indirect spillover to firms: local retailers learn from “pioneer” consumers which new varieties are most likely to succeed and adjust their product offerings accordingly. We study this process in the context of direct-to-consumer imports. Using customs records on individuals’ purchases matched to population-wide social networks, international migrant links, and retailer catchment areas, we document economically meaningful demand externalities. Product-specific expenditure shocks abroad transmit through migrant networks and shift which varieties consumers purchase. Leveraging these shocks as a plausibly exogenous source of local demand variation, we show strong peer effects: prior purchases by close neighbors, coworkers, or friends increase an individual’s likelihood of purchasing the same variety, especially for premium and visible goods. We leverage this result to identify an indirect spillover from consumers to firms: retailers are more likely to add a variety to their assortment when it becomes popular among consumers in their catchment area. Combining the instrument with linked consumer–retailer data and a self-conducted retailer survey, we show that this response reflects learning about latent demand for varieties not yet stocked locally. Together, social diffusion and retailer learning generate demand multipliers that reshape local product availability and expand access to global variety.

papers.title: Why Zoning Is Too Restrictive
papers.authors: Jack Favilukis, Jaehee Song
papers.abstract: Economists estimate that zoning regulations raise house prices, lower productivity, and reduce aggregate welfare, yet regulations remain widespread. We develop and solve a model in which fragmented zoning authority leads to overly strict regulations: Homeowners impose stricter regulations to mitigate local congestion but fail to internalize the broader impact on metro-wide affordability. Empirically, the Herfindahl-Hirschman index of local governments explains 12% of the variation in zoning restrictiveness. Using an instrument based on 19th-century municipal fragmentation, we show that greater fragmentation leads to stricter zoning and higher housing costs. These findings suggest that centralizing zoning decisions could alleviate housing affordability challenges. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: This work was supported by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grant AWD-027881 SSHRC 2023]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02844 .

papers.title: From Bytes to Bites: Examining the Online and Offline Spillover Impacts of Online Food Delivery Platform Subscriptions
papers.authors: Jaeho Myeong, Yongjin Park, Francis Joseph Costello, Keongtae Kim, Jae‐Hyeon Ahn
papers.abstract: With the rapid expansion of online food delivery (OFD) platforms, subscription models have emerged as a strategic tool to retain users and shape consumption behavior. Despite their growing prevalence, the broader impacts of these subscriptions—both within the OFD sector and across downstream consumer activities—remain underexplored. Leveraging a difference-in-differences approach and a large-scale individual-level transaction data set, we identify a significant shift in consumption from a competing platform to the focal platform following the introduction of a subscription service. This shift did not result in cannibalization; instead, overall food consumption within the OFD market increased. Geospatial analysis shows that subscribers were more likely to engage in offline spillovers, including increased local dining and activity in nearby noncompeting economic sectors. These patterns suggest that subscriptions in physical services, like OFD, not only reshape digital engagement, but also, they influence consumer mobility and stimulate localized economic ecosystems. Mechanistic testing supports the interpretation that these effects are driven by increased variety-seeking behavior for offline restaurants that predominantly serve non-OFD cuisines within a proximal location, suggesting that such behavior is constrained by transportation costs. Overall, this study offers novel insights into how subscription models in physical service platforms can expand market demand, foster crosschannel engagement, and generate positive spillovers in adjacent sectors. The findings offer actionable guidance for platform designers and policymakers to enhance consumer welfare and support local economic vitality. They also provide new evidence for restaurants that additional platform usage cost

papers.title: Information Transparency, Choice Confidence, and Customer Retention: Field and Laboratory Evidence from Markets for Credence Goods
papers.authors: Zhi Cheng, Ting Li, Paul A. Pavlou
papers.abstract: How does information transparency affect customer retention in markets where quality is difficult to verify? Conventional wisdom suggests that transparency intensifies price competition and increases customer churn. We challenge this view by showing that acquisition-stage transparency can strengthen retention in markets for credence goods characterized by delayed feedback and persistent uncertainty, where customers revisit their decisions without clear quality signals. We develop a transparency-confidence-retention framework, in which transparency at acquisition builds choice confidence, a psychological switching cost that anchors customers to their initial decisions. Using 83,835 auto insurance contracts from a European insurer and multiple identification strategies, we find that customers acquired through transparent channels are 4.6%–11.8% less likely to churn than those acquired through less transparent channels. A randomized, controlled experiment with 1,515 participants shows that transparency reduces customer churn primarily by strengthening choice confidence rather than increasing conventional switching costs, such as brand trust or product fit. Decomposing transparency into attribute, comparative, and evaluative dimensions reveals that evaluative transparency exerts the strongest influence. Analyses of boundary conditions indicate that the retention effect of transparency is amplified when public and private signals remain congruent with earlier informational cues. These findings reconceptualize transparency as a relational mechanism that fosters decisional assurance and stabilizes retention under quality uncertainty. This paper was accepted by Anindya Ghose, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https:/

papers.title: From Winning to Giving: The Effect of Gold Medals in Crowdsourcing Contests
papers.authors: Shan Liu, Fan Zhang, Jing Wang, Baojun Gao
papers.abstract: We examine how users respond to winning symbolic awards in online crowdsourcing contests. Our setting is a machine learning competition platform that grants symbolic medals to recognize participants’ contest achievements. Employing a regression discontinuity design, we find that gold medal winners participate less in subsequent contests but engage more in prosocial activities, evidenced by a greater volume and length of posts, as well as more substantial and frequent code contributions. In contrast, bronze and silver medals do not seem to exert a significant influence on recipients’ subsequent behaviors. Drawing on self-determination theory and the needs-as-motives hypothesis, we provide evidence that need-driven goal shifting plays an important role in driving the dual effects of gold medals—diminished contest participation but enhanced prosocial contributions.
