Furthermore, conditional upon filing for bankruptcy, borrowers whose loans are held by CLOs with institutional- or individual-level relationships are more likely to successfully reorganize under Chapter 11. Collectively, our findings highlight the dual information channels, both institutional and personnel based, that mitigate information frictions in the leveraged loan market. Data Availability: Data are available from commercial sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; G32; G34; G12.

papers.title: When Companies Choose Their Reporting Standards: Evidence on SASB Adoption and Associated Outcomes
papers.authors: Khrystyna Bochkay, Seungju Choi, Jeffrey Hales
papers.abstract: We examine companies’ voluntary adoption of sustainability disclosure standards developed by the Sustainability Accounting Standards Board (SASB). Specifically, we study which company characteristics help explain the use of SASB standards and examine whether voluntary use is associated with sustainability-related activities and market outcomes. We find that peer behavior, sustainability-focused institutional ownership, company size, and existing sustainability reporting practices are key determinants associated with SASB adoption. Moreover, SASB adoption appears to be a highly persistent disclosure choice. It is significantly associated with better sustainability performance, such as lower sustainability violations, greenhouse gas emissions, and pollution levels, particularly when the SASB standards identify those issues as financially material for the company's industry. Finally, SASB adoption is associated with more extensive sustainability disclosure and greater price informativeness, consistent with investors getting additional firm-specific information from SASB-based reporting. JEL Classifications: M41; M14; G32; Q56.

papers.title: Circuitousness in Disclosure Narratives
papers.authors: Nicholas M. Guest, Jiawen Yan
papers.abstract: This paper examines circuitousness, which reflects related information being spread throughout a narrative as opposed to being grouped together. Circuitousness in the MD&A is higher for underperforming firms facing an imminent recovery, a difficult scenario for managers to describe and reconcile. Such firms’ disclosures are accompanied by heightened information processing activity, such as EDGAR downloads and analyst forecast revisions. Additionally, initial return reactions are faster but incomplete, consistent with recoveries and the ensuing circuitousness increasing processing costs that delay price discovery. Changes in institutional ownership are concentrated among quasi-indexers, who rely on public disclosure but rebalance only gradually. Circuitousness is incrementally and more consistently predictive than other textual characteristics that are related but are typically associated with obfuscation, such as the Fog index and repetition. Overall, circuitousness in financial disclosure signals that a turnaround is imminent and corresponds to more costly information processing. JEL Classifications: D83; D84; G14; G30; M40; M41.

papers.title: Domestic Product Market Impacts of Politically Motivated Foreign Tariffs
papers.authors: Victor Ferguson, Carlyle Burd
papers.abstract: We examine how foreign non-income tax shocks affect U.S. product markets. Our setting is the politically motivated tariffs on U.S. whiskey exports levied during the 2018 trade war, which created an exogenous negative foreign demand shock for domestic producers. Using a difference-in-differences design we show that, on average, U.S. whiskey producers decrease U.S. product prices and thus increase domestic sales volume following the export tariffs. However, we find evidence of strategic pricing, as producers increase prices of locally produced products in primary production states (Kentucky and Tennessee) and more significantly decrease prices in states where whiskey consumption is less popular. Further, we show that U.S. whiskey producers implement smaller product price decreases in states with greater tariff-related media exposure and reduce advertising spending nationwide but not in Kentucky and Tennessee. Taken together, these findings provide timely evidence regarding how foreign trade restrictions impact the U.S. product market and consumer outcomes. Data Availability: NielsenIQ Retail Scanner Data are available through the Kilts Center for Marketing at the University of Chicago Booth School of Business (http://research.chicagobooth.edu/nielsen). Kantar Advertising Insights data are available by subscription. GDELT data are available at https://www.gdeltproject.org/. JEL Classifications: M40; M41; F10; F13; F14.

papers.title: Collective Activism
papers.authors: Craig Doidge, Alexander Dyck, Liyan Yang
papers.abstract: Can investor stewardship codes that call for coordinated activism be satisfied by an Investor Collective Action Organization (ICAO)? In an ICAO, investors work collectively, like a large shareholder, to monitor management and increase value. We analyze the endogenous formation of an ICAO and its equilibrium size, considering free-rider problems and coordination costs. While the ICAO overcomes free-rider problems among its members, it exacerbates them between the ICAO and solo activists. The benefit of joining an ICAO is hump-shaped in size. With moderate coordination costs, ICAO formation features multiple equilibria. Small changes in coordination costs significantly influence ICAO formation and activism. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: L. Yang thanks the support from the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council of Canada [Grants 435-2021-0040, 435-2026-0060] and the Bank of Canada [Fellowship]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.02975 .

papers.title: Worker Repositioning and Technological Change: Evidence from an Online Labor Market
papers.authors: Shun Yiu, Robert Seamans, Manav Raj, Teng Liu
papers.abstract: Technological change reshapes labor markets not only by changing labor demand but also by altering labor supply as workers reallocate effort across tasks and opportunities in response to technological advances. Yet research focuses more on demand-side effects than on how workers themselves adapt. In this research, we examine worker repositioning on a large online labor market following the launch of ChatGPT in November 2022. We argue that the launch of ChatGPT reduced expected returns to labor in exposed skill domains and develop and test a series of hypotheses regarding how this shock is associated with participation, horizontal positioning, and vertical positioning among workers on the platform. Using proprietary data on incumbent freelancers and a difference-in-differences design that leverages cross-sectional variation in preperiod AI exposure and skill level, we show that freelancers more exposed to AI shift away from prior domains and reorient bidding toward higher value contracts. In contrast, high skill-level freelancers, who face greater adjustment costs, are less likely to reduce participation on the platform, reposition across domains, and move upmarket. These findings highlight how technological shocks reshape labor markets through supply-side adaptation and how domain-specific human capital constrains worker responses. Funding: This work was supported by the Mack Institute for Innovation Management, Wharton School, University of Pennsylvania and the Smith-Richardson Foundation. Supplemental Material: The online appendix is available at https://doi.org/10.1287/orsc.2025.20566 .

papers.title: Feedback and Contagion through Distressed Competition
papers.authors: Hui Chen, Winston Wei Dou, 郭洪业, Yan Ji
papers.abstract: Firms tend to compete more aggressively when facing financial distress. This intensified competition reduces profit margins, pushing them further into distress and adversely affecting their industry peers. To study such feedback and contagion effects, we incorporate strategic competition in a dynamic model with long‐term defaultable debt, exploring various peer interactions such as predation and price wars. The feedback effect represents a novel source of financial distress costs associated with leverage, which helps explain the negative profitability‐leverage relation across industries. Owing to the contagion effect, firms' optimal leverage is often excessively high from an industry perspective, undermining the industry's financial stability.

papers.title: Generative AI and Firm Values
papers.authors: Andrea L. Eisfeldt, Gregor Schubert, Miao Ben Zhang, Bledi Taska
papers.abstract: How do recent advances in Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) affect firm value? We construct the first measure of firms' workforce exposures to Generative AI and show that an “Artificial‐Minus‐Human” portfolio earned 5% in the two weeks following the release of ChatGPT. The labor‐exposure effect is more pronounced for firms with greater data assets and is distinct from the effect of firms' product exposures to AI. We assess whether exposed workforces are substituted or complemented by Generative AI based on whether their exposed tasks are core or supplemental. Examining firms' labor demand and profitability following the release of ChatGPT supports a labor‐technology substitution channel.

papers.title: Choosing the Stage: The Strategic Role of Disclosure Venues in Guidance Revisions
papers.authors: Akash Chattopadhyay, Nayana Reiter, Mani Sethuraman
papers.abstract: When managers revise earnings guidance between earnings announcements, they choose not only what to disclose but also where to disclose—in a standalone release, a guidance call, an investor conference, or an analyst/investor (A/I) day. These venues differ in audience, format, and visibility, raising the question of whether venue choice is a strategic communication decision. In a large sample of unbundled revisions, we find that managers use calls for relatively large negative revisions and when litigation risk is higher and that they use conferences and A/I days for smaller revisions and when analyst disagreement is greater. Textual analysis reveals that calls feature cautious, litigious language for both upward and downward revisions, whereas conference and A/I day communications remain optimistic. In line with these framing differences, calls are associated with amplified reaction to negative news and are followed by more favorable earnings surprises, suggestive of effective expectation management, whereas conferences and A/I days are associated with muted reactions and reduced analyst dispersion and are followed by less favorable surprises. Our findings suggest that venue choice is a dimension of disclosure strategy for managers and an informative signal for investors.

papers.title: Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation for Ad Measurement
papers.authors: Brett R. Gordon, Robert Moakler, Florian Zettelmeyer
papers.abstract: Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) provide the most credible estimates of advertising incrementality but are difficult to scale. We propose Predicted Incrementality by Experimentation (PIE), which reframes ad measurement as a campaign-level prediction problem. PIE uses a sample of RCTs to learn a mapping from campaign features to causal effects, then applies it to campaigns not run as RCTs. Because the RCTs identify the causal effects, PIE can incorporate post-determined features—campaign-level aggregates such as test-group outcomes, exposure rates, and last-click conversions, computed after campaign completion. These metrics reflect the consumer behaviors that generate treatment effects, so they carry predictive information about incrementality, even though they would be invalid controls in a causal model. Using 2,226 Meta ad experiments, PIE achieves an out-of-sample [Formula: see text] for incremental conversions per dollar, compared with [Formula: see text] for industry-standard seven-day last-click attribution. In a decision-making framework, PIE disagrees with RCT-based decisions in only 8%–12% of campaigns, compared with 12%–20% for last-click attribution. We conclude that PIE can help scale causal measurement from a limited number of RCTs to a large set of nonexperimental campaigns. This paper was accepted by Raphael Thomadsen, marketing. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.01108 .

papers.title: The Power of Identity Pause: Perimenopause and the Embodiment Process
papers.authors: Madeline Toubiana, P. Devereaux Jennings
papers.abstract: A growing volume of identity scholarship has started to challenge the Cartesian separation of body and mind, highlighting the importance of embodiment. While such research is enlightening, studies do not provide in-depth understanding of how some workers, but not others, are able to develop embodied identities (i.e., identities that are bonded with and bounded by their physical body). In particular, little is known about how this embodiment process occurs—or fails to do so—when changes within a worker’s body threaten their idealized identities (who they want and believe they should be). We examine this puzzle through an inductive study of perimenopause, which is a naturally occurring physiological transition experienced by most women. Unlike studies that have emphasized the importance of remedial identity or body work, our findings point to the criticality of an identity pause, which involves taking respite from striving to enact idealized identities. We illuminate how an identity pause gives workers the space to develop somatic attunement: the capacity to connect with, listen to, and respect their changing bodies. In so doing, our study calls attention to distinctive mechanisms that help develop embodied identities, advancing research on the body–identity nexus, embodiment, and women and work.

papers.title: Repatterning Interactions in Remote Work Environments: Bolstering Psychological Safety Through Mutually Humanizing Self-Disclosure
papers.authors: Vanessa M. Conzon
papers.abstract: Existing research on psychological safety suggests that remote work might make it more challenging for workers to engage in the sorts of interactions that promote psychological safety. This raises the question: How is psychological safety bolstered when groups work remotely? Drawing on data from a seven-year longitudinal qualitative study—including 275 interviews and approximately 330 hours of observations—of a professional services organization that shifted from an in-person work environment to a remote work environment, I present a process model of how psychological safety can be strengthened among workers interacting virtually. I find that remote work supports interactional patterns that facilitate self-disclosure among group members. Learning more about one another, workers become mutually humanized, and psychological safety is bolstered. This psychological safety is accompanied by a set of associated practices that help people coordinate on work tasks while also sustaining flexibility in where and when they work. Reflecting improved psychological safety and associated practices, group members attend to and accomplish both work tasks and nonwork activities. This study contributes to the psychological safety literature by identifying a distinct process through which psychological safety can be promoted in remote work environments: mutual humanization via self-disclosure, which is supported through interactional patterns facilitated by remote work. Importantly, this distinct group-initiated process expands theorization beyond its current focus on leader-initiated social learning. This study also identifies how psychological safety supports role management, integrating theories of psychological safety and work-nonwork roles to expand understanding of psychological safe

papers.title: Dominant Deceptions: How Future-Oriented Narratives Transform into Deception
papers.authors: Tiona Žužul, Aharon Cohen Mohliver
papers.abstract: Drawing on a multiyear, qualitative study of a promising venture in a nascent industry, we develop a process model tracing how future-oriented narratives can transform into deception. In the venture that we studied, the founder’s future-oriented narratives were initially viewed as evidence of his visionary foresight. As these narratives traveled downward through the organization, employees responsible for operations translated this broad vision into specific targets and metrics. Some details described an attainable future; others were so far-fetched that they became liminal, falling into a gray zone between right and wrong. As internal and external demands for tangible progress grew, this expectations-reality gap prompted employees to engage in temporal reorientation, shifting their statements from “we will” to “we have.” Their statements crossed from liminal to deceptive, asserting as fact something that did not exist. Once formalized in presentations, websites, and other artefacts, the claims became dominant deceptions: codified, specific, past- or present-tense deceptions deliberately reproduced across the organization. In this codified form, the deceptions became misconduct that, if detected, could have been acted on by social control agents. We propose that three enabling conditions sustained this transformation: visionary attribution (belief in the founder’s unique foresight), interpretive flexibility (the ambiguity of new technologies that allows for multiple plausible meanings), and moral justification (the framing of deception as serving a higher mission). Because the process unfolded diffusely and incrementally, the transformation could only be observed retrospectively in the accumulation of actions across individuals and over time. papers.title: From Scarce Resources to Resourcing Spirals: A Theory of Mindful Resourcing
papers.authors: Cristina Rubino, Sara Jansen Perry, Ravi S. Kudesia, Ari A. Malka
papers.abstract: People in organizations often face demands in excess of their resources. Psychological theories of resources reflect this scarcity, emphasizing how people conserve or balance resources. Although they acknowledge that interventions, like mindfulness training, can create resources, these theories struggle to explain how as they assume that resources are necessarily scarce. In this study, we introduce a theory of mindful resourcing. Rather than reducing mindfulness to a scarce psychological resource that a person has, it reveals mindfulness to be a skillful practice that a person does to enhance their agency to create resources. Mindful resourcing theory shows how mindfulness skills form a foundation for resourcing—the ability to create and enact resources—and how resourcing reciprocally enhances mindfulness skills such that the practices of mindfulness and resourcing intertwine as mutually sustaining and supporting practices. We develop this theory across a three-phase research design that (1) introduces a conceptual model that sequences how these practices intertwine and (2) uses this sequencing to surface the otherwise implicit design structure of mindfulness trainings before (3) abductively building theory on how people enact and develop competence in mindful resourcing from longitudinal qualitative data of 98 nonprofit employees undergoing training. Our theory-building discovers the critical role of resourcing spirals—showing how employees create and enact resources by skillfully assembling spirals and recursively expanding those spirals into longer and more impactful sequences as they gain competence. Taken together, our study illuminates the understudied human activities by which people not only create and enact resources but learn to do so more mindfully. Funding:

papers.title: Feel Free to Chat About Your Kids? Exploring the Effects of Workplace Parenting Conversations
papers.authors: Yuxin Lin, Allison S. Gabriel, Katina B. Sawyer, Zhengguang Liu
papers.abstract: Workplace conversations are essential for collaboration, knowledge sharing, and relationship building. Although much of the literature has focused on work-related discussions, recent shifts toward the blurring of professional and personal boundaries suggest that employees may increasingly converse about aspects of their nonwork lives. One such topic of conversation—parenting—presents a unique and understudied type of workplace exchange given the central role of the parental identity for working parents and the opportunity for them to highlight this important identity through dialogue. In the current set of studies, we introduce workplace parenting conversations as dialogical, in-depth exchanges about parenting-related topics between coworkers who are parents. Drawing from identity management and boundary management theories, we propose that these conversations offer instrumental, affective, and relational benefits that positively impact behaviors across work and parenting role domains. Using a mixed-methods triangulation approach, we first explore the content and processes of workplace parenting conversations through qualitative interviews (Study 1A), followed by an experience sampling study testing our model, complete with behavioral outcomes at work and home (Study 1B). We then explore the underlying micromechanisms connecting workplace parenting conversations to the mechanisms in our model through additional interviews (Study 2A) and a field experiment (Study 2B). Our findings contribute to the literature on workplace conversations by identifying an overlooked yet impactful form of workplace dialogue, exploring its primarily positive effects on employees’ behaviors in both work and home contexts and uncovering unique micromechanisms associated with this specific type

papers.title: From trade-off to paradox: a configurational theorizing and “quantum” approach to the resilience–sustainability tension in global sourcing
papers.authors: G. Grassi, Stefano Elia, Cristina Di Stefano, Michela Guida, Federico Francesco Angelo Caniato
papers.abstract: Global sourcing is increasingly caught between two persistent pressures: to be sustainable and resilient. While this relationship is often framed as a trade-off, we draw on paradox theory to conceptualize it as a persistent paradox, especially for MNEs coordinating complex supplier networks. Most paradox research addresses either how tensions are embedded in organizational systems or how they are socially constructed by managers, but rarely both. Drawing on the "quantum" approach to paradox, we bridge these ontological and epistemological perspectives, arguing that the resilience–sustainability tension is rooted in the structure of global sourcing systems and made salient through how managers interpret and combine sourcing decisions. Following a configurational roadmap of three stages—scoping, linking, and naming—we theorize five systemic sourcing factors (location choice, supplier redundancy, inventory buffer, green certification, and the sustainability premium) and examine how they are evaluated by 72 Italian procurement managers through a factorial survey, a fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis, and interviews. Managers favor coherent bundles over standalone levers, combining certification-based sustainability assurance alongside resilience-oriented levers such as proximity, redundancy, and buffers. We conceptualize three archetypal sourcing logics— integrator, resilience-first, and cost-only —offering managers a practical vocabulary for framing and legitimating sourcing choices when both pressures collide.

papers.title: Targeted Philanthropy: Evidence from M&As
papers.authors: Cara Vansteenkiste
papers.abstract: I show how firms optimize the allocation of charitable funds around investments that require external stakeholder support, such as mergers and acquisitions. Acquirers increase donations to target‐related charities before making a takeover offer, but scale funds back after withdrawing from a deal. Firms redistribute funds from nontakeover‐related areas to target insider–affiliated charities, employee communities, and counties with a regulatory presence. Targeted donations that encourage blockholder reciprocity and employee commitment are associated with better deal performance through decreased merger premiums and lower integration costs. Overall, the results highlight firms’ use of philanthropy to manage stakeholder relations in takeover decisions.

papers.title: When Do Treasuries Earn the Convenience Yield?—A Hedging Perspective
papers.authors: Viral V. Acharya, Toomas Laarits
papers.abstract: We document that the convenience yield of U.S. Treasuries exhibits properties consistent with a hedging perspective of safe assets, that is, Treasuries are valued highly if they appreciate with poor aggregate shocks. In particular, the convenience yield tends to be low when the covariance of Treasury returns with the aggregate stock market returns is high. A decomposition of the aggregate stock‐bond covariance into terms corresponding to the convenience yield, the frictionless risk‐free rate, and default risk reveals that the covariance between stock returns and the convenience yield itself drives the effect in a substantive capacity.

papers.title: Flow‐Driven ESG Returns
papers.authors: PHILIPPE VAN DER BECK
papers.abstract: I show that the recent returns to environmental, social, and governance (ESG) investing are strongly driven by price impact from flows toward ESG portfolios. Using data on trades, I estimate the market's ability to accommodate ESG flows, which is given by the elasticity of substitution between ESG and other stocks. I show that every dollar flowing toward a representative ESG portfolio increases the market value of ESG stocks by $0.8. The growing institutional flows into the ESG portfolio are the main driver of ESG returns and have caused an annual flow‐driven return of 1.9%. In the absence of flows, ESG stocks would not have outperformed the market from 2012 to 2023.

papers.title: Are Markups Too High? Competition, Strategic Innovation, and Industry Dynamics
papers.authors: Laurent Cavenaile, Murat Alp Celik, Xu Tian
papers.abstract: To study competition, innovation, and industry dynamics that arise as a result of their interaction, we develop a new oligopolistic general-equilibrium Schumpeterian growth model. This model ties together the endogenous growth, oligopolistic competition, and dynamic industrial organization literatures in a single unified framework. Within each industry, there are an endogenously determined number of large firms (“superstars”) that compete à la Cournot and a continuum of small firms which collectively constitute a competitive fringe. Firms dynamically choose their innovation strategies, cognizant of other firms’ choices, and their entry and exit are endogenous. The model is consistent with the macroeconomic trends observed in the US since the 1970s, such as the domination of industries by a small number of superstar firms, the rise of markups, market concentration, profits, and R&D spending, and the decline in business dynamism, productivity growth, and the labour share. It replicates the empirical relationship between innovation and competition within and across industries. As an application, we estimate the model to disentangle the effects of separate mechanisms on the structural transition observed in the US, which yields striking results: (1) While the increase in the average markup causes a significant static welfare loss, this loss is overshadowed by the dynamic welfare gains from increased innovation in response to higher profit opportunities. (2) The increasing costs of innovation are found to be the primary determinant of lacklustre productivity growth, i.e. ideas are getting harder to find.

papers.title: Using Representation Learning and Website Text to Identify Competitor Networks
papers.authors: Gerard Hoberg, Craig A. Knoblock, Gordon M. Phillips, Jay Pujara, Zhiqiang Qiu, Louiqa Raschid
papers.abstract: This paper introduces a new approach to identify competitors using company websites to map competitive relationships among public and private firms. We apply representation learning techniques to create embeddings of companies based on website content, emphasizing information about industry-specific products and services. By placing all firms, public and private, within the same embedding space, we construct a peer competitor network that supports analysis of company interactions and market evolution. We label this new approach and set of network competitors as the website text-based network industry classification (WTNIC). We evaluate the quality of the network using multiple ground truth datasets and benchmarks and show that it offers a robust alternative for understanding competition at scale. Despite using noisy website data, WTNIC matches or outperforms prior approaches that rely on curated data. We demonstrate the value of WTNIC through a case study examining how competition from China affects the public and private peers of a focal firm, highlighting the importance of placing both public and private companies within the same embedding space. Funding: This work was supported by the National Science Foundation [Grants 1561068 and 1937153], the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth College, the USC Marshall Institute for Outlier Research in Business (iORB), and the Smith School of Business at the University of Maryland. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06516 .

papers.title: Personalization, Engagement, and Content Quality on Social Media: An Evaluation of Reddit’s News Feed
papers.authors: Alex Moehring
papers.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly curate their content through personalized algorithmic feeds. Platforms have an incentive to promote content that increases the predicted engagement of each user to lift advertising revenues. This paper studies how ranking content to maximize engagement affects the credibility of news content with which users engage. In addition, I evaluate how the ranking algorithm itself can be designed to promote engagement with high-credibility content. Using data from the Reddit politics community, I exploit a novel discontinuity in the ranking algorithm to identify the causal effect of a post’s rank on the number of comments it receives. I use this discontinuity to identify a model of user comment decisions and estimate the credibility of news content that users engage with under a personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm. The personalized engagement-maximizing algorithm exacerbates differences in the credibility of news content with which users engage. I then evaluate a credibility-aware algorithm that explicitly promotes credible news publishers and find the platform can substantially increase the share of engagement with high-credibility publishers for a small reduction in total engagement. These findings suggest algorithmic interventions can be a useful tool for managers to balance engagement quantity and content quality. This paper was accepted by Hemant Bhargava, information systems. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.06298 .

papers.title: Chronologically consistent large language models
papers.authors: Songrun He, Linying Lv, Asaf Manela, Jimmy Wu
papers.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used in social sciences, but their training data can introduce lookahead bias and training leakage. A good chronologically consistent language model requires efficient use of training data to maintain accuracy despite time-restricted data. Here, we overcome this challenge by training a suite of chronologically consistent large language models, ChronoBERT and ChronoGPT, which incorporate only the text data that would have been available at each point in time. Despite this strict temporal constraint, our models achieve strong performance on natural language processing benchmarks, outperforming or matching widely used models (e.g., BERT), and remain competitive with larger open-weight models. Lookahead bias is model and application-specific because even if a chronologically consistent language model has poorer language comprehension, a regression or prediction model applied on top of the language model can compensate. In an asset pricing application predicting next-day stock returns from financial news embeddings, we find that ChronoBERT and ChronoGPT’s real-time outputs achieve Sharpe ratios comparable to a much larger and potentially biased Llama model. Our results demonstrate a scalable, practical framework to mitigate training leakage, ensuring more credible backtests and predictions across finance and other social science domains.

papers.title: The decline of branch banking
papers.authors: Rajesh P Narayanan, Dimuthu Ratnadiwakara, Philip E. Strahan

papers.title: Trading Off Business and Family Investments: Evidence from U.S. Entrepreneurial Households
papers.authors: Olivia Kim
papers.abstract: Investing in children’s human capital reduces business investments for U.S. entrepreneurial households. Using financial account data of 90,000 small businesses linked to their owners and a regression discontinuity design that compares the business performance of households with college-aged dependents (18–22) to those with near-college-aged dependents (14–17), I show that business revenues and expenses decline sharply when owners’ children reach age 18. Despite the declines, profitability and productivity remain largely unaffected, suggesting a general downsizing rather than a loss in efficiency. Heterogeneity analysis shows that downsizing is concentrated among highly indebted owner households and businesses with volatile cash flows. For each dollar increase in household spending associated with a child turning 18, business expenses decline by $2.26. These findings are consistent with entrepreneurial parents reallocating capital from business investments toward their children’s human capital, as both compete for the same pool of internal family financial resources. This paper was accepted by Camelia Kuhnen, finance. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.04789 .

papers.title: Money Creation for Crypto Space: Stablecoins or Central Bank Digital Currencies?
papers.authors: Jonathan Chiu, Cyril Monnet
papers.abstract: Stablecoins are the current go-to digital money to settle transactions on the blockchain. We explore the implications of introducing competing tokenized public digital monies (i.e., tokenized central bank digital currencies (CBDCs)). When they pay a moderate interest rate and guarantee users’ anonymity, tokenized CBDCs crowd out stablecoins. However, when they pay a high interest rate and have low anonymity features, stablecoin issuers could use tokenized CBDCs as collateral, promoting the creation of stablecoins. We identify conditions under which introducing a CBDC to compete with stablecoins in the crypto sector would be socially optimal. This paper was accepted by Will Cong for the Virtual Special Issue on Digital Finance. Funding: Support from Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) [Grant 100018 219835].

papers.title: Creation after destruction? Financial intermediation and firm entry after bank cleanups
papers.authors: Nishant Kashyap, Prasanna L. Tantri
papers.abstract: We study a large and unanticipated bank cleanup in India after prolonged zombie lending under regulatory forbearance. The cleanup forced widespread zombie exits through bankruptcy. In contrast to a frictionless world where entry automatically follows exit, we show that with financial frictions, local banking conditions shape creation after destruction. New firm entry occurs primarily in regions where banks are present, well-capitalized, competitive, and possess sectoral expertise. We further find a decline in the dispersion of total factor productivity in regions with stronger financial intermediation, consistent with a reduction in misallocation in such areas.

papers.title: The Welfare Effects of Selling Leads in a Two-Sided Marketplace
papers.authors: Peng Shi
papers.abstract: Digital platforms that connect customers with service providers often monetize by selling customer leads to interested providers. Examples include Bark, Google Local Services, HomeAdvisor, Modernize, Porch, and Thumbtack. This paper develops a game-theoretic model to analyze how lead pricing affects customer and provider welfare. When the platform raises the fee-per-lead for a customer-type, those customers—conditional on receiving the same number of provider quotes—are quoted lower prices. However, if the fee is sufficiently high, providers purchase fewer of these leads, which can reduce the number of quotes and diminish customer surplus. To maximize social welfare, a simple policy that sets a market-clearing fee-per-lead for each customer-type guarantees at least [Formula: see text] of the first-best welfare and at least [Formula: see text] of the welfare under the welfare-optimal fees. The first-best outcome can be achieved by subsidizing providers for each job well done, so that experienced providers with cheaper sources of leads do not exit the platform. Understanding these welfare trade-offs can help platforms design policies that support balanced marketplace growth and preserve a sustainable revenue stream. This paper was accepted by Srikanth Jagabathula, market design, platform, and demand analytics. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07399 .

papers.title: Early Environmental Shocks and Organizational Reconfiguration in High-Growth Ventures
papers.authors: Sunasir Dutta, Pyung Nahm, Luis Adrian Rios
papers.abstract: We study whether shocks from local natural disasters can leave durable organizational traces in young high-growth ventures. In principle, such firms may be relatively resilient to localized disruption because they are designed to scale beyond local markets and rely heavily on knowledge-based assets. We examine this possibility using a panel of 19,984 U.S. startups founded between 1985 and 2010 that subsequently received venture financing. We identify ventures whose founding counties experience natural disasters within 12 months of founding using FEMA Major Disaster Declarations. Ventures exposed to disasters at an early stage exhibit higher subsequent failure hazards and no general advantage in follow-on financing, yet show higher IPO hazards in favorable market windows, a pattern consistent with greater responsiveness to opportunities requiring substantial organizational reconfiguration. Descriptive employee-level evidence further documents differences in organizational structure and composition consistent with greater retained fluidity among exposed ventures. Drawing on organization design and imprinting theory, we interpret these patterns as consistent with the possibility that disasters function as forcing environments that entrench early-stage coordination features such as flatness, role fluidity, and broader expertise that would otherwise attenuate as ventures mature. These durable organizational traces may, in turn, shape ventures’ subsequent capacity for reconfiguration. We discuss implications for organizational adaptation, imprinting, entrepreneurial geography, and organizational responses to crises.

papers.title: Specialists' Evidence Evaluation and Judgments in Audits
papers.authors: Tim D. Bauer, Cassandra Estep, Emily Elaine Griffith
papers.abstract: Audits of complex fair value estimates involve evaluating and challenging key client assumptions. Auditors generally lack the necessary expertise to perform this work, and thus, they often engage valuation specialists to perform this audit work. However, valuation specialists primarily perform advisory work and may not put enough care into their audit work. We examine whether valuation specialists' psychological ownership of audit work and auditors' infringement on that work affect specialists' judgment quality. Using a survey and an experiment with practicing valuation specialists, we find that higher psychological ownership improves specialists' evidence evaluation and judgments, but only when auditors do not behave intrusively by infringing on their work. When auditors behave intrusively, the benefits of specialists' higher psychological ownership disappear. Our findings show that audit quality depends not only on specialist behavior but also on auditor interactions with specialists. Our study offers practical guidance to audit firms on how to organize audit work and manage internal working relationships between auditors and valuation specialists.

papers.title: Climate regulatory risks and corporate bonds
papers.authors: Lee Seltzer, Laura T. Starks, Qifei Zhu

papers.title: Analysts’ Perspectives on Climate Change: An Examination of Analyst Reports
papers.authors: Jesse Y. Chan
papers.abstract: I explore the nature of analysts’ climate-related discussion in their reports. Focusing on industries most exposed to climate change, I find very few reports (less than 2 percent) and a minority of analysts (less than 11 percent) discuss climate-related topics. Analysts concentrate climate-related discussion among utilities, mostly discussing renewable energy and regulatory issues. These discussions exhibit no significant association with short-term earnings forecasts and a weak association with more pessimistic long-term growth forecast revisions. Climate-related discussion is also associated with more optimistic target prices when analysts do not issue long-term growth forecasts, suggesting the development of a long-term perspective correlates with views on climate-related issues. Discussions of solar-, emissions-, and automotive-related topics are associated with this greater target price optimism. These findings highlight how analysts’ climate-related discussion relates to long-term expectations and concentrates among highly exposed firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. A detailed listing of how each large language model (LLM) classified each climate-related report, a document describing the details of this listing, a firm-year summary of climate-related discussion and subtopical classifications, and a description document of this firm-year summary are available upon request. JEL Classifications: Q56; G24; M41.

papers.title: Sales-Based CEO Incentives and Their Effect Across the Supply Chain
papers.authors: Jae Eun Choi
papers.abstract: I examine how the use of sales performance measures in CEO incentive contracts affects the operations of a firm and its suppliers. A growing number of firms are evaluating and compensating their CEOs based on sales performance. However, because sales performance measures are narrow measures that do not incentivize cost control, they can influence operational decisions that affect not only the firm but also its suppliers. I show that the use of sales performance measures in CEO bonus contracts is associated with inventory fluctuations that increase the bullwhip effect, a phenomenon in which a firm exhibits greater volatility in production than in demand, thereby increasing the order volatility faced by its suppliers. Instrumental variable tests using the firm’s network connections through compensation consultants mitigate concerns that the results are driven by omitted factors. Collectively, my findings illuminate spillover effects of CEO incentive contracts on economically linked firms. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: M10; M12; M40; M41; M52.

papers.title: Enabling Employee Adaptability to Change: The Joint Effect of Compensation Contract and Process Accountability
papers.authors: M. Abts, Martine Cools, Sabra Khajehnejad, Alexandra G. H. L. Van den Abbeele
papers.abstract: Organizations increasingly operate in uncertain environments, requiring employees to revise task strategies to remain effective. We examine how pay for performance (PFP) influences adaptive performance following unanticipated change and argue that process accountability moderates this effect. Although PFP increases effort, it hinders adaptation by reinforcing persistence with an existing task strategy. Process accountability channels PFP-induced motivation into deeper strategic deliberation, enabling adaptation. We test our predictions in an experiment manipulating compensation (PFP versus flat wage) and process accountability (absent, reflection-only, and present), with participants in the reflection-only condition privately reflecting on their decision-making to isolate the social-evaluative component. Results show that PFP, relative to a flat wage, decreases adaptive performance when process accountability is absent, has no significant effect under reflection-only, and increases it when process accountability is present. Additional analyses suggest that strategic deliberation partially explains this effect. The findings underscore pairing PFP with process accountability to foster adaptation. Data Availability: Data are available upon request. JEL Classifications: D91; M21; M41; M52.

papers.title: The Signaling Role of Seemingly Myopic Investment Behavior
papers.authors: Cyrus Aghamolla, Vivian W. Fang, Renhui Fu
papers.abstract: This paper analytically and empirically investigates managerial investment responses to negative shocks in firm value. In the model, managers are privately informed about the shocks’ persistence, and those facing transitory shocks strategically underinvest to boost earnings and signal financial strength to investors. The model also predicts counter-signaling: firms with strong fundamentals do not need to cut investment to convey strength. We exploit the 2003 mutual fund trading scandal as a plausibly exogenous source of price pressure. Consistent with signaling, we find that firms with greater tainted-fund ownership are more likely to meet or narrowly beat analyst forecasts by cutting R&D, and that this behavior is associated with more favorable earnings announcement returns and better long-run performance. Consistent with counter-signaling, these firms are less likely to cut R&D when they beat analyst forecasts by a wide margin. Cross-sectional tests also support the model’s comparative statics. Data Availability: All data used in the study are publicly available from the sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: C73; D82; G23; G31; G34.

papers.title: CEO Tax Lock-In and Share Pledging
papers.authors: Jonathan Underwood, BENJAMIN P. YOST
papers.abstract: We study how CEOs’ personal tax incentives shape their share pledging decisions and firms’ restrictions on the practice. Pledging shares entails using company stock as collateral for personal loans, enabling executives to obtain liquidity without making a taxable sale of appreciated shares. Using pledging data from 2006 to 2024, we find a robust positive relation between CEOs’ unrealized capital gains tax liabilities, or tax burdens, and share pledging. This relation is weaker when interest rates are high, consistent with CEOs’ trading off tax benefits against borrowing costs. After Institutional Shareholder Services discouraged share pledging in 2012, firms with high-tax-burden CEOs were slower to adopt antipledging policies and, when they did adopt, chose less restrictive policies. Firms that adopted strong antipledging policies subsequently increased CEO cash pay and stock awards. Our evidence suggests that share pledging helps executives manage personal tax lock-in and that firms consider this benefit when restricting pledging. Data Availability: Data are available from the public and subscription sources identified in the text, subject to applicable data-use restrictions. JEL Classifications: G30; H24; J33; M52.

papers.title: Do Commercial Property Taxes Affect Business Microlocation Decisions?
papers.authors: Brayden Bulloch, Fabio B. Gaertner, Jeffrey L. Hoopes
papers.abstract: Do commercial property taxes affect business microlocation decisions? Using precise geolocations for 2.8 million U.S. establishments, we employ a spatial discontinuity density design, comparing for-profit establishments to nonprofits, which are generally exempt from property taxes. Relative to nonprofit establishments, for-profit establishments disproportionately locate on the low-tax side of county borders. This effect strengthens with the size of the tax differential. At borders with differentials in the top decile (quartile), we estimate a 6–7 (5–6) percent shift in establishment location toward the low-tax side over a 10-km band. Businesses move from as far as 10 km away on the high-tax side but concentrate within 1 km on the low-tax side. Firms trade off tax savings with customer access: low-foot-traffic establishments respond more to tax differentials than high-foot-traffic ones. A survey of U.S. mayors finds that perceptions of property taxes’ importance for business location rise with cross-border tax differentials. Data Availability: Survey data are available upon request. All other data were obtained from publicly and commercially available sources described in the manuscript. JEL Classifications: H25; H71; H73; R32.

papers.title: Unwinding Loan Prospecting Pressure through Renegotiation: The Role of Loan Officer Changes in Debt Contracting
papers.authors: Jessie Cheong, Jung Koo Kang, Regina Wittenberg Moerman
papers.abstract: We examine the impact of loan officer changes on debt contract design. Loan officers face pressure to originate new loans, incentivizing them to offer loan terms that are more favorable than warranted by borrowers’ creditworthiness. Because a loan officer who replaces the originating loan officer is not subject to this loan prospecting pressure, we predict that she reverses the favorable discretion exercised at loan origination. Consistent with this prediction, we find that the first renegotiation following the replacement of the originating loan officer is associated with more unfavorable renegotiation outcomes. This effect is more pronounced when loan prospecting pressure at loan origination is greater—when the originating loan officer is less experienced, when the lead arranger faces tight performance benchmarks or lower income growth, and when credit market competition is more intense. Overall, we provide novel insights into how loan officer changes restore contracting efficiency through renegotiations. Data Availability: Syndicated loan data are from DealScan; borrower financial data are from Compustat and CRSP; bank financial data are from the Call Report and Compustat; loan agreements are from Morningstar, FactSet, and SEC filings; analyst data are from I/B/E/S; credit rating data are from S&P Global Ratings and the Mergent Fixed Income Securities Database (FISD); media coverage data are from RavenPack; covenant violation data are from Nini, Smith, and Sufi (2012); and loan officer employment histories were hand collected from LinkedIn. JEL Classifications: G21; G30; G32; J24.

papers.title: Tax-Related Key Audit Matters and Changes in Multinational Income Shifting
papers.authors: Christof Beuselinck, Nathan C. Goldman, Jochen Pierk, Cinthia Valle Ruiz
papers.abstract: Key audit matters (KAMs) increase the salience of uncertainty surrounding the underlying accounts. We examine KAMs related to uncertain tax positions (UTPs), which highlight potential concerns to external stakeholders about uncertain tax planning activities such as multinational income shifting. Increased scrutiny may reduce the expected benefits of these strategies and discourage firms from pursuing them. Using KAM disclosures in the expanded audit reports, we find that group-level KAM disclosures are associated with a decline in multinational income shifting when the KAMs relate to UTPs. This relation is stronger when firms are financially unconstrained, when the institutional environment features strong tax enforcement, and when KAMs highlight specific risk statements and auditors provide explicit assurance. Overall, our findings reveal a novel and potentially unintended real effect of expanded audit reports: the salience of tax-related KAM disclosures influences multinational tax planning, highlighting broader consequences of this regulatory intervention. Data Availability: Data are available from the public sources cited in the text. JEL Classifications: H25; H26; H40.

papers.title: The Effect of Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income Tax on U.S. Multinational Companies’ Cross-Border Tangible Investments
papers.authors: Jing Yang Huang, Benjamin Osswald, Ryan J. Wilson
papers.abstract: The Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income (GILTI) provision, enacted under the 2017 U.S. tax reform, aimed to deter profit shifting by U.S. multinational corporations (MNCs) but has raised concerns about unintended incentives to shift tangible investments abroad. Using an ex ante identification strategy based on public financial statements, we document that an average MNC increases foreign tangible investment by approximately $256.2 million relative to 2017 levels to minimize GILTI tax. Although this finding could raise concerns that firms are reducing domestic tangible investment for foreign expansion, we find no significant decline in domestic tangible investment. Furthermore, we find GILTI firms increase both foreign and domestic innovation, including capital-intensive technologies. The positive domestic innovation spillovers support the intended effect of the U.S. tax reform in boosting domestic economic growth. Our evidence reveals how international tax provisions, though aimed at curbing profit shifting, can simultaneously create unintended incentives. JEL Classifications: M41; H25; H26.

papers.title: From Text to Beta: Macroeconomic Disclosures and Firm-Level Systematic Risk
papers.authors: Cameron Holstead, Alon Kalay, Gil Sadka, Federico Siano
papers.abstract: Using news text from The Wall Street Journal and macroeconomic disclosures in 10-K filings, we address the challenge of characterizing both time-varying aggregate risks and firm-level risk exposures. We develop a disclosure-based measure of systematic risk that (1) reveals salient macro risks in each period, (2) provides a text-based estimate of earnings exposure to these risks, and (3) explains the cross-section of stock returns. We also show that macro disclosures are pervasive across the annual report, grow over time, vary with the business cycle, and exhibit within-firm variation, consistent with the time-varying nature of systematic risk exposure. Overall, disclosures yield transparent and economically interpretable estimates of firm-level systematic risk. Data Availability: Data are obtained from SEC filings, Bureau of Economic Analysis, The Wall Street Journal, Compustat, CRSP, I/B/E/S. JEL Classifications: E31; E32; G11; G12; M21; M41.

papers.title: Social Media Toxicity and Capital Markets
papers.authors: Elizabeth Blankespoor, Jedson Pereira Pinto, Kirti Sinha
papers.abstract: This paper asks about the existence, determinants, and implications of toxic content in financial social media. Using machine learning algorithms to measure toxicity in Seeking Alpha articles and comments, we find measurable toxicity concentrated primarily in user-generated comments rather than articles. Comment toxicity is greater for firms with more investor attention or uncertainty. We document three key results about toxicity in capital markets. First, toxicity displays a feedback loop in platform participation: past toxicity is associated with more future toxic contributors for a given firm. Second, firms receiving more toxic comments have greater retail trading volume but less informative retail trades, especially when comments disagree. Third, toxicity is associated with slower price discovery around earnings announcements. Our findings suggest that financial social media toxicity relates to both user behavior and market outcomes and raise important considerations for platform governance in financial markets. Data Availability: The Seeking Alpha articles and comments used in this study were obtained directly from Seeking Alpha under a data-sharing arrangement and are proprietary; we are not permitted to redistribute them. These data may be requested from Seeking Alpha. Compustat, Execucomp, CRSP, and New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) Trade and Quote (TAQ) data are available through Wharton Research Data Services (WRDS) to subscribing institutions. JEL Classifications: G14; G41; D83; D91.

papers.title: Building Better Information: Reporting Technology, Internal Information Frictions, and Investment Efficiency
papers.authors: Philip G. Berger, Feng Li, Lisa Yao Liu, M.H. Franco Wong
papers.abstract: We assess how firms use spending on reporting infrastructure to improve managerial reporting quality (MRQ) and whether doing so improves investment efficiency. Using the Sarbanes-Oxley Act’s internal control provisions (SOX 404) as a shock to MRQ demand, we find that treated firms increase reporting infrastructure spending, including for information technology and communications. We next examine variation across segments in the benefits and costs of improving reporting infrastructure. Segments increase spending more when facing larger internal moral hazard frictions and when they are less likely to have voluntarily improved MRQ before SOX (including segments insulated from competition, facing difficulty obtaining enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, or lacking internal control personnel). Finally, we find that treated firms improve investment efficiency post-SOX 404, with larger gains among firms with higher spending on reporting infrastructure. Our findings indicate that regulatory mandates can improve investment efficiency by inducing reporting infrastructure improvements that enhance MRQ. JEL Classifications: D83; G15; G18; G38; L15; M41; M42.

papers.title: Determinants and Consequences of Auditors’ Consultations with the National Office
papers.authors: Matthew G. Sherwood, Miguel Minutti‐Meza, Aleksandra B. Zimmerman
papers.abstract: Audit teams may consult with their firm’s national office to obtain specialized expertise, satisfy regulatory and quality control requirements, and demonstrate due professional care. We describe the consultation process based on PCAOB standards, firm methodologies, and auditor interviews. We explain different types of consultations and highlight differences in the determinants and usefulness of mandatory versus voluntary consultations. Using PCAOB inspection data, we show that formal consultations are largely predictable based on engagement characteristics and, on average, are not associated with audit quality. However, two subsets of formal consultations that focus on accounting issues and occur earlier in the engagement process are associated with greater regulatory compliance and higher audit quality. Hence, an increasing reliance on all types of consultations does not automatically translate into higher audit quality. Collectively, our findings deepen our understanding of auditors’ use of national office consultations and their implications for audit practice. Data Availability: Audit engagement data from the PCAOB are proprietary; other data are from public sources. JEL Classification: M4.

papers.title: Beyond Greenwashing: Environmental Commitments and Gas Flaring in the African Oil Sector
papers.authors: Samuel Chang, Hans Bonde Christensen, Andrew J. Mckinley
papers.abstract: Corporations make substantial progress toward their Zero Routine Flaring commitments globally, particularly in Africa where preexisting environmental standards are weak. Moreover, committers’ flaring reductions on the continent are driven primarily by operational improvements rather than offloading assets and are concentrated among committers facing greater stakeholder pressure. Although flaring is higher for assets continuously operated by, awarded to, or divested to noncommitters, corporate actions to uphold commitments are associated with a conservatively estimated 10 percent net reduction in flaring in Africa without a corresponding reduction in oil production or local economic activity in extraction communities. Our findings suggest that environmental commitments are backed by corporate policies akin to establishing a uniform cost of pollution across the firm’s global operations and therefore may alleviate the problems posed by globally fragmented regulation. Data Availability: All data except for Enverus oil and gas are publicly available. Enverus is available for purchase on a subscription basis. JEL Classifications: F18; K23; K32; L71; M14; M48; N57; O13; Q35; Q52; Q53; Q56.

papers.title: Productivity versus Efficiency: The Effect of Incentive Focus on Target Setting in Participative Budgets
papers.authors: Jake Andrassy, Jason L. Brown, Timothy Mallon, Ashley Sauciuc
papers.abstract: Firms typically design incentive systems to motivate employees and advance firm objectives, including productivity (i.e., maximizing output) and efficiency (i.e., minimizing input). However, there remains little empirical research on the potential psychological effects of adopting a productivity versus efficiency focus on employee risk perceptions and decision-making. To address this important gap, we examine how these different incentive foci affect employee target setting under participative budgets. We predict and find that employees perceive efficiency incentives as riskier than productivity incentives, leading to lower target setting. Moreover, consistent with our theory, this effect disappears in the absence of outcome uncertainty. We also find employees are less likely to achieve their target and have higher error rates under efficiency incentives, despite setting easier targets. Overall, our findings suggest that efficiency incentives, relative to productivity incentives, can have detrimental effects on target setting and subsequent performance in participative budgeting settings. Data Availability: Contact the authors. JEL Classifications: M41; M52; J33.

papers.title: Internal Control over Financial Reporting and Mortgage Fraud
papers.authors: Yiwei Dou, Danye Wang, Xi Wu
papers.abstract: Mortgage fraud was a leading force behind the 2008 financial crisis. We measure the fraudulent income overstatement at the bank-ZIP Code-year level as the difference in the local growth between reported income in mortgage applications and the income based on IRS data. We find that overstated income is positively associated with banks’ internal control weaknesses over financial reporting and negatively associated with subsequent remediation of such weaknesses. The associations are concentrated among banks that integrate their accounting and operation processes, as proxied by the adoption of an Enterprise Resource Planning system. Finally, using the removal of internal control provisions in the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Improvement Act in 2005 as a shock to internal control quality, we find that affected banks experience increased income overstatement on mortgage applications. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from the public and proprietary sources identified in the article. Access to proprietary data is subject to the relevant providers’ licensing restrictions. JEL Classifications: G01; G21; G28; G51; M41.

papers.title: How Black Accounting Faculty Exercise Agency to Navigate Career Advancement within Institutional Structures
papers.authors: Michelle K. Harding, Jennifer R. Joe, Kerri‐Ann Sanderson
papers.abstract: This study examines how tenured BAF experience and navigate institutional structures while advancing their careers. Leveraging a qualitative approach, we find BAF encounter recurring forms of marginalization embedded in organizational structures that lead to social identity threats that destabilize their identities as scholars and teachers. BAF respond to these threats by employing agentic and self-preserving coping responses designed to affirm identity and negotiate career advancement. Although coping responses can be effective on an individual level, they do not transform institutional structures and can provoke pushback that reinscribes marginalization. The findings unsettle common assumptions that effort in conditions marked by objectivity and neutrality drives career advancement and highlight the institutional structures and invisible labor that BAF navigate to achieve career advancement. We fill the void in the literature examining how career advancement unfolds within racialized conditions of academic institutions and advance research on minoritized group status in accounting academia.

papers.title: IPOs and Foreign Tax Structures
papers.authors: Christine L. Dobridge, Rebecca Lester, Andrew Whitten
papers.abstract: Does going public affect the amount and type of corporate international tax planning? Using a panel of U.S. corporate tax return data from 2004 to 2018, we show that IPO completion is associated with the rapid implementation of multinational foreign tax structures. Specifically, within three years after filing for an IPO, firms (1) expand their presence in low-tax jurisdictions, (2) enter into cross-border agreements that accompany intangible asset transfers to foreign subsidiaries, and (3) increase the likelihood and level of foreign related-party income-shifting payments. Effects are strongest among firms with strong capital market pressure to hit post-IPO earnings targets, firms with high R&D spending pre-IPO, and firms with limited ability to use net operating loss carryforwards. We contribute to the nascent literature studying tax implications of IPOs by documenting the types and timing of specific tax strategies that enable public firms to remain lightly taxed in the post-IPO period. JEL Classifications: F23; H25; H26.

papers.title: Balancing Act: How Unaffiliated Analysts Navigate Private Information Disadvantages
papers.authors: Leila Peyravan, Brian Robert Rountree, K. Sivaramakrishnan
papers.abstract: Using analyst-lender affiliation in syndicated loans as a proxy for differential access to private information, we examine how unaffiliated analysts respond to this disadvantage. We find that unaffiliated analysts are more likely to herd toward affiliated analysts following loan origination, leading to improved forecast accuracy but weaker market reactions, consistent with reduced information content. In addition, herding analysts improve their forecast accuracy for other firms in their portfolios relative to nonherding analysts, suggesting a reallocation of effort. To capture information acquisition directly, we analyze IP address data from SEC EDGAR log files and find that unaffiliated analysts increase search activity, driven primarily by those not designated as herding. Although herding behavior wanes after the first year post-loan, elevated EDGAR searches persist for three years. Overall, our study provides novel evidence on how selective access to private information influences analysts’ competitive behavior. Data Availability: Data used in this study are available from public sources identified in the text, subject to the terms and conditions of those sources. JEL Classifications: G24; G14; G29.

papers.title: Capital Market Pressure and Racial Inequality in Labor Violations
papers.authors: Seth Carnahan, Sarah E. McVay, MaryJane Rabier
papers.abstract: Managers can boost reported earnings to meet capital market expectations by pursuing aggressive cost-minimization strategies that violate labor laws, such as pressuring frontline employees to forgo safety protocols or work off the clock. We investigate whether labor law violations, which benefit the firm at the expense of employees, fall disproportionately on nonwhite frontline employees. Across similar locations (e.g., stores or plants) within the same firm, we predict and find that locations with a higher share of nonwhite frontline employees are more likely to experience a labor law violation. This racial inequality in labor violations is especially pronounced in settings more prone to racial discrimination and during periods of acute capital market pressure to meet earnings benchmarks, providing insight into the mechanisms underlying the observed disparity. Our evidence suggests that capital market pressure is associated not only with labor violations but also with racial inequality in exposure to those violations. Data Availability: Data are available from the sources cited in the text.

papers.title: Audit Quality and Audit Partner Ownership of Non-Audit Businesses: Evidence from China
papers.authors: Clive S. Lennox, Zanyue Qi, Xi Wu
papers.abstract: We examine whether audit partners’ ownership stakes in affiliated non-audit businesses are related to audit quality. We argue that non-audit ownership is a relatively sharp measure of auditor-client economic bonding, which can impair auditor independence. Using a unique setting in China where we observe partners’ equity stakes in both audit and non-audit businesses, we find that audit adjustments are significantly smaller when engagement partners hold larger ownership stakes in non-audit businesses. Audit adjustments are further reduced when the entire audit partnership holds greater ownership in affiliated non-audit businesses, suggesting that non-audit ownership matters at the audit firm level as well. Additional analyses suggest that these results are driven by impaired independence, rather than partner distraction or endogenous partner-client matching. Our study informs ongoing policy debates on the structuring of audit and non-audit businesses as well as the investments of non-audit entities in accounting practices. Data Availability: The authors have nondisclosure and confidentiality agreements for their use of proprietary data, which were provided to the authors for independent academic research only. Nonproprietary data are available from sources identified in the text. JEL Classifications: M41; M42; M48; M52.

papers.title: Managerial delegation within firms and peer information environment
papers.authors: Jalal Sani
papers.abstract: This paper examines whether and how the peer information environment – generated by peer firms’ disclosures and by the information intermediaries covering them – affects the CEO’s delegation of decision rights to division managers (DMs). Using an international survey dataset, I measure within-firm delegation of decision-making over capital investment, human capital investment, investment in new products, and sales. I find that CEOs delegate more to managers of divisions in country-industries with richer peer information environments. Cross-sectional tests highlight three underlying channels. Specifically, the results suggest that peer information (i) helps the CEO acquire information to reduce potential information disadvantages relative to DMs (CEO learning), (ii) mitigates CEO-DM agency frictions (agency mitigation), and (iii) provides DMs with relevant information to make better decisions (DM learning). While CEO learning reduces delegation, agency mitigation and DM learning increase it. These findings provide evidence that information about peers influences the internal organization of firms.

papers.title: Macroeconomic implications of accounting standards
papers.authors: Hyun Young Hwang, Eunhee Kim, Volker Laux

papers.title: Video-based deception detection and financial fraud
papers.authors: Binglei Duan, Danqi Hu, Hai Lu
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Based on a comprehensive visual deception score constructed from China’s mandatorily disclosed IPO roadshow videos using computer vision and machine learning, we find that visual cues embedded in these videos predict IPO financial fraud. The predictive power is incremental to financial, textual, and audio indicators. Further analyses show that these cues are well grounded in psychology research and focusing on the psychology-based deception-cue-area features improves fraud predicting performance. Furthermore, decomposing each video into five topics, we find that only the deception score of the topic on financial performance is positively associated with financial fraud. We further show that insiders of firms with higher visual deception scores are more likely to sell shares shortly after lock-up periods expire, and these firms experience significantly lower subsequent stock returns. Our study demonstrates the feasibility and potential value of using video information for fraud detection in accounting and finance.

papers.title: Judge financial holdings and case outcomes: Evidence from judge financial disclosures
papers.authors: Tuhin Harit, Sunil Parupati, Jedson Pereira Pinto, Gil Sadka

papers.title: The good idea dilemma
papers.authors: Eti Einhorn, Nisan Langberg, Tsahi Versano
papers.abstract: Once a good idea comes to mind, it is hard to avoid wondering why no one else has already taken advantage of it. Is it because the idea is not as good as it initially appears? This concern gives rise to a dilemma over whether to pursue the idea or abandon it despite its apparent promise, a dilemma we call “the good idea dilemma”. Paradoxically, the more compelling an idea appears, the more puzzling it becomes that others have not exploited it, thereby deepening the dilemma. We study this dilemma in a continuous-time game with multiple players, analyzing idea adoption dynamics and their economic implications. The dilemma yields both under-implementation of good ideas and over-implementation of bad ideas. Its adverse consequences equally affect trivial ideas that arise frequently and creative ideas that rarely do, but intensify for ideas accessible to larger audiences or with riskier outcomes, even under risk neutrality.

papers.title: Unaffiliated component auditors and audit fee models: The case of lowballing
papers.authors: Angela Pettinicchio, Peter F. Pope, Alessandra Scimeca
papers.abstract: Disclosure rules in many countries require public companies to report fees paid to the principal audit firm and its affiliates, but not to unaffiliated component auditors (UCAs). Reported fees thus depend on component auditor affiliation. We show that UCA involvement is significant in many countries. Using Italian private companies’ public filings, we find that UCA involvement is a statistically and economically significant source of bias in audit fee models. This bias is particularly relevant around principal auditor changes, when some subsidiaries temporarily retain UCAs before switching to auditors affiliated with the new principal auditor. The exclusion of fees paid to temporary UCAs explains the initial-year audit fee discount (lowballing) previously documented, which disappears once these omitted fees are accounted for. Our results suggest that lowballing reflects measurement bias rather than systematic strategic pricing. Because UCAs are common internationally and disclosure rules similarly exclude these fees, this bias extends beyond Italy.

papers.title: Diversification versus consumption motives for early exercise of employee stock options
papers.authors: Kevin J. Murphy, Marshall D. Vance

papers.title: Do bonus deferral and bonus recovery affect employee effort?
papers.authors: Mandy Cheng, Tami Dinh, Maria Lotze, Alexander Schäffer, Wolfgang Schultze
papers.abstract: We examine how bonus deferral and bonus recovery affect performance in an effort-sensitive task, where improving overall performance requires effort towards output quantity and output quality. Deferred bonuses and bonus recovery are important elements in contemporary incentive schemes designed to motivate employees to act in the best interest of the firm. We propose that bonus deferral improves performance by encouraging employees to adopt an abstract mindset that focuses on behavior for the good of the firm (“to do the right thing”) and thus to exert more effort. In contrast, bonus recovery serves an effort-directing role by indicating undesirable behavior that should be avoided. Bonus recovery activates a mindset that focuses on the monetary implications of their behavior and thus supersedes the abstract mindset of bonus deferral and its positive effects. Our experimental results show that bonus deferral leads to higher performance quantity; in contrast, bonus recovery increases performance quality, the performance domain related to bonus recovery, but at the expense of performance quantity. Furthermore, we find that bonus recovery counteracts the positive effects of bonus deferral and leads to a reduction in overall performance. Two supplemental experiments provide direct process evidence supporting the proposed theoretical mechanism. Our study contributes to the debate on effective compensation by showing that combining bonus deferral and bonus recovery may have undesirable consequences on effort provision and allocation.

papers.title: Screening and Segmenting: A Consumer Surplus Perspective
papers.authors: Dirk Bergemann, Tibor Heumann, Michael C. Wang
papers.abstract: We analyze consumer surplus when a monopolist can adjust both prices and product qualities across segments, engaging in secondand third-degree price discrimination simultaneously. We characterize the consumer-optimal segmentation and show that it has a striking structure: Consumers with the same value receive the same quality in every segment, though prices differ. Under mild conditions, any segmentation harms consumers if and only if demand is sufficiently more elastic than supply. Hence, potential benefits for consumers depend critically on demand and supply elasticities. These findings have implications for regulatory policy regarding price discrimination and market segmentation. (JEL D42, D83, K21, L12, L15)

papers.title: Truth Elicitation in a Nonstrategic Environment
papers.authors: Jacob Glazer, Ariel Rubinstein
papers.abstract: A principal decides which party deserves a prize. Only the parties observe the state that determines who is deserving. The principal gives each party a text describing the conditions under which that party deserves the prize and asks each to report the state. The parties are nonstrategic. Each activates a known cheating procedure whose outcome depends on the state and on the text. Implementation is achieved if, whenever the parties disagree, the liar is identified by the “one-way cheating principle”: The truthful party is the unique party who could not have produced his story had the rival's story been true. (JEL D82, D91)

papers.title: Taxing Top Wealth: Migration Responses and Their Aggregate Economic Implications
papers.authors: Katrine Jakobsen, Henrik Kleven, Jonas Kolsrud, Camille Landais, Mathilde Muñoz
papers.abstract: Using administrative data from Scandinavian countries, we provide evidence on international migration responses to wealth taxes and evaluate their aggregate economic implications. We find significant migration responses among the wealthy: A 1 percentage point increase in the top wealth tax rate decreases the stock of wealthy taxpayers by about 2 percent. A large fraction of the wealthy are business owners, and their businesses are negatively affected by owner out-migration.
